THE STRENGTH OF THE HILLS. My thoughts go home to that old brown house, With its low roof sloping down to the east, And its garden fragrant with roses and thyme, That blossom no longer, except in rhyme, Where the honey-bees used to feast. Marin' the west the great hills rose. , Silent and steadfast and gloomy and gray I thought they were giants, and doomed to keep Their watch, while the world shodld wake or sleep, , Till the trumpet should sound on the Judgment Day. I used to wonder of what they dreamed As they brooded there in their silent might, While March winds smote them or June rams fell, Or the snows of winter their ghostly spell ' Wrolight in the long and lonesome night. They remembered a younger world than ours, Before the trees on their top wen born, When the old brown house was itself a.tree, And waste were the fields where now they see The winds astir in the tasseled corn. And I was as young as the hills were old, And the world was warm with the breath of spring, And the roses red and the lilies white ' Budded and bloomed for my heart's delight, And the birds in my heart began to sing. But calm in the distance the great hills rose, Deaf unto raptures and dumb unto pain, s Since they knew that Joy is the mother of Grief, And remembered a butterfly's life is brief, And the sun sets only to rise again. They will brood, and dream, and be silent, as now, When the youngest children alive to-day Have grown to be women and men, crown old, And:goile from the world like a tale that is told, And even whose echo forgets to stay. —Harper's Magazine.
AN IIArL. _Bonnie Nellie standing. At the open door, Shapely shadow falling On the sanded floor. Young and fair is Nelly, Yet her eyes are sad— Nelly's absent lover
Is a sailor lad. Loving hearts will quiver, Though no tempest blow— Gallant ships have foundered When the breeze was low.l Sailor lads are fickle,
Changing like the wind; Nelly's lover far away Another love may find. Nelly, fie! thus doubting— Sailor lads are true; I can see a gallant barque Breast the billows blue.
I can hear her anchor chain'
Rattling o'er her side— I see a sailor leap ashore, Outstripping time and tide.

Nelly, woman, hasten, Put on your freshest gown, A sailor lad is coming up - The road that's from the town; He's looking for a place he loves, A little garden stile, A little homely cottage door, • A little lassie's smile. , Oh, faithful sailor laddie, _ A king might envy thee! For such a welcome home as thine I'd gladly cross the sea.

money. "What is laughter?" asked a philosopher. It is the sound you hear when your hat blows off. Owl is the name of an East Riding young man. When he goes to see his girl he has an object in view—to witSto 'Woo. . "There are good and bad points about , this coffee!" said the boarder in 'a judicial tone. "The good point is that there is no chicory in it; the bad that there is no coffee in it." Young hopeful (to his sister) :—" I say, Nell, pass me the butter." Nell (in a tone of sisterly reproof) If what, Johnny?" Johnny (goaded to desperation by the delay:—" If you can reach it." An absent-minded professor was sitting at his desk writing. one evening, when one of his children entered. " What do you want? I can't be disturbed now." "I only want to say godd-night." "Never mind now; to- morrow morning will do as well." They are talking of abandoning the system of giving: prizes to Sunday school scholars in Liverpool, since they found recently that thieboy who won a copy of Paley's "Evidences of Christinnity" had swapped it off for a meerschaum pipe and a quart of peanuts. Call t girl a chink, and she smiles; call a woman a hen, and she howls. Call a young woman a witch, and she is pleased; call an old woman a witch, and she is in- dignant. Call a girl a kitten and: she rateer likes it; call a woman a cat, and she will hatelyou. Queer Sex. FEARFUL Wm)) Fows.—A Sunday school teacher, read- ing the words "The fowls of the air" to her class, pro- ceeded to ask them, "What are the fowls of the air'?" After a pause, one little girl solved the problem,. by re- plying, "Please, miss, it's the bad smells !" • TRUE LIVING. ' Still in mutual sufferance lies The secret of true living; Love scarce is love, that never knOws The sweetness of forgiving.— Whittier. A Nashua man sang, "Don't be angry with me, darling." while he larruped his wife with a stirrup strap. But she got the better of himsand stood on his stomach, while she strewed his hyperion curls about the kitchen ' Soar, and warbled while she twined her lily fingers in his auburn locks, "Darling, you are growing bald.' Worees.—lt is deplorable when a man uses words he does not understand, but it is more so when a lady makes slips in conversation. A gentlewoman at Dundee gave a party, which was kept up to a late hour. Next morning a young gentleman called to ask for her two daughters, who, not having got up, requested their mother to say that they were indisposed. The worthy. matron, unaccustomed to learned phrase, informed the visitor that her daughters were deceased. A lady in Fife, being informed by a visitor that he was suffering from a cold, prescribed this, "Just take some hot gruel, sir, and get into bed, and you'll expire directly e She no doubt meant perspire. A gentlewoman in WigtonShire employed a house carpenter who became an architect. She complained to a neighbour that he Was much leas attentive since he had become an artichoke. An honest Scotch woman remarked to her master that she had seen all about a certain case in the Olcerated—she meant the Illustrated News. SUICIDE IN NATURE—EarIy in becember, 1879, an ap- parent epidemic of suicide attacked the herrings and sprats in Deal Roads, and they rushed ashore in such myriads at Weimer that the fishermen got tired of cart- ing them off, and they were left on the beach for all W&) cared to help. themselves. Nature seems now and then to put bounds to over-population, but if this be the easa, no herrineamines need be feared, for economical Nature would never have played into the hands of the I fishermen who are always at war with her. Such wholesale I suicides occur among other forms of animal life. In Africa regiments of ants have been seen deliberately marching into streams, where they were immediately devoured by fish. Rats have migrated' in myriad's, stopping- nowhere neither day nor night, and have been preyod upon by both large birds and beasts of prey. In the Seychelles some years ago, several hundred turtleg con- spired to die together on the island in front of the har- bour, and carried out their decision. Were they the vic- tims of hydrophobia, delirium tremens, or some other. disease? Even the gay and sprighty butterfly has been known to migrate in immense clouds from the land straight out to sea, without the remotest chance of ever reaching another shore. What could be the reason for such a suicidal act?—" The Sea: Its Stirring Story I *of Adventure, Peril, and Heroism." MaceoNase's DAUGHTEIL—In the Castle, General Haw- ley lodged his sole trophy, the brave Major Donald Mac- , donald of Teindreich, who struck the first blow in the revolt at the Speen Bridge, and who had bee& captured in the smoke at Falkirk. He was brought in bound with ropes, and kept in a dungeon till he was sent in chains to Carlisle, to be butchered with many others. He was a handsome man, and bore his sufferings with great cheerfulness. "It was principle, and a thorough con- viction of its being my duty to .God, my injured king and oppressed country," said he, "which induced nee to take up' arms under the standard of his Royal Highness 'Charles Prince of Wales, and I solemnly declare I had no bye views in drawing my sword in his just and honourable cause." His wife pleaded for his pardon at the feet of George 11. in vain, and, like the others, "he died with his last breath imploring a bles- sing on Prince Charles." Lord Arundel of Wardour re- lates the following anecdote:—" Many years after the Stuart rising, the puke of Cumberland being present at a ball at Bath. indicated as a person with whom he would like to dance, a beautiful girl, the daughter of Major M,acdonald who was executed at Carlisle, and the circumstance of whose last moments supplied Sir Walter Scott with the incidents of M'lvor's eiecution in Waverley.' The lady rose in deference to the prince, but replied in a tone which utterly discomfited his Royal Highness No, sir, I will never dance with the murderer of my father r "—Casselrs Old and New Edinburgh. „Onoteassears-Gtrastes.—Sanitary Importance of Washing at '7ome.—Ttlte c.m be done .with ease and economy and the olothes made beautitully sweet, wholesome, lily-white, and f esti as sea breezes, by using Hudson's Extract of Soap, avoid- 1r all risk of contagion with infected clothes at Laundries, or where the wastong is put out. THE TRADES UNION CONGRESS. In the Cambridge Hall, S'euthport, on Saturday, the 18tit annual Trades Union Congre.s, the best attended meeting of the kind that has been held for several years, was continued and conclu- ded. The chair was again occupied by Mr. T. R. Threll- fall, the president, A resolution was passed urging on Government the adoption of workmen assessors to assist in all stipendiary magisterial courts when workmen's ques- tions are before them. The following resolution was adop• ted :—"That. in the opinion of this congress, the time has arrived for the Government to establish a thorough system of national education, and that, in order to accomplish this object, the public elementary schools must necessarily be made free." This concluded the business of the congress, and thanks were voted to the president, vice-president, and other congress officers, and to the Mayor and Corporation 1 of Southport for the loan of the Cambridge Hall and other attentions paid to congress, and the annual meeting of the delegates for 1885 was declared to be at an end. •• The inhabitants of the ocean were linked with many singular beliefs. A shoal of porpoises or dolphins sporting in the sea proclaimed an impending gale, and the superstition yet lingers among seamen.- Plutarch says, When porpoises sport and chase one another about ships, expect then some stormy weather. Dolphins, in fair and calm weather, pursuing one another in one of their wat,erish pastimes' foreshow wind, and from that part whence they fetch their tricks; but if they play ' thus when the seas are high and tumbled, it is a sign of fair and calm weather.' It was believed that cuttle-fish swimming on the top of the water presages .a. storm. Somd fish had magical powers. In the " Magick of Birami " 1685, "a work much sought by the learned," we read of a fish called the remora checking the progress of a vessel under full sail. "If you sew a little of the bones of the fish remora in a horse's hide, and have -it with you when you take shipping, the ship will not budge in the water at hoisting sail, unless what is put there be taken away, or you go out of the ship." Spenser, in one of his poems, 1591, alludes to the super- stition :

A little fish that men call remora Which stopped her course. . . That wind nor tide could move her. Sailors believed that a barnacle broken off a ship's keel turned into a goose. In "The Maleeontent," 1604, Mar- ston says :
Like your flootob barnacle, now a block, netantly.a worm, and present'y a goose.

- - --- The idea of birds portending the'approach of weather changes has been contradicted by scientific writers. But why cannot birds have the power of recognising atmospheric changes ? Those Close observers of birdlife, who write of their migratory and other habits, record wonderful instances which almost confirm the ancient belief ; and, until good evidence is produced to the contrary, many must indulge the fancy of wild fowl being so gifted. In ancient times the weather was foretold from the flight of birds; and the credulous sailors believed they had dealings also with the storm-spirit. Seagulls cleantng their feathers was a sign of bad weather. It was deemed exceedingly un- lucky to kill one, and especially an albatross. Coleridge makes use of this particular superstition in the "Ancient Marider "
And I had done an evil thing, And it would work 'em woe For all avered I had kili'd the bird That made the breeze to blow Ah wretch! said they, the bird to slay That made the breeze to blow.

A 1! well-a-day ! What evil looks Had I from old and young! Instead of a cross, the albatross About my neck was hung. The appearance of that well-known little laird, the stormy petrel—called Mother Carey's chicken by sailors— was regarded with great disfavour. The name petrel is from the Italian Petrello, or Little Peter, so called on , account of its supposed power of walking the water like the saint of that name. The bird:figures in many tradi- tions of the sea, and always unfavourably. It foretold of stormy weather:— The petrel telleth her tale in valn, For the mariner eurseth the warning bird, Who bringeth him news of storms we heard. THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDIENT ACT. SHOCKING CASE OF ABDUCTION. At Warrington Borough Court on Monday, a man, appa- rently a little over SO years of age, named Thomas Jones, a teamsrnan, of Ellesmere, Shropshire, was charged under the new Criminal Law Ameechnent Act, 1885, on remand from Saturday, with unlawfully abducting a girl under the age of sixteen years, named Margaret Judson, also of Ellesmere. The court was cleared during the hearing of the charge, which was preferred under sub-section 1 of section 5 of the Act. This was the first case at Warrington under the row Act. The magistrates on the Bench were the Mayor (Alder- man Harrison), Alderman Burgess, and Councillor Greening. Mr. J. L. Whittle said that it was his duty to prosecute prisoner for a serious offence under the new Criminal Law Amendment Act, the section under which proceedings were taken being that dealing with the defilement of a girl be- tween the age of thirteen and sixteen years. The magis- trates had no power to deal with the case summarily, and if the facts were proved to them it would be their duty to commit the prisoner for trial at the Assizes. When the case was before the court on Saturday, the facts were stated by Mr. Hunt (chief constable) somewhat as follows. Early in August Mr. Hunt had a letter from the Shropshire police giving information that prisoner had stolen the sum of £9 10s, belonging to his wife. The commueication said that he would probably be found accompanied by a young woman of sixteen years. The letter was placed in the hands of Inspector Spinks, who had instructions to make inquiries. Another letter received on the 7th August resulted in the circumstances of the prisoner being carefully inquired into. It was found that he was living at Atherton's-quay with a Carter named Williams, who is in the employ of Mr.fleaton, contractor. Prisoner, the girl, and her parents all came from Ellesmere, and were pretty well acquainted with each other. He was found lodging with the girl at Williams' place at Atherton's-quay, where Inspector Spinks found them in bed together. The girl was formerly in service at a farmer's named Reeve, as nurse girl, and prisoner at the same time was employed there as teamsrnan. About two years ago be seduced the girl. The Mayor: She would only be fourteen then! Mr. Whittle: It is over two years ago, she told me this morning, and he has been intimate with her ever since. Six weeks ago on Saturday last he induced her to leave her father's house and come with him to Warringtoe. They travelled by rail, and at Crewe they got out, and he there purchased a ring out of the money he had stolen from his wife, saying that he would marry her. Mr. White (magistrates clerk) : She admits that she knew he was a married man. Mr. Whittle said prisoner had been twice married, and his second wife was now alive. Nothing was alleged against Williams. The Mayor: He must have been struck with the great disparity of years. Mr. Hunt: Williams did not know but what this man was married. Mr. Whittle: Mrs. Williams will tell you that prisoner came to Warrington before, and said that he was zoing to be married by license, and was going to fetch his wife. The two returned together as though married. Mr. White: With the consent of her parents she might be married. Mr. Hunt: They had no idea he had married a woman previously. Joseph Judson, father of the girl, of Hampton's Wood, Ellesmere, said that he had a small farm of his own, and kept a cow. He had known prisoner about two years. Prisoner was a teamsman with Mr. Reeve, and witness's daughter also lived there. His daughter was fifteen years old in March. 1885. Prisoner never asked permission to keep company with her, and never spoke to witness about her. His daughter left home six weeks ago last Saturday. He had no idea where she went. He knew with whom she had gone, but did not take steps to have her brought back. Mr. Whittle: Did not you think it your duty to take steps to find her, or were you content to leave it in the hands of the police? I left it in the hands of the police.—Your daughter has net been home since she went away? No.— .You have not seen her before this morning? No.—Your daughter Margaret is the person mentioned in that certificate of birth (preduced) ? Yes. ) Alderman Burgess: Had you any reason to suppose that there was anything of an improper character between your ' daughter and the prisoner before she went away? I never saw anything myself.—Had you reason to suppose there was? Yes.—Will you explain why you had reason to sup- pose so? The reason I had was because people told me he was seen with her.—Your neighbours could say they had seen him with her. Under what conditions? Not under very good conditions. In company with her.—And when he ought not to have been with her; is that what you mean ? Yes.—Or in other words that there was strong around of suspicion that there was an improper connection between them? Yes. Mr. Whittle: Did you know he was a married man? Yes. —How often has he been married? Twice.—ls his second wife alive? Yes. The Mayor: Did you ever speak to him of what you heard in reference to your daughter? No.—And you had an opportunity of seeing him every day ? No; after I knew anything about it I never saw him. I did see him once, I think. Alderman Burgess : How long ago is it since it came to your knowledge? About four months age, I think.—She ' was not then living at Reeve's farm, and this improper in- tercourse was going on while she was living in your own home ? Yes.—Did you speak to her, or did her mother I speak to her ? I spoke to her about it at different times.— What did she say? Nothing to me. The Mayor; She must have said something. Mr. Whittle: Did she deny it? No. The Mayor: Did she say it Was true? She did not say whether or no.—Surely you should have taken means to have pressed her to tell the truth about it. You seem to lihave been very indifferent. div.p: LORD-RIPON- AT-ST. HELENS. - -- B4ITQUET AND PRESENTATION OF AN

tti'Vlt! eitcliat 441 Lexpressing their...approval. h .np.n tip . . a. .. n Ilt. tration. He had recently had occasion in , another part of 'thiS great conatfy[to 'enbmjf to the[piablielomeftteinents connected with 'the measures of his 'Viceroyalty in 'lndia, rti and the policy he pursued in that country; and he would [ not, therefore, now attempt to go over again the ground which he had lately traversed. ,It would be sufficient for , him to Fay that they were right when they stated in the addreis that above all things the happiness and prosperity of the people of India was what he set before himself. (Cheers.) He could honestly say, that that was the guid- ing purpose of' his administration, and—successful or 'unsuccessful—he had honeetly laboured for it. (Applause.) He rejoiced to observe the approval they gave, in their address, to a policy having,,that great object for its aim, for he helieved that they Were right When they re- corded their opinion that it was by such policy that we might hope to deepen permanently that feeling of confi- dence in the justice of the Imperial Administration. in which alone lay the future hope 'of our safe connection with that unique dependency. (Applause.) It was very acceptable to him to find in this address, and in other cir- cumstances which he had witnessed since his return to England, not i few marks which tended to convince him that the people of England were at length awakening to the vast responsibilities which lay upon them in connection with the government of India ; that they were at length becoming alive to the magnitude and the difficulty of the duty which was imposed upon a people who held the government of 250 Millions of their fellowmen; and to see the dawn of a hope that the English people would hence- forth cleaely watch the administration of Indian affairs, and would take care that they should be constantly conduc- ted upon just and equal principles. (Applause.) These principles bad been laid down for Indian rulers long ago by representatives of the English people, and what they had to do wart to see that they were applied wisely. With them, be rejoiced to observe that they had recently received official assurance that, in the present Ameer of Afghanistan, they, bad an ally whose attachment and good faith could not be estimated, On the assuniPtion of his Viceroyalty it was his earnest endeavour to cement a firrp and sincere alliapce between the British Government and the ruler of Afghanistan. (Cheats.) He rejoiced to observe that that alliance so commenced had been confirmed and strengthened lately by the exercise of the eminent diplematic'talents of his noble friend and successor, Lord Dufferin—(oheers),— ' whose recent communication with the Atr4er they bad every reason to believe had been of a satisfactory and gratifying , character. (Hear, hear.) He sincerely booed that our friend- ship with that remarkable man would be maintained and extended ; that it would not be permitted to bscome a bur- den either to him or to us. In such an alliance we had an immense advantage if we were called upon to encotinter- difficul ties upon our north-west frontier ; and in the maintenance of a friendship with an independent Afghanistan lay in his judgment, the true key of the fron- tier policy for India. They Would share the satisfaction with whichthe country had lately learned that these diffi- culties which had arisen in respect to one portion of the north-western frontier of Afghanistan, in the neighbourhood of the Zulficar Pass, had bsen brought to a conclusion. These difficulties were in a fair way of settlement when the Government of Mr. Gladstone—(loud cheers)—retired from office and they bad been mainly brought to a conclusion upon the lines that were being proceeded upon by the Go- vernment of Mr. Gladstone' by the Administration of Lord Salisbury. (Cheers.) He had seen it said that the present arrangement was not the best that might have been made, and that a better line of frontier might have been obtained. He understood it the principle upon which Mr. Gladstone's Government went was this : That they would labour to secure for the Ameer of Afghanistan those frontier points to which he himself attached importance. (Hear, hear.) Those frontier points which he told Lord Defferin be thought he ought to'retain. • What more could any reason- able man require? (Hear, hear.) ~But there was another reason for great satisfaction that these negociations had been brought to a successful conclusion, and that was be- cause there was removed any sort of justification for hasty • or extravagant action on the part either of .the Rome Go- vernment or the Government of India. (Applause.) His lordship then referred to the prayer in the address that he might longed be spared to fill those good offices of philan- thropy with which his name was associated, and said if it pleased God to continue to him the health and strength he now enjoyed, he should always consider it his duty to em- ploy them in the advancement of those great pelitical princi- ples to which for ' the last 40 years be had been devoted. (Loud cheers.) His attachment to those principles had grown with advancing years. He heard it sometimes said that -ae men ,got' older they became more Conservative. (Laughter.) Certainly he could say that he bad not observed any such affect of old age in his case. (Applause.) And why not? Because as time bad gone on he had witnessed more and more the many beuefite which the policy of, the Liberal party had conferred upon this country. (Cheers.) Their attachment to Liberal principles was altogether independent of their temporary' success. Whatever might be the result of the next general election they would remain Liberal still —(applause)—but for his part he looked forward with no little confidence to see the result of that election terminate in a triumph of the Liberal cause. (Applause.) Their Conservative friends were interesting themselves very much just Itow in their (the Liberal) prospects; and they had die- I covered that there existed in the Liberal party many very dangerous differences and divisions of opinion. No doubt, in a party of progress and reform there always had been, and always would be, different shades of opinion. But they had held together for many yeses; they had fought many good battles—(cheers)—and they, had given their opponents many a fall. If that triumph, which he ventured to anti- cipate, ensued, individual members of the Liberal party. must he prepared to make a sacrifice of personal interests. of secondary opinions, and of class prejudices. They must all work together for the attainment of one common end. I Tney must take to heart the lessons taught by the disaster I of 1874, and the success of 1830; and he had every cond. I deuce that if they did this they would once more with un- broken ranks and hearty co-operation march forward to a signal victory of those principles of popular govern- , ment for which, through the long lapse of centuries, 1 the great party of progress, under whatever name it had ' been known, had unceasingly laboured. (Prolonged cheer- ' ing ) 1 The CHAIRMAN then said he bad to give them a toast which he was sure they would receive with as great cor- diality as they had already shown at that meeting. He proposed the health of a gentleman whom they all hoped would represent St. Helens in Parliament—Colonel Gamble. ' (Cheerti.) I The toast was enthusiastically drank, and those present sang "For he's a jolly good fellow." . Colonel CrAsintia on rising to respond, was received with loud cheers. He said he was much obliged to them for the manner in which they had wished him good health, It was a matter of considerable importance to the Liberal party end to the Conservative party in St. Helens at that moment. , He did not suppose anyone wished he should not bays good health, but be had heard hints that be should not be able to parry on the contest, and he hoped there was not much chance of any such result being arrived at. (Applause.) ' He had been asked to propose a vote which he was sure they Would receive with great acclamation, and that was a vote of thanks to the Marquis of Ripon for his attendance at tb:rt meeting and his ready response to the invitation to attend. (Applause.) He alluded to Lord Ripon's valuable services as Under Secretary for War in 1860, when he was the principle promoter of the volunteer forces—(cheers) —and, subsequently as Secretary for War, Secretary for India, and President of the Council. it was while Lord Ripon occupied the last named office that tbe great Education Act was passed which first practically provided for the education of the whole of'Our youthful population, and Which is now giving such unqualified satis- faction to the whole country. It was while bolding that 1 office that he accepted the position of chairman of the I hoyal Commission which negotiated the Treaty of Wash- ington, thus putting an end to the very bitter disputes that had arisen in consequence of the unfortunate escape of the. Alabama from our shores, and which seriously threstenecl oar friendly relations with oar cousins across the water. They were now able to rejoice that the manner in which that dispute was settled had brought about a more friendly feeling beta cep the two countties than had ever existed since the' first, declaration of the independence ot America. In spite of certain wild attacks, there could be no doubt, that 1.44 Ripon's Government in India conduced more than that of any of his predecessors to the happiness and comfort of the people of India, and of their loyalty to the English Crown ; and it was proved by all the great demonstrations of regret shown by all classes of the natives when he left India, and the expressions of adproval which followed him to this country when he left India. (Cheers.) Alderman E. Jonsson, who was received with applause, in seconding the vote of thanks, said the life of the noble lord had been one of usefulness and service to his party and his country. He had spoken not alone to the people of St. Helens but to the whole of England, and he hoped that when the speech was read all over England it would knit together the Liberal party, and that they would achieve a great rvictoryisin in Nov'ember next. (Cheers.) The I esointion was carried with enthusiastic cheers. Os g to respond, Lord RIPON was loudly cheered. He said be was very much obliged to them for the honour afternifo,w. h e havingHe would k, poe diueldadt dhtdhce rmoeeni srtme content nit lomts" ttehhsebii they bad just paid him, and he would very ill repay them a anmy:eaaerlnt etylybf afconsiderabletsrhaeytrbi saying ge Irme cva lengtherepkrrs i.osni(mit.jhpui leis simply TII19."t)11.3 had given him that day, and they would, he trusted, not think that the fewn,ess of the words indicated any want of gratitude on his part. He concluded by proposing a vote praising hhAiseydociaohned(AnsuecirdtveiirnetnestahnoefTcmh.aat ji;,?•:.rokt.) of thanks to Major Pilkington for presiding, and warmly iikseincogntodned, anthdeamppeetaiolend. resent whether We presiding at that meeting had tlt eTI . .. eh ue thoseio p I 1 1g not ensured a very successful and satisfactory meeting (Chsers.)—The resolution was passed with acclamation. The Cretatmusx, in responding, said he felt that the speech of Lord Ripon would do iocalculabhs good, not only to Liberalism in the county but in the ranks of the. Liberal party throughout the country. (Applause.) This concluded the programme, but there were load cries of "Percy," and Mr. C. M. PERCY. the Liberal candidate innthe Inca division, litiefly addrersed the meeting. .The security of indiadepsoded, he said, noon the loyalty •it I its people, and Lord Ripon in his viceroyalty of India had made for himself a name which would be revered foncen- toles to come as one-who, whilet an Englishman, dealt out even-banded justice between Indians and Englishmen. and in :de the Indian population loyal and strong in their loy- alty to the English empire. (Cheers.) The meeting then concluded. .
ADDRESS.

- • The visit of Lard Ripon to St. Helens was signalised on Tuesday by a successful banquet in the Volunteer Hall, tinder the auspices of the St. Helens Liberal Association. The primary object of his Lordship's visit to the town was to take part Wa public meetinglfOt adianaidg the claims to public sympathy and support of the Providence Hospital at Hardshair fleids. • The latter • gathering vas held in the 'Volunteer Hall, in the evening of the day named, but prior thereto his LordsWp was entertained to a banquet by- his political trial:Alt and: eiPporters, and he was also presented with a handsome illuminated address of welcome. The latter was is book form, and had been brilliantly illuminated and prepared by Mr. C. H. H. Walker, of Church-street, , Liverpool. Lord Ripon arrived at St. Helens railway station by the train due from Manchester at 12-40. He was met at St. Helens Junction by Major Richard Pilkington, J.P., chairman of the Liberal Council, and on the platform at St. Helens station was Colonel David Gamble, J.P., president of the Liberal Association. and Liberal candidate for the borough. A fairly large number of persons had assembled outside the station to witness the arrival of the noble mar- quis, but there was no demonstration of any kind. Ile • entered the carriage of Major R. Pilkington, and was driven to the Volunteer Hall. The interior of the building had been ettractiVely decorated. Oa the p/atfOrm was a choice assortment of plants and flowers from the conservatory of Major Richard •Pilkingtori, Rainfoid. =while the three tables were also similarly bedecked. Lord Ripon, Major .Pilkington, and Tether, friebds 'were ac- corded a hearty welcome. Major Pilkington, J.P., presided. On his right hand were the Marquis of Ripon, His Worship the Mayor (Alderman T. Cook), Rev. G. Lakeman, M.A. (St. Mark's), 'Rev. Lt. J. Ward (Cerigregatkinil), Mr.: C. M. Percy (Liberal labour candidate for the Ince division),. and Alderman E. Johnson. On the left of the chairman were Colonel D. Gamble, . fir. V. Crosfield, J.P. (Liberal candidate for Warrington): Dr. E. P. Twyford, J.P., Councillor C. Breaclbent (president of the Warring. ton Liberal Executive), Dr. It. A. Gaskell, J.P., Rev. Father Byrne (Peasley Cross), Captain Brunner (Wid- nes), and Lieut.-Col. W. W. Pilkington, J.P. The invited guests, the majority of whom were present, included the following :—Sir Thomas Brecklebank, Bart, the Rev. Wil- liam Flaherty (Holy Trinity), the Rev. John Barton (Rain- ' hill), the Rev. Father Ullathorne (Lowe House), the Rev. Fathers Cardwell Dignam and Egger (Holy Cross), the Rey. Fathers Walmslev, Kavanah, and Kelly (Sacred Heart), the Rev. There were also present Coungillors,J. C. earable, Belsher, McKechnie, John Forster' HatiteitOrieber, Dr. Mc- Nicoll (medical officer of health), Messrs. H. S. Hall, J.P., Li. I. THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY SEPTEMBER 19 1885 1.1:1;11 ,ro4r mA ING AT - - --• iWARGTON. , . • IMPORTANT AUDIOS'S. ON ' TEMPERANCE. THE DUTY OF ELECTORS. O Mondat evening Cardinal Manning, addressed a large • meeting in furtherance of the temperance cause in the Drill Malt, Warrington. Prior to the meeting a procession was formed in front of: the Catholic League of the Criss Hall, in Bewsey-street, and afterwards paraded the principal streets of the town headed by the bands of the League Ithtwithstanding thiannfavourable weather, a large number of people joined the procession. The Drill Hall was pro- fusely and taitefullt hung with flags, crests, and religious , pictures and emblem, and in consequence presented a cheer- ful and attractive appearance. The chair was occupied by the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), 'who was supported by a large number of gentlemen, including Cardinal Manning, the Rests. Fathers Sumner, 0.8.8., Scannell, 0.8 8., Fish. wick, 0.8.8., Brown, 0.8.8., Murphy, 0.8.8., Thompson (St. Mary% Latchford) '; the Revs. J. Yonge, S. Wilkin- son, and Appleton (Cambridge) ; ' Dr. Gorman, J P., Dr.' Fox, Dr. Spinks ; Aldermen Burgess, J.P., Holmes, J.P., Webster, J.P.; Councillors C. Broadbent, J.P., Litton, J.P., J. Greening, J.P., A. Mackie, H. Roberts, Burgess; Francomb, and Fleming; Messrs. W. Beamont, B. Henin (Liverpool), T. Wallington, F. Deacon, Voisey, R. Hind, Garnett, J.P., J. W. Hall, E. J. Guest, J.P., T. Morris IL Naylor, W. Roberts, P. Caldwell, in. Cardinal Manning, on coming on to the platform, was greeted with loud cheer- ing. ' The MAYOR, who waif received with applause, said he I did not think there was anyone in that room who had` been I. more pleased or better astisfied by the reception which bad just been accorded Cardinal Manning than he (the mayor) was. (Applause.) If he were not transgressing the canon of good taste, seeing his eminence was present, he might say that they greatly appreciated him for many reasons. (Hear, hear.) In the first place they claimed him as a distinguished countryman of their o wa—(applause)—and in the second Place he was'recognised throughout Christen- dom sea prince of the ancient church to which he belonged. (Loud spo'lause.) In addition to that his unselfish and valuable life was devoted to the spiritual interests of , mankind, and his high patriotism entitled 'him to teceive wherever he went the homage of the people. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He was proud to be there that night, and thought it a great honour to be Invited to preside at that meeting, although be was afraid he should be criticised to some extent for it. (Laughter.) There were friends of his both in that room and out of it .who thought there was some little Incongruity about it, and why ? Forsooth because he did not happen to be a total abstainer himself. If he was not a total abstainer himself, he was not so blind as not to see that a great Amount of good arose from the efforts being made in this tioun'ry by the various temperance organisations—(hear, !fear, and applause)—and he should, be thought, be wanting greatly in public spirit and patriotism if he did not appreciate those efforts the very ' great good ef which he was enabled to see almost every day. (Hear, hear.), He thorght the temcor- ance organisations of this country had very great reason in- deed to look with satisfaction upon • the successful efforts they had made to make people sober and better members of society. (Applause.) As they progressed there could be no doubt that drunkenness would practically cease to exist in this country. But of course many things would have to take place before that came to pass. They would have to provide some counter-attractions, but until those counter- attractions bad been molded be had not much faith in the efforts to turn drunkards into teetotallers. Tnere might be differences of opinion as to whether it was desirable to con- vert England into a nation of teetotallers, but there could be no difference of opinion that to convert Englishmen into a nation of temperate, prudent, thrifty people (which he believed the efforts of those societies was fast bringing about) would be ' a blessing to all of them, hot only a blessing to those who would be more directly interested, but a blessing to the whole community. (Loud applause:, Caintstan MANNING, who Was received with continued applause,,apologised for having disappointed them at the last moment last year. He was enabled to call upon his friend, Father Scannell; to be a personal witness that be was entirely unable to keep the promise he had made so long ago. They in their kindness did not find fault with him, and he hoped that he received at that time their for- giveness, and from the number he saw there that night he ,thought that forgiveness was ratified. (Loud applause.) He had also to thank the Mayor personally, and he was glad to see the Mayor of Warrington tike the chair at that meeting. (Applause.) It gave to the meeting a larger ,character, and it included Warrington at large. (Repo] ' hear.) He had another reason for being glad to see the I Mayor occoptthe chair that night, and 'that was that the Mayer of last year is the Mayor of to-day—(applause)—and he received from the Mayor of Warrington last year a letter only too, kind, as his speech had been that night. (Ap- plause.) Well, he came amongst them hardly sea stranger, , and yet he might say in an entirely new character, and he hoped ass peace maker. A friendly hand had sent to him by the post which reached him that morning certain para• graphs from a Warrington newspaper. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) He was therefore holding a brief, and he hoped that in the discharge of his office he should be able to reconcile the two parties without a verdict. (Laughter and applause.) He found that the Chief Constable of War- rington, whom he mast believe was, the highest authority who could pronounce, had given to a certain part of the Warringtou population a somewhat unfavourable character, and he (Cardinal Manning) begged to say that it was mot only Warrington that suffered. (Hear, hear.) He could tell them that London suffered in the same way, and what he read in the Warrington newspaper , was to him no astonishment and no surprise; it was nothing I new to him. But he found that in Warrington a certain number of very zealous ladies did what he would invite ladies in London to do likewise. (Hear, hear.) He only Wished that he had in his flock, and around about his flock those who would with such earnestness—laying aside for the time that sensitiveness, which, he was sure, restrained them, when the great cause of the moral life of the people around them was at stake—dare to make public representa- tion. (Applause.) He knew that was a sudden invasion before the tribunals of justice which their courts were not accustomed to, perhaps it would be better for them if they , were, and he thought, as far as he could ascertain, that the statement they made, which was founded upon the evidence lof the chief constable, was borne out by fact. (Hear, hear.) He would wish them to keep in mind that what he said about Warrington he should ,also be able to say of London, and they must not think he was bringing an impeachment, , or that anyone had brought an impeachment against the old and venerable town of Warringtoo. (Hear, hear.) It was stated that on the authority of the chief conetable that in- , toxication was spreading amongst women; it was alsa said that it was spreading among young women, and that it was I to be found among children between the age of 12 and 20. Well, he was sorry to Bay that that was n 6 new fact, he could verify it in other cities and towns in England, and hayinet received etatietics upon which the statement rested, he learned in them, and without going to any detail, he , would state very briefly what appeared to•him to be the re- ' stilt In the year 1864 there were 211 men and 39 women ' convicted for drunkenness and disorder; he leaped over 10 years and be found that in 1874 there were 720 men and 145 women, whereas 10 years before the proportion was one in five, so again after ten years it was about the same. In the year 1880 the number of men was 470. and of women 145; again in 1881, 445 men and women 138, that was one in three rough:y ; in the year 1882, 602 men and women I 172, which again, roughly, was one in three; in 1883, 42 men and 185 women, that was, roughly, one in two; and in 1884, 392 men and 114 women, which he would pet again roughly, one in two; in the present year, 417 men and 174 1 women, which once more was, roughly speaking, one in two. Well, he was afraid that statement showed that whereas the number of men had fluctuated and varied—in one year he found 700, in another 600, and then 400, 300, and 400 , again ' • the number of women reached 145, 172. 185, 174, and 174. He was afraid, therefore he must acknowledge, that those statistics bore out the statement. (Hear, bear.) Next, he found, and he believed it came from the same paper on nearly the same date, that of four young women three were of the age of 20, one of the age of 23, and one of them had been brought up and convicted the incredible number of 83 times. He mentioned that fact, and he knew the returns from the borough gaol of Liverpool would bring facto of the same kind, and facts even more terrible than that. It was also stated that there were I seen sitting around the room of a public-house some forty or fifty girls, and the reason as- signed was that a friend was going to America. He was afraid that next it would be a friend going t,) Liverpool or Manchester ; excuses were never wanting. It reminded him of the old story of the fifteen reasons for drinking, A friend, good wine, or being dry, Cr any other reason why. (Hear, bear, and laughter.) He mentioned these facts be- cause it seemed to him that the action taken by those pod and zealous ladies was not without a cause. (Applause.) He believed they (the League of the Cross) had, whether 'from the same ladies or not he could not say, an invitation to write and co-operate in the efforts that were being made especially for the reclainfing of women from the most fatal and most miserable habit, and now he could say that the League of the Cross most heartily accepted that invitation. (Loud applause.) With the Mayor' e words as to the good thine by the temperance societies all ever England he very heartily concurred, and though the League of the Cross was kin organisation of a strictly religious character, and therefore could not combine itself with any other organisa- tion whatever, they did with the largest and warmest heart hid God speed to every society and to every man wbo laboured in the same cause. (Loud applause.) He was happy to say that since he came into Warrington there was to him a most beautiful sight presented, that was the enrol- ling in the League of the Cross of some 100 or 600 of the children of the schools attached to their churches. (Ap• please.) He dwelt especially upon that, because if they wished to have sober men and women, make sober children. (Applause.) He believed then that the League of the Cross had given its first earnest of the good will with which it would co-operate with the people of Warrington in that undertaking. (Hear, hear ) The League of the Cross also intended to combine the Women who were enrolled tegether and so to employ them not only in their own homes and among their own children, but also in lending whatever lielp they could to that work of common interest in which they Were all engaged. (Applause.) He would now ask them to allow him to turn to ansther topic, and he must first protest that he was no politician. He did not in the least know what the Mayor's politics were, and further he had no

(Hear;b-ear.) If they asked what his politics were be would tell them, in a word—the -welfare of the people. (Loud applause.) He «lithely accepted the words that were spoken the other day, he did not know whether it was in that room or elsewhere,” the greatest hap- pinees of the greatest number"—(hear, bear,)--thortgli he acknowledged that was a formula which he believed came from Jeremy Bentham and he had no love of his philosophy, and it seemed to him to be a very imperfect and commercial translation of the old Latin saying that 'Saluspopuli wipe= lex,"—the welfare of the people is the supreme law. (applause.) The question of how they were to mule that end would be the drafting of a number of Acts of Perim- meat, and that he did not undertake. There would be cer- tain things he would put in his political creed, and the first would be to give houses to the people fit for human habita- tion. (Loud applause.) Secondly, and they must bear with him, and he dare say the majority there would agree with him—Christian and religious educatiot. (Hear, hear, and applause.) And lastly, and they must bear with him, for he must be sincere, local option or the popular veto upon the multiplication of public-houses. (Lend applause.) He Was not going to enter into the question of housing the people; he was not going to enter into the question of Chris- tian education, but with their leave he would enter upon the question of local option or the popular veto. (Applause.) He did so because the last time he bed the pleasure of be- ing in Warriegton he touched on it quite by the way, and he had no opportunity of fully justifying what he believed. There was a great cause pending between the drink traffic on the one hand, and the people of England on the other. He could not remember baying said a word against brewers, distillers or publicans. (Hear, hear.) He had said much against their trade, and was afraid he would never be peni- tent, but it would be unjust should he make any personal denunciations against them as individuals. For centuries the traffic had been recogeised and protected by the law of the land, aided, abetted, and encouraged by public opinion, and therefore it would be unjust to censure individuals. But he could deal unsparingly with the trade. He believed that at the present moment there was a great crisis. The first crisis was the immense accumulation of the "ewer of the drink itself, such as was never before known in the history of England. He wee himself old enough to remember the time when the number of placee in England where intoxicating drink was sold was put at 50,000, and he had lived long enough to see the time when, including the grocers' shops and provision places where drink was sold, the number had reached 200,000. Whereas these places had increased fourefold, the people of England had scarcely doubled. The capital invested in the production and sale of drink in 1830 was a proportion re the present amount of capital he was afraid to say how small, but he would give them some idea of the way in which that capital had been increasing. Twenty years ago it amounted teo 180,000, now it was between £130,000 and £140,000. It Vras, therefore, going on multiplying the production of in- toxicating drink with a rapidity and with a volume of which, be believed, these figures gave only a very insuffie dent idea. Drink, they knew, would not be pro- duced at that rate were it not consumed, and a man must be of a very credulous nature who could believe that it was consumed and that intemper- ance was not increasing. This enormous traffic was a power in the land, and he asked what could check it? If there were no demand he did not believe there would be a supply, add he did not believe there would be such demand if that knormous capital had not the power of multiplying and planting by anticipation in places where as yet there was not a single habitation built, a public-house, in anticipation of a future population that should come and build there (Hear, hear.) The people of England spent in intoxicating drink twice as much as in bread, four and a half times as much as in milk, and bread and milk were the primitive food of man. They spent in drink a sum equal to the I rent of all the farms and houses in Pngland,• and they spent, or employed in the traffic a capital equal to what I was employed in the cloth, cotton, and linen traders He believed that trade to be the greatest political power in England. They were told of the great power of the land and the landlords, but he believed that enormous capital , governed the elections down to some six years ago—go- verned the electors and the elected, and paralysed the Go- vernment. (Applause) They were at a crisis in which, if there could be found no power greater or more wide- spread than the drink traffic, he BAW nothing before them but a continual incresee of every form of the peril and danger, the havob and devastatinn that resulted from that traffic. Two millions more Englishmen, Irishmen, and Scotchmeu would now be able to say openly what they thought upon this subject. He did not think that the moat inoorrupt and the firmest body of magistrates had power to control the question. He asked that every license should have no effect until the people of the town, village, or ham- let which it aff cted should have the opportunity of saying whether they desired such public-house or nor. (Applause.) Local option simply meant that the people should have a voice in the matter, and the popular veto that they should be able to say no. I That seemed a very reasonable demand—a most constitu- tional and just one. If the welfare of the people Was the , highest law, stately on that ground it was moat jest that they should have this power of self-defence. (Hear, hear.) Who paid for all this evil ? Who paid the rates, and who paid for the insane, the diseased and the criminal? It all came back again upon the people and the sober working- , man paid for the drunken man. (Applause.) Another rea- son for local option was that it was the only adequate and effective remedy. (Hear, hear.) On what did the whole of our commonwealth and constitutional law rest but upon the unwritten law which descended to us from our Saxon an- cestors, and was the result of their free will and perfect liberty. Upon evhat did the great statute law rest but upon the Parliament elected every seven years by the vote of the , people, returning every seven years to those who elected them? (Cheers.) Who gained by the multiplication of r public-houses? The defendant at the bar, the drink traf- fic. Who suffered? The plaintiffs at the bar, the people of England. (Cheers.) Whose homes were wrecked, and whose sons and whose daughters were demoralised ? Whose homes were made uninhabitable Who were they who were sometimes spell-bound, fascinated, and drawn into the same bottomless pit but the people of England? Therefore had not they a just right to protect themselves from the in- vasion of that moral pestilence? (Applause) He put the matter before them on the ground of justice. The magis- trates all over the country were upright and excellent men, and had put before them the petitions for houses, on the renewal of licenses, and they were isolated. They wanted a power behind and all around them. The greatest misery I of the greatest number was to be found in intoxicating drink, manufactured, distriduted, and sold by the enor- mous impulse, the voluminous momentum, of the vast tut& fie. 'there was now a rising all over the country against ; this matter. He believed those who were total abstainers I might be counted by millions, and those who were temper- ate by millions. He hoped that the reasons he had given showed plainly that to give the people the power of self- protection was constitutional, just, end alone commensurate with the evil it had to control. He believed that the mean- ing of time rising against drink was because there Was an as- piration after higher and better things. There was a sense of shame that they, as a Christian people, should be so de- famed, and there WM in many hearts a longing for some- thing nobler, better, and purer, Whence did this come? i,He could speak of the working-men of London. as they r could of the working-men of Warrington, he cculd speak of women—wives, mothers, daughters, and sisters—who for the sake of those who were dear to them had given up once and for ever all taste of intoxicating drink. They aspired to a higher life in the hope of saving those dear to them who were in danger. Fathers and mothers had done the same for their children, and little children had done the same for their fathers and mothers. (Applause.) He be- lieved that this aspiration of the people after higher things was the inspiration of God. (Loud applause.) The Rev. Father BROWN, who received a cordial recep- tion, moved a vote of thanks to Cardinal Manning for hav- ing come to Warrington, and for his interesting and elo- wet address. (Applause.) Certainly they had not the pleasure of hearing his voice, but they who took an interest in that great question of the day, read for themselves in their newspapers all that he said, and they did eo with much interest. They all knew that his eminence was no light and mean worker, that he was one of the foremoet in the great battle against intemperance that was being waged in this ountry. (Applause.) In spite of ell that had been done, however, his eminence knew that there Was still !Mich work to be done and that there was need for each one of them to be zealous and earnest workers in that grand and noble cause.. (Applause.) Mr. C. BROADBENT, J.P.,who was received with applause, said he felt its great honour to he called upon to second that vote of thanks to his eminence Cardinal Manning. They were very much Indebted to him for sparing part of his valuable time and strength to come and aid the cause of temperance in Warrington. (Applause.) Its (Mr. Broad- bent) had heard many speeches on that subject, but be had I never been so much impressed as he had been on the two occasions that he had heard his eminence Cardinal Man- fling. (Hear, hear.) They did not now waste time in argu- ing that intemperance was a bad thing, and that temperance was a good thing, but, as his emin- ence had done, they gave attention to the important subject bow they might best relieve their fellow countrymen from the temptation. He was not going to introduce poli- tics, but he thought that the new eleciors would be more impatient on that subject perhaps than the old ones had been, and he thought they should see before very long- a determination to lessen the temptations now offered to their fellow countrymen, and, he was sorry to add, to their countrywomen—(hear, hear)-40r it was a painful thing to reflect upon that while drunkenness was decreasing amongst men, it was, he feared, increasing amongst women. (Hear, hear.) What was recommended by his eminence with regard to one part of his subject was already being carried out in some country districts by the land owners closing public houses in villages very much to the advent- age of the inhabitants. (Applause.) He could soy some- thing of 'another branch ef the same subject, that in their modern civilisation where they had people crowded together in great cities, the condition of life in crowded and un- healthy houses was such as induce a craving for Intoxicat- ing liquor. (Hear, hear.) He hoped they should all join when the time came in such wise measures as might be brought forward to make their towns ane he dwellings of the poor more healthy, and more favourable to life and happiness, than they were at present. (Applause.) There were, he supposed, young children in their large towns who never saw a green field, who perhaps hardly ever saw the sun shine, and under such conditions the craving for drink was almost inevitable. ported the vote of thanks, and mentioned that he had him- self seen the Arabs be Merry noon water, and in fact they never touched anything else. Yet it seemed to him that in hot countries there was a plod deal more excuse for thirst than 'in a country like England. Referring to the closing of public-houses by landowners, he said that Mr. Warburton, one Of the greatest landowners in this neighbourhood, bad four puhlic-honses in his village. There was the White Hart, the Ring o'-Bells, the Saracen's Elbad, which was his own crest, and the George and Dragon, and he (Mr. Bea- mont) received the following letter from him one morn- ing : Great Budworth's squire, the Ring-o'-Bells " unhong, Whence dhc ,rd long had through the village rung. Turned from the "White Hart ' every blackguard out, And sent the drunkards to the right about. The head of "Saracen" in Roy Land, Sir Geoffrey won it with his own ARIA hand: No less exploit may his successors boss-, Who out the head off from the alehouse post. Sill let St. George the red cross shield display. And drive the " Dragon " drunkenness away.

(Loud applause and laughter.) That was not a solitary in- stance of the hind. In the tow!) of linutsford there was a celebrated public•house, and to the great honour of the owner be abut that op. Indeed, there were great many of them died a natural death, and he should be glad to see a great many more expire under the same circumstances. (Loud applause.) The' vote of thanks, en being put, was carried by loud acclamation. '

Cardinal MANNING, in responding, was enthusiastically cheered. Mr. Broadbent, he said, said one word which brought to his memory a matter he had omitted. He bad spoken of many places in which landlords had closed public-houses on their own estates. There were at present about 1,200 parishes where no pabliedmuses existed, and there were large dis- tricts in Liverpool belonging, he believed, to Lord SeftOn, in which there were no public-houses, and into that part of Liverpool people throng and desire to obtain houses, (Hear, hear) In London S.)aftesbury Park and Queen's Park have been founded without any public-houses, and in York- shire Saltaire.was founded in like manner, but be believed that for a short time public-houses bad been admitted, and then by the good sense of the people turned out again (Ap- plause.) What they now wanted was that the poor man should have the right ard power by law which the rich man has at present by the right of property. (dear, hear, and applause) With regard to the enrolling of children he mentioned that a year ago he gave the pledge and enrolled the children ore certain cite' in the League of the Cross to the number of 150 boys and 250 girls, and he found this year that of these 150 boys 10 only bad fallen away from their pledge, and of the 250 girls not one. (Loud anplaese.) tie concluded by moving a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding.

The Rev. Father SCANNELL, who was greeted with loud applause, in seeouding this proposal, spoke ia high terms of the courteey and public spirit of the Mayor. The vote of thanks was cordially poised, and the Mayor having briefly responded, the proceedings closed.

I On Wednesday evening a great meeting, convened by members of the Salford Roman Catholic Crusade against Intemperance, was held in the Circus, Chepstow-street, Manchester, to welcome Cirdinal Manning. The Bishop of z-alford presided, and there were also present many other dignitaries of the Catholic Church. Cardinal Manning delivered an address, in which he commended the work of those preaent in the cause of temperance, and urged them not to relax the eff 'vs they were making to impriiye the condition of the Catholic community.

div.head: Dr. MACKIE : A ahLUSIVE TORY CANDIDATE.
div.p: Dr. MACKIE : A ahLUSIVE TORY CANDIDATE.

We have again had Dr. Mackie, the Conservative candidate, in our midst; and, from all accounts, the Tories in the different burghs, recognising that he is just the sort of candidate as would venture on a "forlorn hope," have made up their minds' to ac- cord him their support. There is generally a diffi- Culty in securing even a respectable politician as a candidate, unless there are some fair chances of suc- cess; and considering the circumstances of the Montrose Burghs, and its recognised position in the political world as a Radical stronghold, we cannot but feel that, however "weak and dawdling" Dr. Mackie is, he is a sufficiently respectable and" pass- able" politician to satisfy. the Conservative minor- ity in the burghs. We are aware that the Tories, in h faint-hearted, blustering sort of fashion, are pro- claiming that there is a tremendous accession to their ranks since the 1874 contest. It is only a piece of schoolboy braggadocio; and if it is in any degree a source of comfort and consolation to their weary and disquieted spirits, we will be the last to dispel the cheery phantom. We are glad to see the Tories putting a good face on the contest. We by no means deprecate their contesting the seat. It is indeed a right and good thing to have every shade of political belief freely and fully ventilated, provided the contest be conducted fairly, and no underhand means or attempts to delude and misconstrue are employed. Dr. Mackie is indeed a novel Tory can- didate. On some points he professes to be essen- tially Radical, and consequently is at variance with his political leaders; while in a great variety of points he is quite willing to accommodate himself to circumstances. While deprecating "political im- morality," he feels at liberty to misconstrue oppo- nents, and make capital out of his misconstruction. His performances on the platform have been to some extent laughable. His manners is that of a bumptious, self-satisfied individual, who tries to keep his audience in. good humour (as they are mostly hostile) by toning down his political ideas, and endeavouring to win esteem for fairness by flattering the champion of the opposite party; while in the next breath he endeavours to counter- act this by not over-scrupulous criticism. His ex- hibitions of ignorance are numerous; his efforts at misconstruction marvellous; and his attempts to pervert history audacious. If his attitude was not so transparently delusive he would deserve encour- agement for his philanthropic (!) endeavours on be- half of the fishermen. At every stage of Dr. Mackie's candidature we have abundant evidence of the de- monstrative way in which "he blows his own horn." Dr. Mackie made k discreditable attempt to mis- construe the attitude of Mr. Will in regard to the Liberal leadership Mr. Will was asked if he would - follow the leadership of Mr. Chamberlain, in the event of that gentleman becoming Premier; and Mr. Will replied in the affirmative. Dr. Mackie, in would-be indignant tones, endeavoured to make his Montrose audience believe that Mr. Will had dis- carded the leadership of Mr. Gladstone, which was as misleading as it was incorrect; but he found that his audience were not so easily deluded, and that they were too fair-minded and honest to be led away by his silly vapourings. Does Dr. Mackie think that in sneering at Mr. Chamberlain he will draw forth the plaudits of a Scotch audience? He has stated that Mr. Chamberlain is unpopular with the working classes. Is it possible he can really believe this? Accounts from all parts of the country amply falsify this assertion. His own town of Warengton furnishes sufficient evidence to controvert his state- ment. So great is Mr. Chamberlain's popularity that, to quote the Warrington Examiner, working- men, too poor to pay train-fare, have walked into Warrington from distant places in order ter secure tickets of admission' for his meeting there, this week. Dr. Mackie detests Mr. Chamberlain, as all good Tories do. The reasons for this are at once evident and apparent. The Tory party are thoroughly afraid of him; and the key to his immense popularity in the country is his manly and outspoken declara- tions for the rights and liberties of the people. Their bitter hatred and untiring denunciation of his attitude but intensify his wide and deserved popu- larity. He is next to Mr. Gladstone in the estima- tion of the people. Mr. Chamberlain is too strong for the Tories. He has brought not a few of them , to their knees, and compelled ample apologies from ,Ithe unwilling lips of many a reckless Tory speaker; but he has not altogether silenced their slanderous tongues. The amount of abuse hurled at him, and the eager desire to slander his name on the part of privileged individuals, is truly marvellous. By the force of their malignity they have vlemonstrated his strength. The Tories would not trouble him if re he we less powerful. We trust that in the fur- ther pursuance of his candidature, Dr. Mackie will prove himself possessed of wider political know- ledge, of a greater desire to deal more honestly and fairly with his political opponents, and less readi- ness to make random assertions which he cannot substantiate.—Montrose:Review.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

Mr. Forster is reported to be slightly better, but still con- fined To his bed. Dr. Walker, of Belmont-road, Liverpool, was on Tuesday kicked to death by his horse in the stable. Before proceediog to Censtentinople as Ambassador, Sir E. Thornton will, it is reported, be made a peer. Mr. Moses Hopkins of North Carolina, who has been appointed American Minister to Liberia, was born a negro slave. The Right Hon. John Bright, M.P., will address a meet- ing at Bury in support of the candidature of Sir Henry James, on the 9th of October. Mr. Talbot, M.P.. father o, the House of Commons, who is staying at Morgan Abbey, is still in ill-health, and has had to abandon his annual yachting cruise. . . -

. - An official notice has been, issued by the Post Office De. partment with respect to sixpenny telegrams. The new rate will come into force on the IA of October. By a tire which occurred on tqturday bight in the warehouse of Messrs. Joseph Pickles and Son, stuff mer- chants, Bradf.rd, damage to the extent of £20,000 wets caused.
A Sheriff's jury at Derby, on Monday, awarded to Mary Ann Collier, a schoolmistress, £350 as damages for breach of promise to marry. 1 he'defeadant was John Shawcroft, a colliery mansger.

Nevrs has been recieved in Liverpool that the iren screw steamer Hermes, which left the Mersey a month ago with a cargo for Monte Video, bee been wrecked within a few miles of that pole, and that four of the crew lost their lives.

The hundred and tenth race for the St. Leger Stakes was wori:on Wednesday, by Lord Hastings's colt Melton, the winner sf last year's Middle Park Plate and this year's ' Derby. The " field " was small, and the race one of the least interesting of the whole series.

SUSPECTED MURDER—At West WORM, near Wisbecht on Wednesday, the body of Mrs. Goodall, the wife of a market gardener, was found in a well. It bore marks of violence, and the husband, Robert Goodall, has been arrested on suspicion of causing tbe woman's death. OLDHAM STRIKE—The Executive Council of the Old- ham operatives have decided to take a ballot of the people on strike on the question of .offering to accept uncondition. ally a five per cent. reduction in place of the ten per cent. proposed by the employers. The latter are still firm M support of their original demand. _ _

At the Old Bailey, on Wednesday, Charles Smith pleaded guilty to obtaining money by false pretences, and was sen- tenced to five years' penal servitude. The prisoner had represented himself to be an agent of the National Life- boat Institution, and had thus obtained several sums of money.
DEEALCATIONS EY AN OFFICIAL ASSIGNEE.—In the Dub.

lin Bankruptcy Court, on Tnesday, Judge Miller, in allud- ing to the defalcations of Mr James, the official assignee, was greatly affected. Be said Mr. Jarms was 26 years in that position. Mr. James had obtained, without counter signatures. £5OO, and personal possession of over £4OO. The other official assignee, Mr. Deering, was above impeachment and the Treasury were making exhaustive inquiry. AN EXTRAORDINILRY BURGLARY.-A. man named Sharpe was committed for trial at Leicester, on Monday, on an ex- traordinary charge of burglary. Prisoner, in May last, broke into a rope warehouse in Leicester, took a heavy safe from its posltion, lowered it down three flights of stairs into a yard, where be stole a truck and conveyed the safe to his house, a distance of a mile, through the principal thoroughfare. After rifling the safe and its contents, valued at over £2OO, he threw the safe and truck away by the road- side.

FATAL STEAM TRAM ACCIDENT.—MqjOr General Hutch. inson opened at Bradford on Wednesday, on behalf of the Board of Trade, an inquiry into the tramway accident be- tween Bradford and -Shelf on Saturday, when a trap con- taining two men was smashed by a runaway MOROI tram engiae and both its occupants were killed. the engine, which had been undergoing repair, started off down the line, and owing to a supposed defect to the brake power was not Stopped until it reached the centre of the town, hav- ing overturned the trap on its way. The inquiry. was adjourned. STRONG LANGUAGE AT A BRITISH ASSOCIATION Marrusa. —At the British Association meeting at Aberdeen, on Tues- day, Mr. Corry read a paper advocating a State guarantee for war risks at sos. Dr. W. .A. Hunter characterised the proposals of shipowners as barefaced and impudent. Ship- owners were most dangerous to the community, and ever ready to lash the country into war. Mr. Corry retorted ti at shipowners were as respectable and independent as any in the community. The President regretted that such strong expressions had been used. Oa Wednesday the meet- ing of the British AssOciation concluded. At a meeting of the General Committee grants to the amount of £1,195 were made to various committees for carrying on their researches and observations, and the Council were instructed to con- sider whether ladies should be admitted on the com- mittees.

SHOCKING SCENI3 AT A PlRE.—About half-past two o'clock on Sunday morning a fire, resulting in injury to five persons, broke out at No. 4, Dv-win-street, Old Kent-road. London, a dwelling-house of which Mr. Thomas Summers is the occupier. The escape of the inmates, who were in the upstairs rooms, was cat off by the fiamPs, and several constables who attempted to rescue them were unable to make their way through the suffocating smoke which filled the lower portion of the premises. The terror-stricken in- mates, who were at a bedroom window appealleg for help, were then directed to jump into blankets held beneath the window. A child named Thomas Summer% nine years old, was thrown from the eecond floor, but, missing the blanket, fell on the pavement and fractured his skull. Alice Sum- mers, aged 12, and Henry Summers, aged three years, were next lowered to the ground, and Mr. Summers then descended. All three were very much hurt. A ledger named Frederick Biuters leaped out of the window on the first floor, but, missing the blanket, struck upon the iron railings and was impaled. His wife was rescued, and escaped with slight injury. All the injured persons were removed to Guy's Hospital. The fire was got under in about three-quarters of an hour, but by that time the house was nearly gutted. . _ .

The latter ad- hered to her statement that she bad not received more than a shilling when Mrs. Jarrett took the child away.—Mrs. Broughton stated that Jarrett told Mrs. Armstrong she would give the girl nethini the first month, but would buy her clothes.-The cross-examination of Mrs. Broughton by Mr. waddy was directed to show that the witness was not a credi bl• one.— n stodnd thatay whenliirs . Lisson-grove, said she was at Mrs. Brough- tco's when Mre. Jarrett came there on June 2. Mrs. Jar- rett said the witness was too big fee her as servant, and Mn. Mrs. Jarrett gave Mrs. Armstrong something—witness heard it was a shilling.—Charles Armstrong, father of the girl Eliza, said that the day his daughter went away his "rife told him she bad gone to service. He had some words with his wife, and then knocked her down. She said nothing about baying seen Mr. Booth. The witness described his jourtiey to France with the police inspector.—The ease was further adjourned till Saturday week. Ma. CHAMBERLAIN IN SCOTLAND. Mr. Chamberlain addressed a great Liberal meeting in Glasgow on Tuesday night. He repeated that be was not willing to afford any coun'enance to Mr. Pernell's proponale—propoeals which would, he said, keep apart nations wh.ch ought to be closely allied. Speaking of the quesnon of disestahlishment in Scotland, he said the subject occupied a peculiar and, be thought, a not altogether sa`istlctory position. The leaders of the Liberal party, Mr. Gladstone and Lord Hartington. had both declared their readiness, without reference to per- sonal feelings or to anything in the nature of English pre- judice. to deal with the subject as a Scottish matter, and he (Mr. Chamberlain) adopted their view. He perceived the differences which reigned in Scotland on this subject, and be advised forbearance on all sides. In view of the prob- ability that this question would not receive its final settle- ment in the next Parliament, he thouebt the Liberals, whether Churchmen or Dissenters, might agree to unite in order to secure the application of Liberal principles for the mere urgent work with which they would be confronted. The right hon. gentleman went on to explain his views on measures of social reform. On Wednesday Mr. Chamber. lain lunched at the Glasgow Liberal Club. Jo a short speech he made he remarked that in Glasgow, as in Bite mingham, they had bad to deal with the minority vote, and they had been able to divide their votes with an accuracy which said a good deal for the *ally of the voters to the Liberal organisation. Before success could be expected their Associations ought to be made thoroughly represeata. tive of the Liberals of a district. There ought to be no at.: tempt to set up a on ilification other than the profession of ~ Liberalism. A subscription to aid in carrying on theme,. , eiation's work might be welcome, but it ought not to be tn.:. despensable to membership. The amciatiou ought freslyr, to elect its council of two or three hundred, the majority a whom should determine what candidate should be dapper. ted ; and a man who would not accept as decistvi• t%', re solution of this majority Was a traitor to the Liberal canna avociatiOn in the word, 6. The right hon. gentle.. 81 nNadne oughtveraddressed e ntro hb ee ' the l' peopleer:e:: mine.Y t Th by one or two villages through which he passed in the course of the afternoon. He said he was glad to state that Mr. Gladstone as once more restored to health, and would he able again to lead the Liberal party .0 victory. in the coming el. ction.—On Thureay, Mr. Chamberlain, in journeying from Balluchney to Bridge of Allan, had a most entouslastic reception on reaching the railway station at Callender, the hem@ being taken- from the carriage and the vehicle drawn along the street be a crowd of the right hon. gentiemanta admirers. In a•lirief speech be dwelt on the importance of a universal extension ,of local ,government, and upon the necessity for the Liberals of Scotlandmaking their power felt. Mr. Chit IbLdUhCd also a most cordial welcome at Bridge of Allan.
