Mr. GLADSTONE never ,p 15 anYthing, and he is always learning. t,hTe°nScious, painfully conscious, of the qle t;'4,t the Liberals have not accomplished Which they set themselves in 1880 ; ka37 oreseeing that the work of the State (~4,111 be again hindered, and from the it! efause, he points to the necessity nl of the procedure of Parliament th„<,-° Use finding work for the machine, rnachine itself cannot work. Then ISl)° be, what Tories as well as Liberals %)vet t p, necessary, a reform of Local Illak,.."ltent involving changes of great f.,"111 -11,4'cle—not the least important of which those relating to the Licensing t},-°n• Land Law reform comes next, -45gerT.t sweeping away of entail and pri- -iture, the adjustment of taxation and

"the extension in the numbers of those directly interested in the possession of land and its produce." Mr. GLADSTONE points out the need of completing the Reform Acts by improving and simplifying regis- tration ; but we take it that there will be little or no difficulty about this, seeing that the Tories as well as the Liberals are interested in getting rid of existing anomalies. Mr. GLADSTONE points out the need of reform of the House of Lords—a subject which many politicians seem of late to have lost sight of; but he hopes—and this is a bit of genuine Conservatism—" that in the reconstruction of the House of Peers, when it arrives, a reasonable share of power may be allowed under wise conditions to the principle of birth." Mr. GLADSTONE treats the problems of the Disestablishment of the Church and of Free Education as scarcely ready for solution. This, we confess, is somewhat dis- appointing, but at the same time we must frankly own that they have not as yet been brought as prominently before the electors as the proposals which he stamps with his approval. There is this to be said about the new Programme, that it will not divide the Liberal party, and that it will provide as much work for the next Liberal Parliament as it will be possible for it to accomplish.

MR. CHAIABERLAIN roused the enthusiasm of his Glasgow audience by the vigorous speech on Tuesday, in which he dealt with the question of the Disestablishment of the Church, and expounded his scheme for deal- ing with the land in such a way as to improve the condition not only of the agricultural labourer, but the poorest of the poor in our large towns. It is remarkable what progress the question of F ee Education has made since Mr. CHAMBERLAIN spoke at length on the subject at Warrington. Liberal candi- dates are everywhere showing themselves favourable to the proposal, providing it can be carried out without interfering with de- nominational schools. Even the Marquis of LORNE, who is usually regarded as a Whig politician, has this week declared himself in favour Of Free Education. On Wednes- day Mr. CHAMBERLAIN paid a visit to a Glasgow Liberal Club, and made a short but pertinent speech on the queston of organinsation. " Their whole success," he said, "as Liberal Associations was involved in the spirit of loyalty. Before it could be expected, the as- sociations ought to be made most thoroughly representative of the Liberals of a district. There ought to be no attempt to set up a qualification other than the profes- sion of Liberalism. A subscription from a ' member to carry on the association's wolk might be welcome, but it ought not to be in- dispensable to membership." It is to be hoped these weighty words will be well con- Fidered throughout the country. It is natural that those who find the ways and means should attach importance to the fact ; but , should never be forgotten that when it comes to a question of voting Jack is as good as his master. There are may men, too, of the operative class who cannot afford to give any- thing beyond their services, and this cla.3 should be especially welcomed. There will be plenty of volunteer work for them to do at the General Election. All round, Mr. CHAM BERLAIN shows himself to be far-seeing and sympathetic. It is not to be wondered at that he is growing in popularity.

LOCAL NEWS.

„ NEW WEseETAN Cgarna, FIYE CROSSES.-0a Sunday special sermons were preached in the above chapel by the Rev. George Lupton Alias, formerly a minister in the Frodsham circuit. The services were attended by large congregations, and the collections in aid of ths building fund amounted to upwards of £25. THE VALUE OF PROPERTY IN WIDNES.—MeeStS. J. B. and B. Leach, auctioneers, this week offered for sale at the Central Hotel, Widnes, several lots of house property, situate in Carlisle, Lacey, Walmsley, and William streets, in Widnes and Appleton. The reserve was not reached in any case, and the property was withdrawn. LIQUIEST AT HALZWOOD.—On Saturday last, Mr. W. T. Husband held an inquest at the Eagle and Child, Mile- wood, upon the body of Joseph Birch, Si, a collier from Wigan, who was found lying dead in a lane of the village on the previous Thursday. Evidence bearing out the ac- count was given, and an open verdict was recorded by the jury. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT HALTON.—The annual harvest festival at Halton Parish Church took place on Thursday evening, when a large congregation assernialed to take part in the beautiful and interesting service. The Rev. Canon Greenan, of Grappenhall, rural dean, preached from Mat- thew %Hi., 30th verse—” Let both grow together until the harvest." Special hymns were sung by the choir, Mr. Jeacock presiding at the organ. The sacred edifice was bright with a profusion of fruit, flowers, and canals, which had been arranged in a very tasteful and artistic fashion in all parts of the building. As usual, Lady Brooke decorated the chancel, the adornment of the other portion having been done by many other memhers of the congregation. ,1 ACCIDENTS AT WlDNES.—Michael Maloney, a labourer, living at 7 Caroline-street, was on Saturday employed at a boiler at Messrs. Muspratt's works when the steam forced the top off. He was struck od the side of the face and severely wounded, besides being seriously scalded about the arms, face, and body by the eecaping steam.—Thomae Cran, a labourer, was sitting down on the ground be- tween the railway metals and the wall at the British Alkali works, when the step of a passing locomotive struck him on the head and dragged him a distance of nearly twenty yards. He was picked up in an insensible condition and carried home. He is suffering from a severe scalp wound, concussion of the brain, and general shock to the system. He is under the care of Dr. McCambridge.— William Moss, an innkeeper in Midwood-street, was knocked down by a horse and trap in Gerrard-street, Simms- Cross. He was badly shaken and had lobe carried home. HARVEST THANIEsGIviieGaT WIDNEs.-The annual harvest thanksgiving services of the Primitive Methodists of Widnes took place in Hutchinson-street Chapel o Sunday. The edifice was decorated with a profusion of flower, fruit, and vegetables, which had been generously given by friends. The donors were the following :—Mrs. Wright, Widnes Messrs.'Navlor, Halebank ; Abbott, Halebank ; Peter Long- ton, Ditton - Joseph Longton, Ditton ; Israel Taylor, Dit- ton ; Josepla Taylor, Bitten; Joseph Wilcock, Dittoo ; Richard Hedgeock. Huyton ; Ed. Percy, Widnes ; Ed. Clare, Farnworth ; W. Thomas, Widnes ; C. Hemmingway, Widnes; J. Barker, Bold ; J. Crampton, Warrington ; Hig- ginson, Widnes; S. Whitfield, Widnes ; Owen, Warrington; Leddon, St. Helens ; C. Clifton Widnes ; H. Leer Widnes ; Bradehaw, Farnworth ; Whalley, Bold; Prescott, Farnworth ; T. Aidley, Widnes ; H. Wiliams. Widnes; Hall, Kingsley ; and T. Carr, Widnes. The services were well attended, and Mr. James Peters, of Buckley, two appropriate sermons. The choir renderedm preached cshpeed- cially selected for the occasion. On Monday evening %fruit banquet was held under the presidency of Mr. F. H. Pank- hurst, of Victoria-road. During the evening the Chairman delivered, an address, and said it was always a great pleasure and privilege to him to hold out the hand of fellowship to any denomination. He had been in Widnes about 20 years, and during that time he had been closely identified with the cause of Christ, and he was always ready to do what little he could for the furtherance of Christianity. Addresses were also delivered by the Rey. .1. Calvert, and Messrs. J. Shuttlewortb, J. Swales, J. Whit- ley. Mr. Calvert said there was a debt on the chapel of £360, and they wanted to reduce it from that amount to £2OO this year. He remarked with pleasure upon the har- mony that existed amongst the congregation. In the course of the evening the choir sang several anthems, and fruit was distributed.

MR. BEN DAVIES, late of Carl Resa's Opera Company, is announced to sing in the Drill Hall, Widnes, on Monday, the 28th inst. HARTLAND WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.—The Rev. R. Bardon preached the anniversary sermons on Sunday last to good congregations. SINGING CLASS eer Ruereorter.—lt will be seen from our announcement columns that Mr. Ho!ford is again commenc- ing his singing ekes in Ellesmere-street school. Tne class has achieved much success in former years. ACCIDENT AT WIDNES SOAP WORKS.—A man named Ingram had two of his fingers of his left hand taken off at a circular saw at Messrs. Gossage and Co.'s works on Tues- day. He was attended by Mr. Richards, assistant to Dr. McDonnell. THE DEATH RATE AT RUNCORN.—During the 17 days of the present month only five deaths had occurred in Run- corn, equal to a mortality of 8 per cent per 1,000 per an- num. The death rate for the month will probably be the lowest ever recorded in Runcorn. ACCIDENT WITH A BOTTLE AT WIDNES.—Mr. Joseph Robinson, a prorniment member of Lacey-street Wesleyan Chapel, was out at supper on Tuesday evening. He took hold of a bottle of mineral water for the purpose of un- corking it, when the bottle burst in his hands. The broken glass almost severed the thumb of the left hand, and cut the ends off nearly every finger. He will probably be crippled for some months. THEFT OF WATCH AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Wednesday, Ellis Johnstone, a middle aged man, was charged with stealing from the dwelling-house 53, Cbolmondeley-street, a silver watch, worth £3, the property of John Shuttleworth. On the evening of the Bth inst Mrs. Shuttleworth let the house for ten minutes. On her return the watch was not ti be found. Subsequently the prisoner pawned it for 123 61 to Mr. Neild, Simm's Cross, and he was apprehended by P.C. Evans.--Ile was commit- ted to the quarter sessions for trial. CURIOUS ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—Mr. L. Landenberg, glazier and picture frame dealer, Waterloo-road, Widnes, was carrying two large pictures along Widnes-road, near St. Paul's Church, when a gust of wind caused them to knock against his legs. The glass was :smashed, and a large piece entered the calf of his leg, severing one of the arteries. Blood streamed forth in considerable volumes, but Inspector Wood was near the spot, and bound a hand- kerchief round the wound. He then helped Lindenberg to Dr. O'Keeffe's surgery, where his injuries were further attended to. FATAL ACCIDENT AT HALEWOOD BREWERY.—Au inquest was held at the Coroner's Court, Liverpool, on Wednesday. with reference to the cii cumstances attending the death of James Appleton, 50 years of age, whe lived at Halewood. The deceased was employed at the Halewood Brewery Company's brewery at Halewood, and on Friday last, as he was going down some steps at the brewery, the iron on his clog caught in one of the steps and he fell to the bottom, injuring his hip. He was attended at home until Monday, when he was taken to the Royal Infirmary, where his in- juries terminated fatally the next day. Verdict," Acciden- tal death." WIDNES SAMARITAN LODGE held its weekly session on Monday last. Brother Machin, W.C.T, presided. After the usual routine business had been gone through the Lily Juvenile Temple paid a fraternal visit, and with much credit entertained the lodge. Recitations were given by Sisters Lamb, Hobson, Roughsedge, Galilee, Blease, K. Blease, Atherton, Frith, Buckley, Howson, E. Atherton, and Brothers Blease, Buckley, and F. Buckley. Songs were also given by Brothers and Sisters Smith, Bearding, Atherton, GuYliDavies, Manley, and Ince. On the propo- sition of Brother Machin, seconded by Brother G. Widders, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the visiting lodge, and the respected superintendent of the Temple, Brother Webb, responded. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.—Yesterday Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Railway Hotel, Runcorn, upon the body of Elizabeth Needham, aged 15 months, daughter of Isaac Needham, a hind on board the narrow boat Hotspur, belonging to Mr. H. Finch, of Marple. Needham and his wife and family, consisting of three chil- dren, live on board the boat. Early on Thursday morning he observed the deceased to be foaming at the mouth. At seven o'clock the father took the child to Dr. MacDougall's surgery, and Mr. Ansbro, the assistant, administered an emetic, and instructed the father to apply mustard plasters to the stomach, and besides giving the child some medicine, he prescribed. Later, the father took the child to Dr. Robin- son, who approved of the treatment, and ordered it to be continued. The child was then in a state of collapse, and died about an hour subsequently. In accordance with an order from the coroner Dr. Robinson had made a post- mortem examination, and be informed the jury that the cause of death was fatty disease of the kidneys, resulting in congestion of the brain.—A verdict in accordance with the med ical ettldenett waS rettittied. UNJUST WEIGHTS AND SCALES AT RUNCORN.—At RUH. corn Police Court on Monday, Joseph Burnand, a hawker, pleaded guilty to being in possession of a 2lb weight five drachms, and two llb weights each three drachms light. Superintendent Leah said they were very old weights.— The prisoner, who stated be had lost his own weights and borrowed those in question at Chester was fined 10s and costs. --Martin Loughlin, greengrocer, Mersey-street, was brought up on a similar charge. Superintendent Leah had found a 71b weight 6 drachms, and a llb weight 91 drachms light.—The defendant said he knew nothing about the busi- ness. The big weight was used for keeping the door open. He was fined 53 and costs.--Samuel Ward, grocer, Ten- nant-street, was charged with having unjust scales. Su- perintendent Leah said on the sth September he found two scales at the defendant's shop which were out of balance against the purchaser. Each scale had a piece of lead which could be removed at will attached. One scale when the lead was removed was an ounce and a half against the 1 purchaser.—The defendant said he had kept a shop for 40 I years and this was the first information ever laid against him. He was fined ss, end costs 9s 6d. A BOY DROWNED AT WIDNES.—Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Thursday, held an iuquest at the Com- mercial Hotel, kept by Mark Wright, upon the body of Edward Roberts, sine years of age, who was drowned in the St. Helens canal on Tuesday. Evidence was given by Mary Roberts, wife of Thomas Roberts, engineer, of Milli Brow Old Marsh ; Elizabeth Ellen Fox, dress,naker, Dock Cottages; and John Hartles, flatman, 51, Gerrard-street. It appeared that a Birkenhead Hatman, who is unknown, saw ; the boy in the'water with his bands up. He drew Rattles I attention to the boy, and stated that he could not swim. I Hartles, who was on the opposite side of the canal, obtained a boat hook, as did several other persons, and in a few minutes the body was recovered. Mr. Richards, assistant to Dr. McDonnell, was quickly on the spot, and used every possible means to restore animation, but without effect.—A discussion took place amongst the jurymen as to the dangerous nature of the place. It was stated thalt boys had to go backwards and forwards to school along the bank of the "canal, and yet it was not a public road.—The ' Deputy Coroner said the property owners ought to see to I it. It was for them to get a right of way, to maintain it, and keep it clear. It the railway company owned the houses they were responsible, and bound to provide a pro- , per road.—A juryman: The house the boylbad lived in be- I longed to the Limestone company.—The Deputy Coroner said it was sad these accidents should occur continually, I and there was no doubt something should be done.—A vet- ' diet of accidental death was recorded. BOWLING MATCH AT RUNCORN.—CAPTAIN It. WRIGHT'S TEAM V. CAPTAIN S. YanwOon's TE&M.—The match be- tween the teams of the Runcorn Bowling Club, chosen by the two captains above named, and which was brought off , on Tuesday afternoon on the green of Mr. George Hayes, I Bridge Hotel, resulted in favour of Mr. Wright's team by 13 points The game was 15 up, and from the start to the finish great interest prevailed, the bowling being some of the finest witnessed on the green during the season, particu- larly that between the two captains. The day was fine and the green in splendid condition. The following are the scores : Captain Wright's team. Captain B. Yarwood's team. ldr 13 iso Shaw Mr W Brlmelow Mr J Lewis Mr W Anderton Mr R Wright l5 Mr S Yarwood Mr B Johnson Mr J Abrams l2 Mr Zolan Ravenscraft 15 Mr Wm Jones MrJ Jones ll Mr Rd Jones l5 Mr J Withington Mr Jos Dutton Mr E Turkey

, Total 155 Total t42 At the close of the match the members adjourned to the large tent, where a knife and fork tea was provided by Mr Hayes. On the removal of the cloth Mr. S. Yarvrood was appointed to the chair. Mr. R. Wright occupying the ViCe• chair. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were given and honoured with enthusiasm. The members passed a very pleasant evtning together. THB PAYMENT OP JURYMEN AT WIDNES.—At AR inquest held at the Commercial Hotel, on Thursday, before Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, Mr. Fitzpatrick, of Vic- toria-road, moved that in future jurymen should be paid for their services, as it would tend to make them more care- ful in sifting the details of cases, and also make them more attentive to their duties.—The Deputy Coroner said he had never had this matter mentioned before him without ex- pressing a desire that the law should be altered so that jury- men might be paid. They were paid in some places, and he could not see why a man who gave his time in Widnes should not also be paid. At Garton jurymen were paid half a crown. They had a voluntary rate for the purpose. The rate was printed in the list sent oat by the Local Board at the foot of the different rates and as a rule it was paid without a demur. Of course they could not compel anyone to pay. In the Whines locality the manufacturers would have to pay the bulk of mit a rate, and it was no doubt mostly owing to the manufacturers that these accidents occur. He had no doubt they would not demur to the payment of the voluntary rate, and then the jury could be paid. In some localities they adopted a method that was not straight and above board, and that was to give the collector of taxes a nominal increase on the condition that he gave a certain amount out of the rate for the payment of jurymen. He should recommend a voluntary rate.—A juryman asked bow often a man was liable to be sunuponed on a jury.—The Deputy Coroner said that was a question for the police.— Another juryman remarked that it was a pity the police did not come down upon the managers of works at times a., they could get away without being mach missed. Th subject then dropped. Public Analysts have submitted CADBURY'S Coooa. to close tests. and the result has always proved its great value as a sus taming and nourishing beverage. Bewaref:of

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 19, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 19, 1885.

, DEPRAVITY AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. J. Brock, at Widnes , Police Court, on Monday, Thomas Johnson, a stone mason from Birkenhead, was committed to the quarter sessions on a charge of committing an unnatural offence on the farm of Mr. James Kelsall, Lower House, Appleton, on Friday. A POLICEMAN ASSAULTED BY A WOMAN.—Mary Grady appeared at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of assaulting P.C. Tweedale. On Satur- day night the constable had a man in custody, when the defendant, who keeps a shop in Bean-street, seized hold of him, and after a struggle succeeded in getting the prisoner into her shoo. A. fine of 2s 61 and costs was imposed. RUNCORN POLICE COURT—Yesterday, before Mr. J. Brundrit, at Runcorn Police Court, Bridget Brown of Fred- sham, who was only released from Knutsford Gaol on Wed- nesday after serving a month for larceny, was charged with begging in Bridge-street on Thursday. P.C. Breeze proved the case. On promising to at once go home to her husband, the was discharged.—Joseph Reyes was sent to gaol for seven days in default of paying a fine of 5s and costs, for being drunk at midnight on Thursday. ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN POLICEMAN.—MichaeI Nichol- son, a young man, was brought before Messrs. Brundrit and Handley, at Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, charged with assaulting P.C. Harper.—On Friday night, at eleven o'clock, the officer dispersed a crowd of persons who were watching a fight in Fryer-street. The prisoner then came up, seized the officer by the throat, struck him in the face, and said, " Now, you clear off." A straggle ensued, and the constable was kicked and bitten by the prisoner. His finger was severely bitten.—ln default of paying £2 Sc 6d, the prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. ROBBBRI FROM RUNCORN NATIONAL SCHOOL.—At Run- corn Police Court, on Saturday, Eliza Whitfield. a married woman living in Lowers-court, Cooper-street, was brought up on remand charged with having on the 7th inst. stolen a shawl, worth Sc, the property of Eleanor Parr, wife of Jos. Parr, Beatiock-street.—Mrs. Parr's daughter took the shawl to the National School, and placed it in the cloak-room. When about to go home at noon she discovered that the shawl bad been stolen, and on Thursday P.S. Neild, in con- sequence of inquiries he bad made, entered the prisoner's house, and found the missing article behind the door.—The prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was fined 20s. A WIDNES FRIED FISII DEALER IN TROUBLE.—On Wed- nesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Alfred Ward, refreshment house keeper, Waterloo-road, was summoned for keeping his place open after hours without a license.—Sergeant Robinson said the defendaat sold fried Ash and chipped potatoes. At half-past eleven on the night of the sth inst. he was selling to about a dozen persons through a hole in the door caused through the removal of a panel.—Superin- tendent Barker said if these places were not closed at the proper time there was no getting the streets clear.—The defendant said the practise he was summoned for was car- ried on in Manchester and Oldham.—Mr. Gibbon said it was against the law, and a fine of 40s and costs was im- posed. THEFT BY A DOMESTIC SERVANT AT HALEMINE. Annie Hostler, 18 years of age, was brought before Mr. T. S. Timmis, at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, charged with stealing a gold pin worth about £3, and a pair of drawers, a pinafore, and several small shirts, two bibles, and other articles, the property of Mrs Elizabeth Duxbury, wife of John Duxbury, who resides at Woodside Villa, Hale- bank. 'The prisoner had been employed as domestic ser- vant for the past month, and during that time many articles had been mimed, but the prisoner stoutly denied all know- ledge of them. On Wednesday Mrs Duabury searched the prisoner's box in her presence, and bend all the articles . enumerated with the exception of the gold pin, which has not yet been recovered. On the application of Inspector Wood the prisoner was remanded until Wednesday next. SAVAGE ASSAULT ON A WOMAN BY A BOY AT. WIDNES.— John McCabe (14) and Margaret McCabe (15), brother and sister, were charged at Widnes Petty Sessions, OR Wednes- day, with assaulting Elizabeth Esmond, a married woman, , living in Midwood-street. Mary Ann Walsh was also charged With threatening her. Mr. J. W. Knowles prose- , anted. On Saturday afternoon last the prisoners, who had some spleen against Mrs. Esmond, set fire to a bundle of straw as an effigy, and threw the burning mass into the lobby of her hones. She was going to the police station to acquaint the authorities of the matter when John McCabo struck her on the side of the bead, knocked her down, and , kicked her, while Margaret palled her hair and struck her on the face, causing a black eye. Walsh uttered violent threats against her.—Mrs. Esmond raid her life was misera- ble through the defendants and some of their friends, and after hearing the evidence the Bench fined John and Mar- 1 garet 108 and costs each, and ordered Walsh to be bound , over to keep the peace, herself in £lO and two sureties In £s.—Mr. Gibbon said John, who made his fourth appearance and had served 21 days for an assault in 1884, deserved a downright good flogging, and he was sorry the law would not permit him. ADULTERATED FOOD AND DRINK AT Rusicoale—Daniel Basnett, grocer, Weston, appeared before the Runcorn ; magistrates to answer a charge of selling adulterated ginger. —On the 14th ult. Superintendent Leah purchased half a , pound of ground ginger, which the public analyst certified contained 10 per cent, of chalk.—Mr. Burton, who repre- sented the defendant, said Mr. Basnett had been in business 27 years, and although samples had been frequently taken , this was the first case against hitn.—A fine of 103 and costs was inflicted.—On the evidence of Superintendent Leah Phoebe Bartow, landlady of the Royal Oak, Weston Point, was ordered to pay £l6B ld for selling a pint of rum which contained 29 per cent, of water, or four per cent, more that is allowed by Act of Parliament.--Joseph Oates, of the Fleetwood Arms, Church-street, was charged with refusing to sell a quantity of whiskey to superintendent Leah.— Acting to instructions, Police-clerk Wallace entered the de- fendant's house and ordered a glass of whiskey. Superin- tendent Leah then appeared upon the scene, and demanded a pint of whiskey from the same keg. Mrs. Oates refused, ' because she said it was "dirty," and the superintendent de- clined to take it from the stock in the cellar, or from a quart bottle on the shelf.—The defendant stated the keg was empty, and as it was an awkward job for a woman to fill it, Mrs. Oates used the quart bottle.—The Bench imposed a 1 fine of £2 and costs.

LORD DERBY AND THE FAIR TRIDERS.--Lord Derby, acknowledging the receipt of a Free Trade pamphlet, says he agrees in the conclusions and in the arguments of the writer, only doubting whether the so-called Fair Trade policy is likely to find general support from the Conservative party at the next election. He cannot bring himself to treat it seriously, especially as most of the Fair Traders repudiate taxes on food, the only kind of protection which the agricultural classes care about, where they care abont any. CARDINAL MANNING.—As the visit to Warrington of Cardinal Manning has led to some inquiry as to the age of his Eminence, we may state, on the authority of "Men of the Time" that he is over 77. He was born at Totteridge, Hertfordshire, on July 15, 1808, the son of William Manning, Esq., M.P., merchant, of London. He joined the Roman Catholic Church in 1851, and was created a cardinal on March 15th, 1875. We may add that Mr. Beamont, who so ably supported the vote of thanks, is older than the Cardinal by eleven years. It is to be hoped both old men will remain on the scene for many years longer to be of service to their kind. THE MARQUIS OF LORNE AND THE RADICAL Pno- GRAMASE.—The Marquis of Lorne, the Liberal can- didate for the new borough of Hampstead, issued I his address to the electors on Saturday. He ex- presses himself in favour of a reform of the House lof Lords by an infusion of elected members; he is I also in favour of free elementary education, dis- establishment of the Church of Scotland, and the compulsory registration of title to land, with a view to cheapening the transfer of land, remarking that the taxation of sales of large amounts of land, leav- ing free the sale of smaller lots, might affect some ' good. As to Ireland, he is in favour of an extension of local self-government. PARLIAMENTARY CANDIDATES AND DISESTAR- LISHMENT.—The Record publishes a return of the opinions of candidates for the new Parliament as to IDisestablishment. There are 1,061 candidates see...- , ing election in England, Scotland, and Wales. Of the Liberal candidates there are 403 in favour of Disestablishment and only 37 against it, while 33 refuse to give any information on the subject. Of the remaining 106 the Record has been unable to obtain any information. There are 482 Conserva- tives before the constituencies, and they to a man are against Disestablishment. Some of the Liberals are in favour of Disestablishment in Wales only and some in Scotland only, whilst others go in for it in Scotland and Wales only. These may be classified thus :—Three in Wales only, fourteen in Scotland only, and ten in Scotland and Wales only. A similar classification may be made of the Liberals who are opposed to Disestablishment; eleven oppose it in England only, and three in England and Wales only. TILE LIBERATION SOCIETY. —At the monthly meeting of the Manchester and District Committee of the Liberation Society, held at the offices, 4, St. James's-square, Manchester, on Monday, September 1885, Mr. Robert Afileck ix the chair, it was moved by Councillor J. H. Crosfield, seconded by Mr. Alderman George Booth, J.P., supported by Mr. Arthur E. Reyner, J.P., and unanimously resolved: —" The committe& have attentively read the dec- larations of various Liberal statesmen as to ques- tions which should be selected out of the crowd waiting to be dealt with by the first Parliament representing the householders of Great Britain and Ireland. They find, however, that as a political i fact, there s a greater agreement of opinion amongst Liberal candidates on Disestablishment and Disendowment than on almost any other topic before the constituencies. They are strongly of opinion that nothing is more likely to check en- thusiasm in the principles of Liberalism, and to diminish confidence in the ability of their leaders to discern the signs of the times, than a refusal to include in their programme a question which at all Liberal gatherings calls forth the warmest response, and which is a measure of. justice and reform that
has been demanded by the blilk of the Liberal party for a generation past.

ICOLONEL MCCORQUODALE'S LIBERALITY. COL McCorquodale, the popular Liberal candidate for the Newton Division, has forwarded a cheque for X-30 towards the election expenses of Mr. C. M. Percy, the Liberal candidate for the Ince Division. ACCIDENT TO SIR PHILIP EGERTON, BART.—While the rejoicings were proceeding at Calton Hall, Cheshire, in honour of the coming of age of Mr. P. 11. D. Egerton, heir to the estates, Sir Philip Grey Egerton stumbled and fell heavily. It was at first thought the leg was fractured, but the ankle only was put out. According to medical advice a month must elapse before Sir Philip will regain the use of his leg. MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND THE PUBLICANS.—Mr. Chamberlain has given an answer to a series of test questions that the Birmingham and District Licensed Victuallers' Association proposed to put to Parliamentary, candidates which will not please "the trade." Ile was invited to give an explicit answer to a series of questions on local option, Sun- day closing, grocers' licenses, clubs, and other mat- ters. His reply is that he does not admit the right of any external organisations to interfere between him and those whom he hopes to represent in the next Parliament, and that he believes the arrogant attempt to extort pledges in the interests of a par- ticular trade will be resented by the electors and by every candidate who has the slightest self-re- spect. A BIG WINDFALL REPORTED.—Some time since a statement was circulated by the Liverpool daily , press that a warehouseman named Robert Tarbuck, in the employ of Messrs. C. and G. Williams, cotton- brokers, Liverpool, was about, to succeed to a for- tune of no less than £BO,OOO which wasin Chancery. The money had been acquired from coal mining pro- perty in the vicinity of St. Helens. It now appears that a Widnes man claims a right to participate in the wealth. Mr. Peter Ince, baker and confectioner, Ann-street West, married a member of the family that laid the foundation of the fortune as did also Tarbuck, and the two men have agreed op co-oper- ate in their endeavours to obtain the money. Several interviews have been held between them, and they are confident of being able to sustain their claim.

MR. IIUGIT MASON, M.P., ox FILER EDUCATION. On Monday night Mr. Hugh Mason, M.P., presided at the opening of the session of the Albion Literary So- ciety, Ashton-under-Lyne. He said the Government grant for education now reached .C 3,500,000 a year, and the School Board rates were about .£2,500,000, or together .£6,000,000 taken from the rates. In addition to that, the children's pence raised every year .£1,700,000, and voluntary contributions .£700,000, making £2,400,000, or a gross total of .£8,400,000 for educational purposes. Those who educated their own children were taxed for educa- ting other people's children, and in some cases the tax fell very heavily indeed upon people of limited fixed incomes, and they did not derive any direct benefit themselves for the education of their own families. Five-sixths of the expenses of educating poor children was already provided for by the taxes, and they might just as well give the other one- sixth,

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Lieut.-Col. Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, present—tha Revs. S. Lockwood, J. J. Bryant, Messrs. Stokes, Aaron' Whit- taker, Speakman, Percival, Lewis, Hadfield, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). THE ESTIMATE.—The Clerk presented an estimate for the half year ending Lady Day next, from which it appeared that £4,985 was required. Ihe rateable value of the union was £214,337, being an increase of £2,321 on the cor- responding peried of last year. A rate of 5i would pro- duce £l9ll 17s 9d, being a penny in the £ less than cor- respono'ng half-year, and a decrease of 2d in the £ as com- pared with the current halt-year. ACCOENTS.—The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £1,333 19a id. The amount included £1.319 for county rare, being a decrease of £196 3s 901 on the corresponding period. The report was passed on the motion of the Rev. J. Lockwood, seconded by Mr. Speakman. THE VISIT TO VIE LINATICS.—The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner forwarded a written report of the visit of the depu- tation appointed for the purvse to the Chester County Asylum on the 3rd inst. There were 38 patients charge- able to the. Union presented to the deputation by Dr. Davidson' medical superintendent. Of these 24 were male I and 14 females, an increase on last year of one female. They were questioned by the deputation individually, and they were all hopeless cases with the exception of ors male. They were clean and well cared for, dud appeared to be treated with tenderness and attention by the officialecon- nected with the institution. As usual, the deputation were received most courteously, and showed all the modern con- trivances used in cases of Innacy.—a. cheques for the costs of the deputation was passed. Ile amount was £2 83 41. —The Clerk observed that many of the cases were really worse than last year.—Mr. Lockwood said a patient in addition to the one mentioned in the report had been recom- mended for dismissal. SIIPHEANNUATION.—The Local Govern net Board gave the formal sanction to the payment to Mr. Wright, formerly relieving officer at Runcorn, of the superannuation allowance of £52 per annum.

div.head: WIDNES PIG DEALER HEAVILY FINED.
div.p: A WIDNES PIG DEALER HEAVILY FINED.

At Widnes Petty Seasioas on Weduesday, before Mr. E. Gibbon and Mr. H. S. Hall, Andrew Quinn, pig dealer, Mess Bank, Widnes, was charged for haying in contraven- tion of an order of the Privy Council, relating to swine fever, sold two pigs to Louis Pfister, eleven pigs to Elwin Hickey, and two to J. Hatton, all butchers, the animals not hiving keen kept upon the prerniees for 28 days before they were disposed of. Mr. .1. W. Knowles defended Q tinn. According to the evidence, the defendant on the 10th inst. brought 60 pigs by the London and North-Western railway from Oswestry to Widnes. In the train he agreed to sell eleven to Hickey at nt per lb., and two days previ- ously he had arranged to let Pfisten and Hickey each have a couple. These persons removed the pigs from the railway station to their own premises. On the same day P.C. Hunter met the defendant driving a large number of Digs along Victoria-road, and asked him if he were allowed to sell pigs, as be had seen him take five into Mr. Sadler& The defendant replied that he had only sold them to but- chers.—Mr. Knowles was contending that because the con- tract for the pigs had been made in two cases before they were brought into the town and in the ether in the train, no breach of the law had been committed.—Mr. Gibbon said wherever, or from whosoever, the defendant purchased the pigs, at that moment liability attached to him under the order, and seeing that the order was made for the protec- tion of the public, it would be perfectly nugatory if it were not so.—Mr. Knowles then pleaded that his client had acted in ignorance ani innocence, and said his trade was so bad that if a heavy penalty were imposed the defendant would have no other course open to him but going to the House of Correction.—Mr. triiishon said, as chairman of the County Committee, he had signed large orders of money durieg the last six months larger orders than he had ever signed before in his life, as compensation to pig dealers, and it was almost entirely to Widnes. It was idle to tell him that Quinn or anybedy else connected with pigs in Widnes could possibly be igno- rant of the serious outbreak caused through the sale of pigs, and of the law upon the subject. If Quinn did not know he was not fit to carry on the business of a pig dealer. He had never known anything worse than the state of things exist- ing in Widnes.--Sunerintendent Barker said the defendant in June, 1883, was fined £3 for a breach of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, and in March of this year £5 for not reporting an outbreak of swine fever upon his premises. Mr. B irker added that the butchers who had purchased pigs from the defendant were just as liable, and he had sum- moned them.—Mr. Gibbon suggested that as they had given evidence in a very fair manner they should not be proceeded against.—Mr. Barker then withdrew the charges against them, and Mr. Gibbon admonished them to use more eau- tion.—Quinn was fined 303 for each pig he had sold, making with costs a total of £25 83.

LECTURE BY MR. T. SNAPE AT RUNCORN. "Heroes of Peace and of War" was the title of a lecture delivered by Mr. T. Snape, of Widnes, in the United Metho- dist Free Church. Ellesmere-street, on Monday evening. There was a very numerous attendance. Mr. J. T. Brun- ner, Liberal candidate for the Northwich Division, presided, and had a very cordial reception. He was supported on the platform by the Revs. W. Vause and J. D. Thomas, and Messrs. J. N. Lello, Carson, and Marsh (Liverpool). The Chairman, in introducing Mr. Snaps, said he desired to have It thoroughly understood that he did not come there to promote the candidature of anybody. (Hear, hear.) He was very glad to hear from Mr. Vause that he considered that buildings erected in the first instance to the glory of God were not rightly used if they were only used for four hours a week. He (the chairman) was very firmly con- doned that politics and religion were coming very near together—(hear, hear, and applause)—and he wished those present never to look coldly upon their minister if he en- deavoured to induce his neighbours to use all the power that had been lately put into their hands in a righteous fashion. Hitherto, they knew, a political parson bad been looked upon as a very second rate parson. But he should he v.ry glad indeed to think that they agreed with him in the wish that politics hereafter should be more righteous, and that religion was not a matter of endowments. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Brunner then referred to the fact that hie rather was president of the Peace Society in Liverpool, and that he attended some lectures given by that society in a , room in Lime-street, Liverpool, now occupied by nigger minstrels, at the time of the Crimean war, when he was a schoolboy aged ten, and mighty little Greek he knew." De idea that they should wbrk and strive for peace was in his very blood. (Applause.) He asked them to join with him in giving Mr. Snape a very hearty welcome. In him tie had never found an',' change or shadow of turning He had been a man who hid never varied in his fight for the right, and who had never abated one jot of his heart and lope in the good time coming. (Loud applause) Mr. Snape, who was heartily received, said by no means be smallest part of the plea,ure that he had in coming to see them was the fact that he appeared under the presi- dency of one of his oldest Mends. For long years they

had been associated, in times none by more closely _ they had recently, aud he was proud that he had risen to occupy a position of their chosen candidate for that divi- sion. (Applause.) He (Mr. Snape) was connected with the Peace Society of Liverpeol, and Mr. Brunner's honoured father, long before his (the speaker's) connection with the
than

society, was one of its officers. lie was very glad indeed to know that Mr. Brunner had not departed from the faith of his fathers. He feared, as be told them before be rose, that possibly he might not go with him the whole length of that which he bad to say, but he was much gratified to know that to a very large extent—should he say altogether? —he agreed with those who were foand noon the Peace platform. (Applause.) Coming to his subject, the lecturer said the profession of war was by no means a heroic one, for Napoleoe, who might be said to be an authority, said that war was the "business of barbarians," and one of their own generals said that the profession of a soldier was an abomi- nable profession. Were war always unavoidable, and were justice always on the side of its decisions, its heroism would be much more commendable; but war wae an admitted evil, and to affirm that evil could not be avoided was to affirm there was no order in the world, and, in fact, to canonize disorder. Everyone would admit that daring was exhibited on the battle field, but it was not alone the dar- ing, but the object and results for which they dared, the animating spirit underlying their actions and its effects, which w re tip standards by which all heroism should be judged. In taking these rules to guide them, he ventured to say that the animating spirit of all war was unheroic and base. Alluding to the Crimean War, the Lecturer eaid on the rumour of the war the funds fell 10 per cent, meaning a loss of 80 millions ; the railway nooks fell 20 per cent, being a loss of 60 millions ; while the diminished value of manufacturers was 60 millions. The war cost them 100 millions, while it added 10 millions yearly to their na- tional expenditure for the army and navy. He mentioned the immense coet of other conflicts, and pointed out that from 1815 to 1870 the country lead spent to maintain the army and navy, on fortifications, and in interest on National Debt £2,700,000,000. Besides the tremendous cost of war, the loss of life was appalling. In the live years before 1852 we killed 5,400 persons by our ships in the East without our having lost a single man by the butcheries. From 1853 to 1871, the Crimean war to the Franco-German war inclusive, two million lives were lost in war, and Ed- mund Burke estimated that since the beginning; of autheia- tm history 35,000 millions of human lives (three times the present population of the globe) had been lost in war. When they spoke of the glary of war they should also not forget that there were attendant horrors which far outweighed in their terrible character all the tinselled glory that war might bring. What of the heroes of peace? Time would fail him to tell how Florexce Nightingale solaced the wounded and the dying—(applause)—how Mrs. Fry visited the forsaken when they were in prison; how John Howard assuaged the sufferings of those who had been immured in deadly gaols; how Thomas Clarkson and William Wilber- force broke the shackles of the slave and let the bondsmen free. (Applause.) The principle that animated their mili- tary hero was not what was right, but what was safe. Now, Instead of seeking to overcome evil as the war-heroes did by means of evil, the peace hero tried to follow out the apos- tolic injunction, and to overcome evil with good. (Ap- plause.) As an example of this teaching, the lecturer referred to the life and labourer of Richard Cobden and John Bright, and dwelt at length on their memorable endeavours to prevent the outbreak of the Crimean war. He alluded to the obloquy which they met, and the bitter reproaches with which these noble men were stung. But above all the triumphs which the peace party had secured was that of Free Trade. (Loud applause.) Before the passing of that great measure of reform agricul- ture and commerce were in a terrible state of depression. In Somersetshire twenty to thirty thousand laboarers were living on charity. In Newcastle-upon-Tyne almost all the working population wanted employment. Lancashire workmen existed to a very large extent on charity. In Leeds thirty to forty thousand men existed on charity. Sheffield was at the lowest stage of distress. Derbyshire was the same. In Stockport the poor-rate of Is 81 in the £ produced £5,000 in 1835, but immediately prior to the passing of the Act, with a rate of 2s in the £, it failed to produce £3,600. Poor-rates increased everywhere, and in Manchester the rate was as high as 3s 41 in the L. There were thousands of wives, and mothers, and children dying of hunger. After Free Trade this condition of things were altered. The exports nee in five years from 50 millions to 100 millions per annum. Manufacturers were rolling in Opulence, and country gentlemen were getting better rents than ever. In the last 23 years they had imported £1,600,000,0:0 more merchandise, and £70,000,000 more in coin and bullion than they had exported. Tee excess of imports and of bullion over and above the exports represen- ted the amount of profit that had been earned. In 1850, the populationyas 27 millions, and in 1831 nearly 35 mil-

In 1850, the 27 million's could scarcely get employ- ment; and in 1831 35 millions could get employment—he would not sty without difficalty, for they knew they bad been Passing under a cloud of depression—at any rate, with far less difficulty and impoverishment than occurred before. (Applause.) The repeal of the taxes on knowledge and light, the widening of re- ligious freedom, and the accomplishment of international arbitration with regard to the Alabama claims were referred to, eloquent tributes being paid to Cobden and Bright. Mr. Snaps asked how long the present state of things was to cmtinue. If the people of England, rising its the might of their moral strength, would make the demand, the day might draw near sooner than they thought when the mutual ' reduction of armaments would dimish the peril and ' frequency of their use in war; wheu the folly and wicked- ness of war should cease to the ends of the civilised earth, and in its place the voice of justice and of reason, speaking through established courts of international arbit-ation, I should rule this world. (Loud applause.) The Rev. J. D. Thomas, in moving that a vote of thanks be accorded to Mr. Snape for his lecture, said there was no doubt a growing feeling in the country against war, and that feeling Wilb to be attributed very largely to the efforts of the Peace Society, of which Mr. Snape was a worthy re- preseatative. (Applause.) The motion was seconded by Mr. J. N. L3llO, and car- ried unanimously. - .

Mr. Snaps, in replying, urged the audience to do all in their power to promote the principles of the Peace Society, and expressed a hope that they support the candidature of Mr. Brunner, who would do them good service in the Legisiature. (Applause.) Lie moved that a vote of thanks be given to Mr. Brunner for presiding over their pro- ceedings. Mr. Marsh (Liverpool) seconded the motion, which was carried by acclamation. . .

Iv reply, Mr. Brunner said he wanted them to work for a better time. Wherever they went he would like them to urge upon their fellow-men and women that it was the duty of every minister of religion to lead the people in every sphere.of life, and that it wee especially their duty to see if that could not induce the men who had the power in their hands to reduce the amount of poverty, of misery, and of wickedness, and to raise the people a step nearer to God. (Applause.) The meeting closed with the singing of the Doxology. A collection on behalf of the circuit fund realised £6 12s 4d.
THE THEATRE ROYAL, RUNCORN.-POLICE PRO-
sEcurioN.—A RUINED MANAGER.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. James Handley, Mr. William Rvchard Waldron, lessee and manager of the Theatre Royal, Wel- lington-etreet, and Mrs. Catherine James, propriatoress of the theatre, were jointly charged with keeping open the theatre on the 26th, 27th, and 31st August, and September let, for the public performance of stage plays without the authority or licence -equired by law, contrary to section 2 of the 6th and 7tn Victoria, c. 68. Mr. Waldron was also separately charged with this offence, and furthef that en the above mentioned dates he did for hire, act or present or did cause permit or suffer to be acted or presented certain parts in stage plays in the theatre, the same not being a patent theatre or duly licensed as a theatre. Mrs. James was also proceeded against under a similar summons.—Mr. Cartwright, Chester, prosecuted on behalf of the police, and Mr. T. H. Ilitchen represented Mrs. James, who was un- able to be present through sickness. Mr. Waldron was un- defended.—Mr. Cartwright read the sections under which the summonses were issued, and pointed out that any per- son offending was liable to a penaly not exceeding £2O for every day on which the house had been kept open without legal authority. The phrase " stage play" was interpreted by the Act to mean every tragedy, comedy, farce, opera, burletta, interlude, melodrama, pantomime, or other enter- tainment of the stage, or any part thereof. Mr. Cartwright quoted two cases, the first and last tried under the Acts for regulating theatres, it which it had been decided that a dia- logue between two persons on the stage was a stage play within the meaning of the Act. He narrated the circum- stances that caused the Bench to refuse a renewal of the license to the theatre, and stated that immediately after- wards Mr. Waldron issued bills headed "Runcorn Music Hall," stating that Messrs. Lomax's and Burgess's ‘• Rip Van Winkle" Company would give a first-class variety and miscellaneous entertainment. Feformances of this descrip- tion had taken place up to the present time.—Pei ice-clerk Wallace said the theatre was a dilapidated wooden building and described the performances that had taken place on three occasions when he had visited it. All the customary scenery and stage accessories were in use. Songs were sung in costume, lines were recited from Richard 111, in imitation of Barry Sullivan, and there was a dialogue between a man and a woman dressed in chara ;ter. On another occasion a court-room was presented, with judge, barrister, policeman, prisoner, and witness, and Wallace caused great amusement by his clever descriP- tion of the piece. P.C. Harper corroborated. Inspector Roche I said by direction of Superintendent Leah he had had con- trol of the details of the case. He was present at the per- formances on the dates mentioned in the summonses, and I • , amplified the evidence given. Mr. George Hayes, manager to the executors of air. C. Gerrard, proved that the notice bills issued were ordered by Mr. Waldron, and Superintend- ent Leah deposed that Mrs. James had applied for a license ' to the building.—Mr. Hitchen said Mrs. James closed the theatre after the service of the summons on Wednesdays and it was broken open again on Thureday.—Superintend- ent Leah said a complaint was made to him to that effect, and he was requested to put Mr. Waldron out. He, how- ever, could take no action in such a matter.—Mr. Hitchen contended that there was not a tittle of evidence against Mrs. James. Mr. Waldron' yearly agreement with Mrs. James expired on the 2nd August. Anticipating that there would be some difficulty about the renewal of the license, Mr. Waldron renewed the agreement for a month, so that Ire was the tenant t,f the theatre to the 2nd September. tWhen Mrs. James renewed the agreement there was a licence

I for the building, and he could produce the agreement in , which Mr. Waldron expressly agreed to do nothing which ' would endanger the licence. Mr. Waldron had also stated that he had the permission of the superintendent of the police to keep open the buildinee—Mr. Waldron denied the last assertion. It was a falsehood. Mr. Cartwright argued that Mrs James, as owner, was equally liable with Mr. Waldron for tbe control of the theatre.—Mr. Waldron said he was quite unprepared for any opposition on the part of Mrs James. He thought that she intended to act in uni- son with him in the matter, as he was her tenant. Mr. Elitchen had stated that he broke into the premises It was the such premises, and He d b had e(rsinr now the kldreV held possession Of of the theatre. The rent was paid until within nine days ago. He went to Mrs James and tendered a month's rent, when she distinctly said, in the presence of a witness, "I shall not charge you any rent until the license is granted." That month did not expire until the let of October, consequently he was etill Mrs James's tenant, and she had no legal right to close the theatre against him, and he did not conceive that he was doing anything wrong in obtaining entrance to his own prernisee. He merely came there that day prepared to answer the summonses issued against himself, Put since it appeared that the whole onus must fall upon his shoulders he must reopectfully point out that he was not the licensee of the theatre, and that he had never applied for the licenee. He could scarcely be held responsible for what bad tran- spired, as he was not the licensee. He bad no desire how- ever, to take any advantage of Mrs James, but he thought the opposition was entirely uncalled for.—Mr. Hitchen : I
am noi prosecuting you.—Mr. Waldron : It looks very much _ _ like it. -
I clme —l2;re. without anyone. to .ddend me,.
knew there was a solicitor employed on behalf of the police, but instead of one I have to face two. Mr. VVal.

dron submitted that he had not infringed or Tii any way violated the Act relating to staxe plays ; and contended that a similar class of of entertainmeet to that produced at the Theatre Royal was given in school-rooms and other unlicensed buildings by local amateurs. The sketches d scribed were merely the

vehicle for extemporaneous nonsense, and during his 4Ct years' experience be had never seen them on the stage of a regular tkeatre. If he had erred it had been in ignorance. Should the magistrates' decision be against him, and that decision wee accepted as a precedent every music hall pro- prietor in the kingdom would be liable to a prosecution which would deprive numbers of dialogue and sketch artistes of the means of livelihood. He stated that the company that had been engaged the week the license was refused writ zined a loss of £3O, and his own 1099 PS amounted to about £2O. He availed himself of the only means of paying then, which was to give a concert.—Mr, Cartwright said he must press the case against Mrs. James qui.e as much as against Mr. Waldron.—The magistrates retired to

consider their decisiontand on returning into court they die missed the cases against Mrs. James. For keeping open the theatre for stage plays Mr. Waldron was fined £2 and costs, £2 15s, and for allowing the pieces to be acted a penalty of Li and costs, is ød, was imposed.—Mr. Waldron asked for leave to appeal.—The .Magistrates' Clerk said the Act gave

this power.—Mr. Waldron said he was not able to pay the money. The proceedings had totally ruined him, and is family were without the means of subsistence.—The Bench allowed the defendant a montn in which to pay the fines.

div.head: RUNCORN STABBING CASE . .
div.p: THE RUNCORN STABBING CASE . .

Before Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Police-- Court, on Tuesday, Mary Ann Brickoall, with several aliases, a native of Widnes, was brought up on remand charged with having, on the 7th September, unlawfully wounded Rose Pearle, domestic servant, in the employ of James Payne, landlord of the Cornwall and Devonshire Arms Inn, Church.street.—The proseoutrix, who appeared to be in a weak condition, said that about half.past eleven on the night in question she went te the railway station to meet her master and mistress, who had gone to Belle Vue. She was accompanied by Prancis Dawe. As they were retnniing they stopped to witness a row that was taking place at the foot of Waterloo-road. The prisoner called her filthy names, and then threatened that she had eomething in her pocket that would do her good, following up her words by striking her. Witness felt pain in the places where she had been struck, and shouted, "Oh, she is using a knife." The prisoner ran down James-wint, near the Theatre. Witness became faint, and Dawe took her home. On going to bed she found a quantity of blood on her clothes (produced). There were boles in the articles corresponding with the posi- tion of the wounds. Dr. Mangan saw her subsequently and ordered her to remain in bed a few days. The prieone; had threatened to do violence to the witness since last Octo- ber.—Evidence of a confirmatory character was given by several witnesses.—Dr. Mangan deposed that he had ex- amined Pearle. He found an incised wound on the back of the left shoulder, another on the left side, and another in the region of the stomach. They were clean cut wounds half an inch bag, and likely to be caused by the knife pro- duced. To cut through the stays and clothing in the man- ner these articles had been cut, considerable f orce mast have been used. The wound on the side was not healed yet.— P.S. Nick! stated that the prisoner, when apprehended, said I used the knife. I did not think it was se bad. I was drunk at the time.—The prisoner called P.S Walley, who stated that he met the prisoner on the night in question. She alleged that she had been held by a sailor whilst the proeecutrix assaulted her. The prisoner's hair was 'tonging down upon her shoulders. She did not appear te be drunk. —The prisoner, who wept bitterly during the hearing of the case, was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

The- for-tn'ghtly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Lieutenant-Colonel Asbton presided, and there were present the Revs. J. Lockwood, J. J. Bryant Messrs. Stokes, Aaron, Hadfield, Lewis Weir, H. Percival, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). , FRODSHAM PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.—At the m-sting held OH Friday at Frodsham the engineer reported that the outfall sewage tanks should be emptied at least once in three months. The Inspector of Nuisances said :he rants had now bees emptied and the necessary rep ars were in pro- gress.—Dr. Steele, of Newton Hall, claimed £7 for damage alleged to have been done to the field in which the trial wells were soak. The Clerk said be had rigaested Dr. Steele to furnish particulars of claim and the matter wan referred. Tau ESTIMATE —The Deputy Clerk read the estlin ate for Lady Day, 1886. The total capital tfhore thhaelfhlaelft; et'aurdennling Michaelmas was £420. and there is• expected to be a balance in hand at the conclusion of the period of £42. The probable expenditure for the ensuing half year was :—Salaries £135, legal expenses £lO, rent £2, sundries £25, Weston drainage (suspense account) £122,. Five Crosses water scheme £177, balance and contingency find making a total amount required of £721. After e educfl2nsgoihe probable balance at Michaelmas the amount was £579. The rateable value of the Union is £162,032. A rate of id in the £ would produce the sum of £675 2e Sd,, and this rate was recommended to be levied, as it would.. provide the authority with a working balance, and so avoid any question of interest on overdraft. The Parliamentary grant of £l3O, which was usually paid in January, had not been taken into account in the estimate. THE WESTON SEWERAGE SCREUE.—The Deputy Clerk read a draft agreement he had prepared between the Au- thority and the Bridgewater Navigation Company with re- spect to providing Weston with a more efficient scheme of sewerage. wo ol ua Thp apa Rvr approved. t He added that he could not advise the Authority to give up the right of crossing the field of the Brine Com- pany, because if a nuisance should arrive from turning the sewage into the canal at the point now proposed they would purchase the right of way again.—The draft vaexdo.OF FEVER AT KINGSLEY AND FRODSHAM.—Dr. Adams, the medical officer, reported the existence of typhoid fever at cottage premises at Kingsley, occupied by George Geffs, who was the only person attacked at present. He had found no sanitary defects at the premises to account for the outbreak. The patient, however, had been in lodg- ings at Weston Point in premises where the whole of the old drainage had been recently taken upend newly laid, and it was more than probable that the noxious exhalations evolved during the process had contributed to induce the disease. He had further to report an outbreak of typhoid fever at Church-street, Frodsham on premises occupied by Mr. Franklin. Two children were at present ill, ag,d seven and five years respectively, and during August an infant was ill for a long time with a disorder of typhoid fever. On inspecting the premises, which were newly built, he discovered a trap in the cellar, from which distinct emanations of sewer gas were escaping into the ' cellar, which the children appeared to have used sea covered playground, and they had thus been breathing sewer gas in all its undiluted vigour. This outbreak was but another instance of those cases where a trap was worse than useless, unless it was kept constantly filled with water. The water had evaporated to a depth of four inches below the level of the trap, and the sewer gas had unimpeded access to the house. He suggested that an inspection be made of the other pre- mises similarly built, and the possibility of further similar occurrences taking place should be obviated. The usual preyentitiye measures had been adopted, and he trusied the onthreak would be arrested.—The report was adopted. FLIIIN'S•LANE, FRODSHAM.—Mr. Hadfield drew attention to the state this lane had been left by the contractor for the sewerage works. The road was in a most disgraceful and almost impassible state for both pedestrians and horses. He desired to know whether the contractor ought not to have put the road in the earns condition in which he Mand it.—The Clerk said the surveyor of highways contemplated making some improvements to that road He intended, he believed, to have a footpath on the easterly side, joining the footpath near Mr. Nibb's property there. Perhaps he did not wish to do anything until the sewerage works were completed.—The Deputy Clerk : He cannot do anything until we have decided about the -water seheme.—The Clerk said the survyor had been in communication with the con- tractor about the road, and the Authority agreed to take no action upon the matter until next meeting. / There was no other business of public interest.

Mr. and Mrs Broadhurst were among the visitors received by Mr. Gladstone at Hawarden Castle on Wednesday, "JUMBO KILLED IN RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—A Central News telegram from New York says intelligence has just been received of the death of the celebrated elephant "Jam. bo," which was brought to America from the London Zo-• logical Gardens by Mr. Barnum. The beast was killed in a railway collision at St. Thomas's, Ontario. It sees that the animal was run into by a freight train when being taken across a line of rails. A taxidermist has gone to St. Thomas, Ontario, for the purpose of stuffing the skin, which will be presented to Tupp's College, Massachusetts. The skeleton will probably be placed in the National Museum at Wasbicgton.

--WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. liostilax—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), in the chair, Alderman Burgess, and Councillor Greening. MISCELLANZotS.—The following were dealt with for being drunk :—John Donlan, in St. James's-street, on Sat- urday night, fined 5a and costs; James Scully (sixth ap- pearance) and Peter Bartuley (79th appearance), fined 5s and costs each; Mary Towey, in Cockhedge-lane, sent to prison for a month; Daniel Neal, In Dixon-street, on Saturday night, fined 5s and costs; Sarah Ellen WillOn- son, in Battermarket-street, on Saturday night (16th ap- pearance), sent to prison for a month ; George Jones, in Winwick-road, on Saturday night, fined Sc, including costs; James Sauce, in Bridge-street, on Saturday night, fined 20s and costs ; Micbael O'Connor, on the platform of the Cen- tral Station, on Saturday, fined 5s and coots; Elizabeth Jones, in Winwick-road. on Suaday morning, fined ss, in- cluding costs; John Hatton, in Tanners-lane, on the 3rd Inst., fined 5s and costs; James Murray, in Naylor-street, on the 4th inst., 4ned 5s and costs; Elizabeth Leyland, in Golborne-street, on the 7th inst., discharged with a caution; Thomas Locker, in Knntsford-road, on the Bth inst., fined 5e and costs; Sarah Burns, in Buttermarket street, on the 6th inst.. fined 5s and coats; Bridget Rooney, in Batter- market, fined 5s and costs.—The following were bound over to be ot good behaviour r—James, Bibby, Robert Taylor, Eichard Smith, and Margaret Wright. &Hoot ATTENDANCH.—Mr. George Riley, school attend- ance officer, prosecuted in the following cases :—Richard Howarth, fined ss; Thomas Walmsley (two cases), fined 55 in each case; John Stapleton, cue adjourned for a month ; John Rooney (two cases), fined 5s in each case ; Joseph Dean. adjourned for a month ; in the cases of John Broderick, William Worrell, and Elizabeth Abraham, orders were made for the children to go to reformatory schools, the evidence showing that they were beyond the control of the parents. TUESDAY.—Before Councillors Greening and Broadbent, and
Mr. F. Monks.

WIFE ASS&ULT..—JOh—E—iililig;;;;- labourer, was charged with assaulting his wife, Bridget, on Saturday.--The wife stated that he dragged her through the strbet by the hair of her head. He was when sober, a very good husband, but there had been no living in the house with him since he broke teetotal a short time ago.—He was ordered to be bound over to be of good behaviour for six months, and the costs were remitted. div.head: DOUBLE MURDER AND SUICIDE.
div.p: DOUBLE MURDER AND SUICIDE.

On Wednesday, Mr. J. the County Borough Coroner, opened an inquiry at the Reindeer Inn. Sutton, near Liverpool, on the bodies of Emily Louisa Mappleton, aged four years and 'iii months; Thomas Mappleton, aged two years and three months; and that of their mother, Louisa Mapple- ton, aged about forty-nine years, who committed sui- cide atter murdering the deceased children.—Thomas William Mappleton, of Glenham Cottages, Spa. avenue, Sutton, farm labourer, deposed that the de- ceased woman was his wife. On Monday morning he left home as usual to go tce• his employctent, leaving the deceased woman and Lwo children in bed asleep. He returned as usual about a quarter-past seven in the eveninz, but after continuous knocking at the door and failing to get-any reply, he got over the wall at the rear of the building. Upon entering the building he called for his wife. Receiving no reply from her, he went upstairs to the bedroom, where he had left her, and was horrified at finding the place covered with blood and his two children and his wife surrounded with gore. He raised an alarm, and medical assis- tance was sent for. It was then discovered that their throats were fearfully our. In answer to the coroner the witness farther said that the deceased woman had I been in a strange condition of mind for some days past, but he had not the slightest suspicion that she would do any harm to herself or the children. She had been of late a great student of the Bible, and he believed that her mind had become deranged in con- sequence. She was very much attached to the chil- dren The jut:, returned a verdict that the deceased children's lives were wilfully destroyed by their mother, who afterwards committed suicide while . under a state of mental derangement. ,

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. '

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was. held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning. There were present— The Rev. U. F. Roberts (chairman), and Messrs. Jolley, Hunt, Brown, Appleton, Derbyshire, Harrison, William Houghton, John Houghton, Broadbent, Bonnet!, Killsball, Greening, and Humphries; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sul- ton (assistant clerk).

_ SCHOOL commtrrEs. The minutes of this committee stated that the committee had had before them the regulations they propose to recom- mend with reference to children visiting their sick parents In the Workhouse and with reference to the admission of children into the schools, and decide in the first place to sabmit the same to the consideration of the ROOS.) Com- mittee for their suggestion thereon.—On the motion of Vie Crtanamarr, seconded by Mr. JOLLEY, these minutes were confirmed. SCHOOL FEES.—DISTRESS IN THE TOWN.

The School Fees Committee reported that school fees had been granted in 46 cases, 38 of which were old, and eight new cases.— Mr. BLacxnuasr moved, and Mr. BROWN seconded, the adoption of these minutes.—ln answer to questions, Mr. JOLLEY said that the number of new applica- tions was considerably less than those of previous occa- sions, but this was owing to peculiar circumstances. At the previous meeting there were a large number of applica- tions, and there was a very great and serious increase over any previous quarter in consequence particularly of the de- pression in the fustian and iron trades of the town.—Mr. BROADBENT said he should like to know whether those who applied for school fees were usually in receiptof other re- lief, that was whether in the majority of cases those who had to apply for assistance in the form of school fees were people who applied for other sort of assistance:—Mr. HAR- RISON pointed out that to persons who were in receipt of any other kind of parochial relief school fees would not bee distinct item, but would be absorbed in the amount of relief given to the recipient. The school fees were, however, a kind of barometer indicating the state and condition of the labour market in Warrington, and therefore it would always be interesting to sae exactly what the state of that barometer was, and he was sore Mr. Blackhurst would be very happy to give them what information he could—Mr. Baiaatinsur said be did not mean exactly whether parents were in-receipt of relief ai the time they were receiving school fees, bat whether those who were. in the habit of receiving school fees were also in the habit of receiving parish relief also. It had been the intention of the legislature that the receipt of school fees should not constitute paupers.—Mr. BLACK.. sustsr said that at the next meeting they would endeavour to give the information asked for, but at present he bat no knowledge of any pauper cases coming before the School Fees Committee. They were principally cases in which the head of the family bad been temporarily thrown out of work.— Mr. DAEBYSHIRE said there were many people came to ask , for school fees who were very glad to repay the amount when they were in a position to do so.—The minutes were then adopted.

div.head: VACCINATION.
div.p: VACCINATION.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board, stating that they enclosed a letter which had been rec-ived by them from Mr. Ho!ford, vaccination officer for the War- rington district. They had also received from Mr. FloHord a statement showing the steps taken by him with regard to the children born in his district during the year 1883 and the first half of the year 1884. It Appeared that the oh- servitions contained In their (the LOOA I Government Board's) letter of the 12th ult. with regard to Mr. Cooper's state- ments equally apply to Mr. Holford's. The Board trusted that the Guardians would see that in future Mr. HoHord issued the notices to pa:rente, and make inquiries into cases of default promptly as required by the Board'a instructions. The statement of Mr. Bollard to the Local Government Board as to cases unvaccinated for the year 1883 and Jan- uary to Jane, 1884, was also read. The Board would per- ceive, Mr. Holford stated, that 21 cases had been postponed, and he would do his very best to have those arrears cleared off by October next. What cases remained unvaccinated then he should repart to the Guardians for their instrtic- tions as to his next action. As he found no reins:ale to have the children vaccinated he had delayed reporting them to the Guardians in the hope that the should get them vaccin- ated without having recourse to proceedings in court. If the Local Government Board would grant him the ex- tension of time, he felt certain he should clear them all off.

RESIGNATION OF DR MEM. The following letter to the clerk was read, viz. :—" Local Government Board,. Whitehall, S.W., 15th September, 1895. —Sir,—l am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of 'your letter of the 10th ult. and of its enclosures, and to transmit for the information of the Guardians of the Warrington Union the enclosed copy of a letter which the Board have this day addressed to Dr. Spinks requesting him to resign the office of medical officer of the schools; and they request that they may be informed as soon as his resignation has been placed in the hands of the Gnardians.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, ALFRED D. ADRIAN, assistant secretary."—The following is a copy of the letter above referred to as having been sent to Dr. Spinks, viz. :—" Local Government Board. Whitehal I, S.W., 15th September, 1885.—Sir,--I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the recept of your letter of the 28th ult. relative to the administration of the schools at Padgate belonging to the Guardians of the IVarrington Union. The Board have given their careful consideraVon to the questions affecting your position as medical officer of the schools which have been submitted to them ; and they now direct me to state that under all the circumstances they deem it undesirable that you should retain that office. The Board therefore direct me to request that you will place your resignation of the office of ' medical officer of the schools in the bands of the Guardians at their next meeting. lam sir, your obedient servant, A. D. Adrian, assistant secretary."—Mr. BLACKEIIIRST : Has Mr. Spinks sent in his resignation yet P—The CLERK said he had not, but he.would only receive his letter that morn- ing.—The subject then dropped, but at a later stage of the meeting a letter was read from Dr. Spinks in which he tendered his resignation of the office of medical officer of Padgate Schools.—The CLERK stated that the matter was one between the Local Government Board and Dr. Spinks, and therefore no resolution on the Dart of the Board was necessary.

div.head: COT/ST! EXPE gDITURE.
div.p: COT/ST! EXPE gDITURE.

The CLERK 'ead-K-1000-178-ta.ci-in-enat—as to the contribu- tions towards county expenditure made by that Union, and he also referred to the manner in which the county funds were expended. In particular he referred to the case of a propoeed bridge at Penwortham which was to cost £50,000 or £60,000, and in connection with which a bill for legal expenses amounting to about £5,000 had already been sub- mitted to the county authorities. The facts he (the clerk) had brought before them only went to show the desirability of their calling in some man who ought to know, and let him explain if that Board would have to pay any part of that £5,000 or the cost of Penwortham bridge if it was car- ried out. He then mentioned that Mr. Bleckley took a good deal of Interest in the financial affairs of the county.—ln answer to a question the CLERK said he did not know whether or not the bill to authorise the erection of the bridge in question pissed Parliament or not, but in any case there would be the question of the £s,ooo.—The CHAIRMAN thought it would be best for the Board to take the advice of the clerk and ask Mr. Bleckley if he would attend their meeting and explain the matter to them. There was no doubt that that kind of thing would not be carried on much longer as county government boards would do away with it.—Mr. HARRISON ti-.onght Mr. Bleckley would come if he were properly invited.—Mr.HARRESHIRE thought that if the bill had not passed Parliament those who insti- gated the proceedings ought to pay the costs. He also mentioned that he thought the Warrington Union was much higher assessed to the county rate than other Unions. The CHAIRMAN said there was no doubt that a greater uniformity of assessment was required.—The CLERK remarked that Mr. Blecklv was one of the committee who went round the county to equalize the assessment, and therefore be would probably be prepared to answer a question of that kind, which was a very fair question.—Mr. DARBYSIIIRE said he knew the Cheshire townships in the Warrington Union were higher assessed to the county rate than townships in other Cheshire Unions.—Mr. APPLETON said the assessment of Newton had been raised about £lo,ooo.—The CLERK said that the Union valuation of Newton was £47,104, while the comity valua- tion was £52,000.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE moved and Mr. GREENING seconded a proposal that Mr. Sleekly be invited to attend the next Board meeting in reference to county ex- penditure.—This proposal was carried unanimously.

div.head: POOR LAW CONFERENCE.
