div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 19, 1885
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 19, 1885
PROVIDENCE HOSPITA,, ST; HELENS. erPl
SPEECH OF THE MARQUIS OF RIPON.

_ On Tuesday evening a Jargely-attended meeting was held I in the Drill Hall, Sr. Helena, in aid of the Providence Hos- pital. The Mayor (Alderman Cook) presided, and there were also present on the platform the Marquis of Ripon, Colonel Gatrible (Liberal candidate for St. Helens), Mf- Seton-Karr. (Conservative candidate), Messrs. NV. Puking. ton, R Pilkington, H. S. Hall, A. Sinclair, .1. C. Gamble, W. Gamble, J. B. Leach, A. Walmaley, Dr. Twyford,-Dr. McNicoll, the local Catholic derv, and several ministers of other denominations, ctn.

The Mayor, who was received with loud applause, said they were met there that night to hear something of the operation and circumstances of the Providence Hospital, and to consider bow far it Was entitled to the generous considera- tion and liberal support of the public of St. Helens. (Hear, hear,) That institution had been founded for the purpose of affording relief to the poor in Cases of sickness, or in cases of accident. Be nerd hardly say that in St. Helens they had another hospital, the terms of admission into which were somewhat different to the one in question. In the St. Helens Cottage Hospital patients were admitted either by the payment of Is per day during their continu- ance in the hospital, or by subscribing Id per week towards the funds of the hospital. Bat in a community like St. Helens there must always be a number of the poor who were unable to subscribe the charge which was necessary for admission into that hospital, and the Providence Hos- pital had been founded for the purpose of relieving such cases. (Hear, hear.) He had in his nand a report of the operations of the hospital during the past year, and he was surprised to find that there had been admitted during that time 152 patients—(bear, hear, and applause)—and judging from the report it must be admitted that the hospital had been doing good and valuable services to the poor. (Ap- plause.) _ _ _

Fath'er Dignam then mentioned the objects of the hos- pital and gave a few details as to its operations up to the present time. Colonel Gamble, who was received with loud applause, moved the following resolution That this meeting cor- dially recognises the benedcent work that has already been done and is being continued by the Providence Hospital at Hardshaw Hall, and avails itself of this opportunity to put on record their feelings of gratitude for the unreniitting care and attention which have been bestowed by the sisters in charge of the institution upon the numerous cases which have been received into the hospital." He was net going to speak to them, he said, as a candidate for Sr. Helens, but in a position of much older standing—a friend of charitable institatious in St. Helens. (Loud applause.) In regard to that hospital he should tell them beforehand that he had never been in it, or in the little institution in George-street' which preceded it, but he happened to know a good deal about the,old institution, and he knew that it was conducted in such a way by the sisters who had charge of it as to receive the admiration of every one. (Applause.) As they were aware, be had taken coesiderable interest in the cottage hospital, and he had taken the trouble of comparing the accounts of the two hospitals for the year 1884, and he was glad he was glad to see that the new hospital with only one year's experience seemed to be worked as economically as the old one. (Hear, hear.) The Providence Hospital reCeived people of all denomination!, and all received the same attention from the sisters in charge, who had been qualified for their post by training in a great London hospital, and be was told by a medical man from whem he had inquired on the subject that they did their work skil- fully and well. (Applause.) He also referred to the fact that patients might be visited by clergymen of their own religious persuasion, and that no attempt whatever was made by the sisters In charge to induce any one to change their religion. As far as be was concerned, he thought they ought to support that .hospital, and he expreseed the inten. tiott to subscribe the same annual sum to it that he did to the Cottage Hospital. (Loud applause.)

MR. &ETON Kean, who was received whit loud ap- plause, in eecouding the motion referred to the necessity of hospital accommodation in the midst of a large working- class copulation like that of S. Helens. The ploulatien of St. Helens, he said, amounted to about 60,000. and was rapidly increasing, as from the number of children he saw in the streets he should be inclined to say that the family of the St. Helens working-man was invariably large. (Hear, hear, and laughter.)

The Marquis of RIPON, on rising to support the resolu- tion, was enthusiastically received, He said that when he was asked some time ago whether he should be willing to visit St. Helens for the purpose of giving what aid he could to that valuable institution, be felt bound to accept the pro- posal if be. could make it at all possible to do so—(cheers) —for it was no small pleasure to men who were engaged in public life, especially duriog these eventful months, when many demands were made upon them, to have an opportu- nity of casting aside those considerations of controversy and of contest with which they had se much to do, and to come forward upon an occasion like that, which united men of all parties and all opinions, to advocate a great and a noble cause. (Cheers. )Nevertheless, he could not conceive that it was necessary for one who, like himself, was a stranger in the borough to occupy any large portion of their time in endeavouring to convince them that it was their duty and their interest as citizens of St. Helens to give their cordial sanction to the resolution which had been moved. (Cheers.) And if he felt somewhat oppres- sed by that c ,nsideration before he came into that hall that evening, he must confess that it had been much more clearly brought home to him since he had been listening to the speeches which had just been delivered. (Hear, bear.) Very little had been left for him to say except that he most cordially agreed with the areuments already submitted to them in favour of that institution. (Cheers.) Some of the speakers who had preceded him had spoken from personal acquaintance of the work which was being done in that hos- pital, and they had borne their testimony to its excellence and efficiency. (Hear, hear.) He was quite confident that no one would dispute that in a great town like that, con- taining some 60,000 inhabitants, mainly of the working classes, men engaged in occupations fraught with frequent occasions of danger, there was a very ample scope and necessity for hospital accommodation. (Cheers.) They had heard that there existed in St. Helens two hospitals and it was very gratifying to find, from the language used by previous speakers, that there existed no rivalry between these institutions, which united in confer- ring the utmost benefits on the inhabitants. That there was ample room for both hospitals was shown by the fact that during twelve months the new institution had relieved 152 persons. Where people could pay, it was desirable that they should do so, but they knew that in a town of the poZ pulation of St. Helens there were only too many who could not afford payment of that kind, and there was only too large a scope for a hospital of that kind. (Cheers) The sisters engaged in it made no concealment of their faith, and he *as very sure that if they were to ask them, these sis- ters would tell them that it was on the strength of that faith that they were able to accomplish the work to which they had devoted their lives. (Hear, hear.) Their minis- trations were freely given to all without distinction, and suffering and distress io every form had a claim upon them; and if they wanted a proof of the appreciation which was entertained in that town for this wise and truly Christian spirit by which these devoted women were actuated, they would find it when they looked round at the assembly gathered is that hall that night, where were brought together in support of this hospital per- sons of all opinions' and of all creeds. (Cheers.) He could conceive no Work 'upon which men of different opinions, religious or political, could batter and more safely unite and work heartily together than with the work affor- ded by an institution of this kind. (Hear, hear.) The re- lief of suffering and the cure of disease was a matter upon which men of all sentiments could agree. It was a work on which at all events, those actuated by a spirit of Christian- ity could unite. (Cheers.) They had entrusted with the nsanarment of this institution, and with the nursing of the patients, a body of ladies of whose devotion to their work in the highest spirit of religion—he could not speak from per- sonal knowledge, but from the testimony of those who had seen them at wort and krie'w what they were doing—testi- mony bad been borne to their labours, and he could well understand what that spirit was from the experience which he, in common with others, had had of the character of the lives of other ladies of the sarne description, who in other parts of the country had given themselves to similar work. Those present, however, were the best judges of what was being done by the sisters, and to them be appealed without hesitation and withont fear. They knew bow great, how untiring, how generous, and how self-sacrificing that devotion was. (Cheers.) He thought that the experience of those who had bad any- thing to do with the sick, especially in these times—he did not anticipate thit the medical gentlemen who might be present weuld contradict him—showed that, in regard to many illnesses, good nursing was at least half the battle. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) But whilst be felt this in the strongest degree, whilst he knew it from his Own personal experience, he acknowledged, of course, that neither hospital buildings, nor skilful nor devoted nurses were alone suffi- cient to make an efficient hospital. They must also have a good medical staff —(mar, hear, and cheers)—and he be- lieved be was right in saying that in this Providence Hos- pital they largely enjoyed that great advantaget and that the medical men who gave their services to it did so in that noble spirit of devotion to the sick which marked the medi- cal profession throughout the world. (Cheers.) This being so, he ventured to submit that its promoters were amply justifi.d in appealing to the public for their support. An institution of that kind ought to have s‘mething of a permanent character. He did not think it needed many general arguments to induce them to feel the duty of giving their support to an institution of that kind. (Cheers.) Sickmas and accidents were common to them all, and they reminded them perhaps more than other of the various circumstances of their changing life, of that ftindamental human relation which underlay all artificial distinctions and bound them all to their fello,w men. (Cheers.) "There were few present that night who did not know something from personal experi- ence af the trials of sickness and the weariness of pains, and it behoved them all tri do what they could to alleviate those trials. (Cheers.) Many persona could' not afford to go to the Cottage Hospital and make the payments which were reasonably expected, having due regard to the work it was intended to do, and they shrank, ' through most honourable motives, from having recourse to the union. (Cheers.) They turned, and rightly en, to theother hospi!al to help them, OD no pauperising conditions, 'and on'tio terms iDCOn. sistent, with self-respect. (Hear, bear) The sitters were doing well their noble work at the hospital, the medical officers were doing theirs, and It remained for the public of Si. Hefena to seize that opportunity which Pod had given them 01 doing something for His service by helping to se-

The match Lancashire v. Sixteen of Enfield and District was concluded on Saturday. On the previous day the Sixteen were at the wickets nearly the whole of the day, but only scored 77. When the stumps were drawn two of the Lancashire wickets had fallen for 47 runs, of which Mr. Hornby had made 39. Owing to the unfavourable weather on Saturday the gime was not commenced until three o'clock, and even then a fresh wicket had to be pitched. Though there was no rain during the rest of the afternoon, the weather was boisterous, and as a consequence the 1111111. her of spectators was comparatively small. Barlow and Mr. Lancashire continued the batting, and the innings closed, after an hour and a hairs play, with the score at 105. The bowling was uniformly good, Crossland taking.five wickets for 35 runs, and Mr. Appleby three for 28. The score was as follows :—Endeld and District. 77 and 33 ; Lancashire, 105.

The season just closed has been the most successful for I the4East Lancashire Cricket Club known for many years. 1 Of the 26 matches played no fewer than 15 were won and five drawn, th., remaining six being lost. The East Lanai- shit. Club have defeated Preston, Burnley, Church, Crane, I and Haslingden twice each; and Darwen, Keighley, Ley- land, Harwood, and Balton once each. They have been defeated bv Nelson twice, and by Leyland, Todmorden, and Darwen once each. The cup tie, which they lost against Darwen, is not reckoned, being played without professionals. The drawn games were with Keighley, Bolton, Harwood, Emeriti. and Todmorden, besides a cup tie drawn with Dar. wen. The season will finally close with a march between Married and Single members of the club, which will not affect the averages. The new professional, Crossland (the ex-County man), heads both the batting and bowling aver- ages. He and Mr. Dixon have been the mainstay of the club in the batting department, while he and Shaw have car- ried off the chief bawling honour.

Major Richard Pilkingtoni J.P., moved" That, in the opinion of this meeting the Providence Hospital is entitled to the confidence and support of the inhabitants and it de- sires to urge its claims to public sympathy and support." He pointed out that in that institution there was no dis- tinction made with regard to religion—that those who en- tered it, entered it apart from what they believed, or to whatever church they belonged. Not only was that great boon conferred, but they entered it without price, and they not only had their physical necessities attended to, but their religious necessities--(applause)—and could have the at- tendance of their own ministers of religion whether they belonged to the Church of Rome, Church of England, or any dissenting body. (Cheers.) He hoped inst.tutions such as that would draw the various sections of the Church of Christ in closer bonds, and would increase and not diminish. All of them knew full well that such a thing as they saw there that night could not have existed fifty years ago and he hoped that when fifty years more had gone, the differ- ences which divided them would be far less than they were to-day—(cheers)—and that it might be possible for the dif- ferent members of the Church of Christ to apiroach so closely that they should almost forget that there was a dif- ference, and that once more there should be one church, one master, and one God. (Cheers.) Dr. McNicoll seconded the motion. He remarked there was one quotation left for him, and that was " One touch of Nature makes the whale world kin." If he (Dr. M'Nicoll) might speak for the medical profes- sion, be would say that they fully agreed not only with the origin, foundation, and principles of the institution, but also with its management. (Cheers.) They knew full well the value of go'od, careful, moral nursing, and that institution was pre-eminently for the poor. (Applause.) Alderman'E.•Johnson, in supporting the resolution, said the ladies who had established the hospital in their midst appealed for their support and asked them to perform a most charitable work, and he (Alderman Johnson) bad every confidence in his fellow townsmen that that appeal would not bnin vain. (Cheers.) The resolution was then passed with acclamation. Mr. W. CLLEIC FOR DANIAOII.—, A SINGULAR CB.Sll.—Patriok Renayne, of Newhin, summoned his brother James Ronayne, at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, for wilfully damaging two doors and a window to the amount of 16s on the Bth inst. The magistrates meth. Bench were Messrs. R..Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and W. F. Gooch. The defendant did not appear.—From the evidence of the com- plainant it appeared that the defendant repeatedly annoyed him. He did not want' to " meddle " with him in any form. His brother had 'coine down to break the windows and commit murder, but he (complainant) did- net want to fight with him.—Superintendent Jackson informed the corn- ptainant that he had charged his brother with breaking doors and windows, sod he asked him to tell the magistrates about the affele-e-The Clerk: How'eid be do the damage ? —Complainant r. He kicked them'when r went for a police- man.—The Clerk: How many panes agiaes did he breek ? —Complainant; I let him first rob me, and then after he had spent all the money, be said he was going to Come down to my place to commit minder, but I. did not want him, and I went for a policeman—The clerk: Have you had the doors and windows repaired 7--Complainant : Oh, yes.—How mach did you pay for it 7—Sixteen shillings. You paid that amount ?--Well, I have not paid it yet, but I have a bill for it. (Laughter.)—Heve you any witnesses ? --Cornplaioant : Witnesses ? No, I have no witnesses only a wife and child. (Loud laughter.)—The Bench made an order for the payment of the damage, amounting to 16s, along with the costs. , PROPOSED SWIMMING BATH AOl3 EARLESTOWN. A movement has. been commenced in Earlestown for supplying the town with public baths. The absence of a swimming bath has long been felt and deplored, and though the Fab- ject has been often considered, no definite steps have hither- , to been taken. The question, however, has latterly come to ' the front, and there Is a prospect of the hopes of a large number of the inhabitants at last being realised.. During the past week or two a gentleman. has thoroughly considered the matter, and plans of a proposed swimming bath have been prepared. The size of the principal bath, ari at pre- sent suggested, will he 40 feet in length and 24' feet wide, while there will be 12 separate dressing rooms for the swim- mers. The building, heating apparatue, and other necessary articles will cost, it is estimated, over £6OO. A great diffi- culty towards the completion of the scheme is the supply of water. The township water is sultplied by the London and North-Western Railway Company, and according to the pre- sent rates the quantity of water required for the proposed bath would be a burdensome charge. It has seen estimated that about 27,000 gallons of water would be wanted to fill the bath, and this would entail a coat of over 13s each time the bath was filled.. With the view of overcoming this drawback, we understand that the Newton Commissioners and the Railway Company are being consulted with the view of having the water supplied aka nominal charge. It is stated that in order to give the proposal a successful start an appeal for subscriptions will be made to the public, for whose benefit the bans will be provided. The movement is certainly one-deserving support. ' BAD . SCALDING FATALIVr.—A sad death by scalding' .was investigated by Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, and a jary, at the Royal Hotel, Cross-lane, Eirlestowo, on Wednesday afternoon. The deceased was Stephen John Partin, 3 years and 9 months old, eon of John Carlin, chim- ney sweep, residing at 22, Derby-street. The first witness was William Carlin. 15 years of age, who said the deceased was his' brother. On the night of the 29th ult, deceased, witness, and other children were playing in front of the' fire. The kettle WAS on the hob. Deceased was seated on the fender, and witness struck at him with his cap. His cap caught the kettle and pulled it off, the water flying on his little brother. His mother and aunt came, and attended 'his brother. The skin peeled off his brother's back when be -was touched. Dr. Niouncey , and Dr. Fox afterwards attended him to his death which occurred on eaturday night —Jane Carlin, wife of Christopher Carlin, 24, Derby-street, deposed that she was called to the house. She asked the mother what was to do, and she said the child had been scalded. Her words were, "Willy bas pulled the kettle of boiling, water on my boy." • The boy did not say amything. He was crying. He, too, had been scalded on the arm. Whitening and oil were applied to the 1 wounds: The water had alighted on the deceased's shoal. demand run dowri his back.—The Deputy ;eoroner thought i he 3 jury would believe the boy William Carlin had stated f exactly what bad occarred. The lad himself was in some eanger. If the jury believed he struck his brotheren anger he was guilty of manslaughter. He thought, howevae what was done was done in fun, and death ensued from an i acCident.—The jury expressed themselves to the same i opinion, and returned a verdict of "Accidental death." • l

NEW ASSEMBLY Ham.—The first of a series of lectures was delivered by Mr. Wright. of Liverpool. on Monday evening, to a large audience of between 400 and 600. on 'A solemn testimony conoerning the second coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the signs of the times." Mineacturun BEHIBITION.—Oo Monday an attraction was afforded by a visit of E. FL Boatock's collection of wiloi beasts contained in a cavalcade drawn by elephants, dromedaries, dm., which entered the town in the afternoon and occupied a portion of the old Park grounds. They were liberally patronised daring their stay, and considerably enlivened the neighbourhood with their band.

The clothing, appointrnents,'and general bearing of the force, were considered satisfactory. Cana Comma? Dreettrne—On Monday a deputation of the Lancashire Miners' Federation, consisting of Messrs. Pickard. Woods, and Aspinwall waited on Mr. S. Davies, chairman of the directors of the Carr Colliery Company, and Mr. Edward Fidler, shareholder, with the object of coming to a mutual arrangement to settle the dispute. The proprietors offered the men work on the old conditions for threensontlas and change of check-weighman. The depute- time asked would they give day wages, and they answered • no. Afterwards, at a meeting of the men-at Prescot, the deputation put three questions to them, in consequence of charges made against John Pagan .by Mr. Fidler:--let, Were they content to work with the riddle? 2nd. Did, Felon prejudice them against the riddle or their employere 3rd, Would they return to work without their cheek-weigh- man being re-instated 2 An unanimous nemitive was re- turned to each question ; and the statement that Fegan had only dose his duty throughout was received with applause. A settlement appears, therefore, as far off as ever. BOARD OF Gueurnews.—The fortnightly meeting of, this Board was held on Tbursday, at the VVeiston Workhouse. Mr. John Leatherbarrow presided. The master reported that there were 399 inmates this week, against 409 last week, and 419 in the corresponding week of last year vagrants relieved 52, against 51 in the corresponding week last year. A letter was read from the Local Government Board en- closing a copy of the report made by Dr. Southey of his visit to the workhouse under an order of the Lunacy Corn. missloners. It stated that all the cases, with one exception, appeared to be proper cases for the workhouse.. Al! the patients appeared to be well cared for and kindly treated ; satisfactory. On on the whole the arrangements were highly sat On the recommendation of the commissioner, it was decided -to prepare a room for the reception of vi•lent lunatics. The clerk read a letter front the Town Clerk of Sr. Helens, en- closing a copy of a resolution of the Health Committee acreeing to receive pauper patients in the St. Helens Borough Infeetious Diseases Hospital, on payment by the guardians of Bs per day, such 'amount not to include to uneditine. Several guardians remarked that the earn was very heavy. Mr. Jackson said -that if a person could pay be was admitted in that institution on payment of is per day, but a poor pauper must be charged 6s per day. Mr. Hall moved that\ the matter be left In the hands of the clerk, and let •him make the best tams I-e contd. The Clerk (Mr. Hartley) said he must decline the responsibility. -It was a matter between the guardians and the Local Government Board, more than between the guardians and • the St; Helens Town Council. He thought the guardians ehould first consider whet er they had reasonably tried to make ,an arrangement with the Corporation, and if so in- struct slim to forward to the Local Government • Board a ropy of the resoletion of the St. Helens Corporation, and • tote that the guardians considered 6s per day an unusual - am. The reason a woman is continually looking in the glass is because she wants to see herself as others see her. Some people are born to ill-luck. An old woman who has pasted nearly 5,000 medical recipes into a book during the pest forty. years, has never been ill a day in her life, and she 18 growing discouraged. Discussion between a wise child and its tutor : " Tbist star you see up there is bigger than the world." "No, it isn't."' Yes, it is." " 'Elvin why don't it keep the rain off?" _ _

CABBAGEL—MOSt cottagers take a pride in producing an early sample of spring cabbages, and there, is a con- siderable amount of chuckling by those who happen to be Cutting in advance of their neighbours. Next to a favourable position there is nothing like plenty of feed- ing for hastening crops; We would' therefore urge upon the attention of cottagers the importance of deep dig- ging or trenching, and a liberal application of half- e- cayed manure. Ws prefer to dig it in reeking hot, to the'decayed cold Clammy substance which farmers de- vote so much labour in preparing by turning it over in , the yard or carting it and forming a heap in the corner of a field or some other convenient spot where most of its fertilising ingredients are washed out of it. Partially decayed manure applied during the operation of trench- I ing acts as temporary drainage, or till such time as its particles remain undecomposed. If digging only is prac- tised in the garden the soil will only be loosened to the depth of a foot, but by resorting to trenching a depth of three feet may be attained.' and at whatever depth we leave off a hardened pan is left. Now it is evident that for a limited period water will percolate the depth the spade. has gone, and if there are no drains it will pro- bably remain there during winter and spring, unless of course the sub--stratum is gravel or sand. Now water logged laud is considerably colder than that which is drained. This has been explained by Mr. Parkes in his "Essay on the Philosophy of Drainage." In draining the Red Moss, near Bolton-le-Moors, the thermometer in the drained land rose in -Dine, 1837, to 68 degrees at seven inches below the surface, while in the adjoining water-logged land it would never rise above 47 degrees. This fast will in a measure account for the starved and stuntediappearance of the vegetable and fruit crops in some of our cottage gardens. It cannot be a matter of surprise if a cabbage bed that has enjoyed four or five degrees, more heat for months than an adjoining one, should be two or three weeks in advance of its neigh- bour. Trenching alone if properly executed will do this. Land with clayey subsoil is a difficult and dangerous subject to deal with, and the inexperienced are apt to bring too much of that crude substance to the surface at a time. Not more than two inches of it or any kind ot subsoil should be introduced to the surface at one time, but the other should be stirred up to the depth of the spade or fork, and when the top spit of the next trench is,thrown on the top of it they become slightly mixed, so that when turned up again another two inches may be brought to the surface, and as trenching is not per- formed oftener than every four years the ground in that tine is dug several times over, and the two inches of . foreign matter becomes by then thoroughly incorporated with the ordinary soil of the garden. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Pansies and Violas have formed cuttings very tardily this season on' account of the dry weather, so that we have had some difficulty in procur- ing sufficient of them for stock. Old plants frequently die off in winter, so that it is of the utmost importance that we should have duplicates. They strike freely in a shady position, and a skeleton frame may be constructed to place over them to support the shading if a naturally sunless corner, is not to be had. Now that we have had more suitable weather for Pansy growth, the cuttings will improve daily, and should be taken off as soon as ready. Our cuttings of the old. double rocket were not very promising, so we took up some old plants and , divided them, securing as much root as possible to each ' piece. Other subjects that may now be increased from cuttings are the Variegated Arabis, Alyssum saxatile—h plant producing yellow flowers that are in great beauty during May and the summer months in this district (Preston), and probably in many other northern parts, but in the south its season is short. Penstemons and Phloxes of sorts will root freely now, though in case of the latter this may only be desirable where large; heads , of bloom are required for exhibition, as the plants are' ' quite hardy and rarely die off in winter. Penstemons are uncertain, and it is safest to put a few cuttings in annually. THE WlNDOW.—Pelargoniums, if outside are in danger of having too much water if not laid on their sides dur- ng, heavy rain. Those cut down in August will soon be fit for potting, and soil and pots must be got in readi- ness, and the former placed under cover, or it may be in II an unfit state when required for use. The Chinese and Fairy Roses are best turned outside for some portion of the season. If this has not been attended to, they should be seen to without delay in order that their wood may get thoroughly matured before the winter. There is too much anxiety to keep plants indoors in the sum- mer for the sake of an odd flower or two that they may have on them.

"How is Jim Bullard getting on ?" asked a stranger at the railroad station of a Dakota town. "Jim kermitted suicide 'bout a month ago," replied a native. "Committed suicide? How did he commit sui‘ide ?" "He called me a liar, stranger." "What on earth can that mean?" asked a friend of Thackeray, pointing to an inscription over a doorway, "Mutual Loan Office." "I thin% know," answered the novelist, unless it means that two men who have nothing agree to lend it to one another." It is said that some men never become irritated, but there
never was a masculine mortal who, while putting up picture

;ids, CO:4 be; in silence his wife's question, "-WitY didn't you hit the nail ?" This is one of the things which has been known to wreck households and fill the divorce courts. Too Mout Fos Has Fertint,—A short time ago a gentleman took his little eon on a railway excursion. The little fellow looked out Of the window, when the father slipped ihe hat off the boy's head. The latter was much , grieved at his supposed loss, when papa consoled him by saying that he would "Whistle it back." A little later he whistled and the hat reappeared. Not long after the little lad flung the hat out of the window, shouting : "Now, papa, whistle it back agaizi? " &roar of laughter served to enhance-the confusion of papa. PROPITIATING BOTH PARTIES—An old French peasant woman whom her parish priest found going into the village church one evening, with a wax taper in each hand, as if to make an offering, was asked : "For whom are those candles, my daughter ?" "This one, my father, is for St. Michael, the Prince of the Angels." "Good, my daughter; but for whom is h other ?" " The other, my father, is for the devil." "For the devil, my daughter ?" echoed the horri- fied ecclesiastic. "To be sure, my father," answered old Lisette, coolly, "it's just as well to have friends on both aid's" _ _

-- - John B. Gough tells the following story, though the joke Is at his own expense. Once, while on a lecturing tour through England, he was introduced to a small village audience in these terms: "Ladies and gentlemen, I 'ave the 'onour to introduce to, you the distinguished lecturer, Mr. John B. Gough, who will haddress us on the subject of tem- perance. You know that temperance is thought to be a very dry subject; but to-night, as we listen to our friend, the hoarator, from the hocean, we 'ope to 'awe the miracle of Samson repeated, and to be refreshed with water from the jawbone of an hass."

SHE Strom OFF.—A quack who in his perambulations around the country was always accompanied by a negro carrying a trombone with which to attract the people and draw them around his employer, was pelted one night, and from" Hobson's choice" was constrained to choose for the night's resting place a barn. There they had barely bes- towed themselves on the top of the straw-pile when an old woman entered and commenced to sweep and clear a portion of the place. Succeeding her came an old man, who first brought a number of chairs and forms and afterwards an empty barrel. Presently a number of people entered and seated themselves, and finally there came one w 4 mounted the barrel. Then the quack and his companion perceived that th ir lodging place was for the nonce the place of wor- shm for some small sect of dissenters. A hymn was duly sung, a prayer offered, and a chapter real, and then the preacher gave out his text, "Blow ye the trumpet in Zion." At the first announcement Sambo nudged his partner, and asked him in a uhisper, "Does he mean me?" When the text was repeated Samba gave another nudge, and whis- pered, "I don't like to, but if he asks again 11l try what I can do on the old trombone." Once more the words were uttered, "Blow ye the trumpet in Zion," and before the preacher had finished Sambo's trombene rang out loud and long. It's effect was striking. The preacher was the first to run, and the flock quickly followed. In the stampede a hobbling old woman was knocked down, and Sambo seeing her predicament, scrembled from the straw-pile and hurried to her assistance. When he reached her, and attempted to help her, she looked up with a frightened face, and said, "0, pray. Mr. Devil, don't take me, I don't come here repi- ne—Chicago World: COURTING A Winow.—There is any amount of fun in courting a, young girl who has not become used to it. She swallows all the soft things a fellow says, but when it comes to popping the question. or something of that kind, she gets frightened, more or less, and wants time to consider, until there are enough loopholes for her lover to slip out without the least bit of trouble, if he happens to see someone he could love a shade or two better. Young girls are timid and shy in earnest, and if the fellow is slot pretty certain that he has found precisely the, angel he is looking for, he can manage so as to have the refusal of her for a year or roore, and at the same time manage to keep his neck out of a breach of promise suit, when he happens to meet some other sweet-faced angel that seems to him to be better suited to his tastes. It is different with a widow. She gets rid of all her shyness at the earliest convenient opportunity, and finds out the principal things she desires to know of him before she allows him to become acquainted. The schoolgirl of 16 trusts herself to a fine young fellow on sixty or ninety days' sight without security, but the widow, like a thrifty whole- sale house, goes out and examines the mercantile reports concerning him, and then sells to him on her own terms for cash. She has him sized IID before he comes to market, and when she looks as if she were a very artless creature and fights shy of him, whenever be happens to sit a little close to her on the sofa, there are ten chances to one that he will never look any further, but will buckle right up to her, and put the question fairly and squarely, and when he has done so she is not going to tremble all over and blush, and ask for a week or a month in which to make up her mind. She will just wind her arms around his neck, and look up into his face with one of Ella Wheeler's fiery yearns, and before he has had time to catch his breath, he will find himself nailed to the cross with a " yes" that pierces him to his very soul. "Where were you born, little girl?" asked a philan- thropist of a street beggar. "I'm not sure, sir," was the reply; "but I've often heard ma say that I was born in poverty." A jubilant voter wrote two letters immediately after the return of his candidate at a late election—one to his son, consisting of a single word, "Hurrah!" and the other a few sentences of condolence to a dear friend who had lost his wife. In his excitement he mixed the envelopes, and the result can be imagMed when the bereaved widower received the wrong letter. Those who are compelled to hire house help will ap- predate the following advertisement, clipped from an Omaha paper:—" A lady wants a first rate tip-top, No. 1, girl, to do house work ; Must thoroughly understand cooking, washing, and ironing. Wages, five dollars per week. All the piano-playing, fine needlework, visiting, and entertaining company will be done bylthe lady of the house." "This looks very nice indeed," remarked Mr. Fitz joy to his better half, as he Uncovered the breakfast dish. "What is it? "This ii the new cook's specialty. Tripe. smothered in crumbs of bread." "Well, I shoulclsay so," as he made an unsuccessful attempt to cut it. "Its mighty tough." "I don't see. The cook has a diploma. She ought to be a good one." "Oh, that accounts for it. She's fried.the diploma." Two Ilighlandmen, being in Glasgow for the first time, were having a walk through the city. Turning a corner, they were much surprised to see a water-cart wetting the,street. Not having seen anything of the kind before, Tougal, under a mistaken idea, ran after the cart and cried out to the driver, "Hey, man—hey, man, you're losin' a' yer water!" His friend, annoyed at Tougal's want of knowledge, ran after him, caught him by the arm, and said rather testily, "Tougal, man Tougal, don't be showin' your ignorance; div you'll no see it's to keep the laddies aff the back o' the cant ?" "Dauvid," a Scotch character, had a big mouth, orna- mented with a big tooth in front. Some of his friends wished him to have it removed, but he would not listen to them. He maintained that Providence had some pur- pose in putting it there, so it did not become him to frustrate that purpose. One day at a public dinner, a maiden lady of uncertain age and appearance, quizzed him about his being a bachelor. With the bluntness of those days she said at last, "If it wert not for that tooth I trtight take ye myself." Looking in his quaint way at he; he quietly replied, "Providence likely put it there, then, to save me from that fate." "I intended to tell Jane to bring a fresh bucket of water," said the wife of Prof. Nottlehead, looking up from her sewing. "You doubtless mean a bucket of fresh w rejoined her husband. "I wish you would paysomater' elA'tle attention to rhetoric; your mistakes are embarrassing!' A few moments later the Professor said, My dear, that picture would show to better advantage if you were to hang it over the clock." "Ali !" she re- phed, "you doubtless mean if I were to hang it above the clock. If I were to hang it over the clock we couldn't tell what time it is. I wish you would pay some little attention to rhetoric; your mistakes are embarrassing." ELECTRIC HOUSE BELLS

div.head: OCR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OCR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON', THURSDAY. Mr. Chamberlain has kept the ,political ball vigorously rolling during the week. His tour through Scotland is in respect of the popular enthu- siasm evinced paralleled only by Mr. Gladstone's triumphal procession. Mr. Chamberlain went North avowedly to kindle that enthusiasm without which, lie justly observes, the battle of the General Eleo- tion may be in danger. He has certainly succeeded in his object. Not only at the various public meet- ingorhe has addressed has the multitude risen at him, but all along the line crowds have gathered to cheer bum on his way. Sir William Harcourt has doubt- less been grimly watching this proceeding. Prior to the last General Election, Mr. Chamberlain, though a prominent figure, had not assumed the commanding attitude from which he now addresses the nation. It was Sir William Harcourt, after Mr. Gladstone, who was the great Liberal platform champion. Sir William will presently issue from his retirement. But he will find it difficult to excel the excitement or the measure of public attention Mr. Chamberlain has created. ' Mr. Chamberlain has within the last two years • very considerably improved as a public speaker. Unlike Sir Charles Dilke, whose improvement upon another line is also noteworthy, he began public life as a platform speaker. It was either as chair- man or as the mover of resolutions on Birmingham platforms that he first learned to command the at- tention and the passions of a crowd. The first time I heard him speak was during the visit of the Prince of Wales to Birmingham, at which time Mr. Chamberlain was mayor and his reputation only lust beginning to emerge beyond the local circle. I was then much struck with the incisive force of his oratory. He was above all things eminently clear, knew what he had at heart to say, and was capable of saying it in a manner that left his mean- ing unmistakeable. But it was eloquence more Un- adorned than Mr. Cobden's. A plain business man talking to his townsmen Mr. Chamberlain essayed' no flights into fancy. There was no trace through- out his speeches of this epoch that he 'had ever read , a book. It will be observed that of late. more particu- larly within thelast twelve months, he has laid him- self out to adorn his oratory with literary references and illustrations drawn from both prose writers and poets. He read up his Burns on the way to Scot- land, and delighted the Glasgow people with an apt quotation. In fact, in his speech at Glasgow he "dropped into poetry" with a frequency that Mr. Silas Wegg, in his most liberal moments, did not exceed. One of the London morning papers, in re- porting the speech, evidently growing a little tired of the repeated introduction of verse, gave a comic effect to the passionate outburst of verse with which Mr. Chamberlain elosed his speech by print- ing it as if it were prose. Mr. Chamberlain is even more happy in his introduction of little anecdotes, which, cleverly dealt with and boldly pointed, are always effective with a crowded audience. Sir Henry Wolff is still enjoying himself at Con- stantinople, a most pleasant place to live in just I now. He occasionally has an interview with the Sultan. But it is admitted that things "get no forrader." That is, however, of the less moment as, it was never seriously intended or hoped that they should. A pleasant occupation has been found fo. a member of the Fourth Party, otherwise unpia- vided for, and so long as Sir Henry does no harni no one will seriously complain of his little outing. It will cost certain sums of money. But vae victie. In English politics the Conservative victor has always claimed the spoils, and Sir' Henry Wolff, a cheery gentleman who likes to make himself comfortable, is taking his share. There is one little episode in his mission which completes its incongruity. The other day the telegraph wires flashed across an awed continent the fact that Sir Henry Wolff had been kept waiting for an hour for an audience with the Sultan, whilst the Russian Minister engaged the attention of His Imperial Majesty During this in- terval of waiting, Sir Henry had time to recall a i little incident that happened n the House of Com- mons early in the month of July. Negotiations were then going forward in St. Petersburg in respect of the Afghan frontier. Sir Edward Thornton, call- ing upon the Russian Minister, was kept waiting for twenty minutes, whilst his Excellency des- patched some business on hand. I remember as if it were but yesterday how Sir Henry Wolff bounded up from his seat below the gangway, and, supported by stentorian cheers from Lord Randolph Churchill, asked Lord E. Fitzmaurice whether this report were true, going on, amid vociferous cheering from the Conservative side, to hint that an insult of this char- acter would, except by a Government of poltroons, be promptly resented. I wonder if Sir Henry thought of this as he kicked his heels in the trite- room of the chamber of his most potent Majesty the Sultan? People are sick to death of the Armstrong case, with its sordid circumstances and its tainted at, mosphere. The reading through the evidence, counsels' question, and witnesses' answer given ver- batim, is like sitting in a cellar in company with a draggletail woman who smells of gin, and a blear- eyed master sweep temporarily exhausted with the effort of beating his wife. Yet the London papers publish it all, not omitting a single turn of inteiro- gation or a minute inflection of reply. The worst of it is that, as far as dramatic interest is concerned, it all leads to nothing. You may wade through column after column of the tedious talk, and are no nearer the heart of the case than after reading Mr. Poland's statement. The whole case, so far as the defence have been able to control it, turns upon the 'question whether Mrs. Armstrong did or did not know the purpose for which her child was engaged. But whether she did or did not will not affect the position of the defendants in the eye of the law. •'There is no attempt to deny the spiriting away of Eliza Armstrong, the examination to which , she was subjected, her visit to a brothel, and her subsequent removal to France. This is the charge against Mr. Stead and his co-workers, and, as it is not denied, and as the law provides certain punish- ment for this kind of thing, it will be seen that the defendants are in a perilous position. London continues empty in the sense that the West End houses flaunt their yellowblinds or guard their windows by manifold sheets of newspaper. Society is just now "at home" in the country or in the fashionable resorts of the continent. The Queen• I is at Balmoral where she has had the advantage of ' the quiet and genial company of Lord Iddesleigh, the minister-in-waiting. Lord Salisbury is at his chateau near Boulogne. Lord Randolph Churchill is fishing in Loch Houle, the guest of Lord Wim- borne. lir. Bright is also fishing at present in the river Cree, but meaning to visit the Tay and the Tweed. The Duke of Argyll is entertaining a large party at Inverary Castle, and Lord St. Oswald, bet- ter known as Mr. Rowland Winn, has this week had Nostell priory filled with a party for the Don- caster week. Mr. Sykes, at Brantingham Thorpe, has also had a party for the race week, his guests inclueing the Marquis of Hartington, whose pre- Bence would not compensate the courtly Chris- topher for the absence of the Prince of Wales. There are great improvements projected in Cler- kenwell. It is one of the poorest districts in cen- tral London, being almost exclusively inhabited by artisans and workmen. The improvements are to be for their behoof. A building which has many associations, and none of them pleasant, is to be • pulled down. We shall soon see the last of the Clerkenwell House of Detention. It has stood for a hundred and ten years, having replaced another prison built on the same site more than a century earlier. The old prison was the more interesting of the two, so far as its inmates contributed to its in- • terest. Jack Sheppard was one of them. They show you still at the prison the fetters he wore and the mark of the file with which the great highway- man freed himself from their grasp. The present building has no such historic romances, but one in- terest clings to its shadowed walls. Here it was that John Howard, the philanthropist, found some of the most disgraceful abuses which he resolutely • battled with and overthrew. The removal of the building is itself a step in the march of philan- thropy. On its site will be erected a whole series of model lodging houses to be occupied by the • working classes of the district. No improvement could be more practical or more beneficient. We , want to get rid of the prison and we want to house •- the poor. The operation will cost a great deal; .but the money will be well and profitably in- vested.

The unfortunate strike at the Elswick Ordnance and Es- gineering Works has practically terminated. At a meeting ci directors and representatives of the mew a series of Proposals for establishing a "council of conciliation" was adopted. ALARMING COLLIERY ACCIDENT.—An accident of a very alarming nature occurred at the Ottswell Colliery. Ilkeston, On Thursday. The winding engise "ran away," and the Cage. was thrown on to the head gear with such force as to partially destroy it. There were 3to men and boys in the mine at the time, and the only means of rescuing them was to utdtse. the furnace shaft. After several hours the whole Of the mine S were safely brought to the bank, before the partial stoppage of ventilation caused by the extinction of the furnaco had any serious effects.

div.head: XettetO to the gditor.
div.p: XettetO to the gditor.

STREET IMPROVEMENTS IN WARRINGTON. Sir,—Some twelve months ago you favoured me with space in your valuable paper to make what I considered a just and reasonable complaint. The condition (at that time) of White-street was indeed disgraceful—and still remains se—and why a street complete in every sense, so far as buildings are concerned, should lie unfinished and in wet weather ankle deep in mud is a problem let our worthy borough surveyor to solve. True, a measurement has been taken and the usual advice note sent to the tenants, but fer twelve months this is all the activity which has been dis- played. Surely the inhabitants of this neighbourhood are entitled to better attention. How many MOTO years, I won- der, have they to wait before being allowed to enjoy ordin• ary comforts for which they have to pay—for our author- ities are not at all backward in their application for rates. ; Trusting, Mr. Editor, that it will be unnecessary for me ; to again implore your aid on behalf of the inhabitants of . the abo'veneighbourhood,—l remaim, yours faithfully, TOM TIT.

SIR GILBERT GREENALL. Sir,—l am informed that Sir Gilbert Greenall is now eighty years old. lam also told that when he was last in Parliament, via., 1874 to 1880, he was hardly ever at his post in the House of Commons after nine o'clock at night, except upon a few special occasions when an urgent" whip" commanded his vote in the interest of his party. As every- body knows, the real business of the House of Commons was then and is now, done very largely after the time when Sir Gilbert knew that it was necessary in the interest of his health that he should be at home and in bed. Sir Gilbert was many years younger then than he is now, although, ac- ' cording to his own professions, be feels so young now, that many of his friends consider that he has attained to his second childhood. Can anybody tell me what credit or ad- vantage it would be to this borough to send to Parliament a man who has long since passed the allotted space of human life, and whose mental as well as physical faculties can hardly be expected to be equal to the strain of Parliamen- tarY life? This is a common sense question, to which, I believe, a common sense answer will be given in Novem- ber next.—Your, &c., A NEW ELECTOR.

REPRESSION VERSUS FREE TRADE IN LIQUOR. Sir,—lt is very much the fashion just now to quote the political economists. When some reformer, Mr. Chamber- lain for instance, ventures to suggest an amelioration in the condition of the poor, he is lectured from a hundred platforms for wanting to violate some of the so-called laws of nature " which certain writers who call themselves poli- tical economists have been pleased to lay down. Seeing that the economists Save become such authorities, it might not be out of place at the present time, when the public-house question is again being thrashed out, to give the opinicn of the greatast of the economists, Ada.o Smith. relating to the drink traffic. Referring to the wine trade Dr. Smith says : —" It is a losing trade, it is said, which a workman carries on with the ale-house. I answer that the trade a th the ale-house is not necessarily a losing trade. In its own nature it is just as advantageous as any other, Oiough per- haps more liable to be abused. The employments of the brewer and even of the retailer of ferment-d liquors are as necessary divisions of labour as any other. It deserves to be remarked, too, that if we consult experience cheap- ness of wine seems to be a cause not of drunkenness, but of sobriety. The inhabitants of the wine countries are in general the soberest people in Europe. People are seldom guilty of excess in what is their daily fare. Nobody affects the character of liberality and goon fellowship by being pro- fuse of a liquor which is as cheap as small be Were the duties upon foreign wines and the excises upon malt beer and ale to be taken away at once it might occasion in Great Britain a pretty general and temporary drunkenness among the middling and inferior ranks of people, which , would probably soon be follower' by a permantst and almost universal sobriety." In this brief extract we have ex- pressed the opinion of one of the keenest of observers and deepest of thinkers, a DM who based his convictions on the , sure foundation of experience and reason, and who was c,,r- -• tainly not addicted to extravagance or fanaticism of any , kind. Would it be too presumptions to insinuate that those who are so zealous, and unquestionably sincere in their zeal, to put down intemperance might learn a lesson from Adam Smith, a writer from whom the world has already learned so much. We all know how true it is in poli- tics that "force is no remedy," and every passing year brings its evidence that the remedy for intemperance is not to be found in intolerant repression. Ills getting very clear • that the old philosopher had a deeper insight into human motives than your modern teetotaller. JAQUES.

FEMALE DRUNKENNESS IN WARRINGTON, Sir,—Leaving the strictures of various correspondents upon the remarks made by me at the annual Licensing Session to the judgment of the public—though a charge of inconsistency ought not to have bees brought against ale on the ground of my having applied for a fresh licence, wben'your report shows that what I did apply for was the transfer of the existing Pelican licence to a new and com- modious inn, to be built at a cost of £2,500, informing the Bench at the same time that it would cause the discontinu- ance of three existing off -licencea—l desire to add a few words to what has been said on this important subject. The ques- tion at issue is this, Is Warrington so full of drinking wo- men as to deserve to be held up to public opprobrium as a place notorious for female drunkenness? A friend ot mine told me last Saturday that having to consult a Liverpool doctor, he was asked if Warrington was not, judging from what had lately appeared in the newspapere, a fearful place to live in. For those who are proud of their native town such things are not pleasant to hear. If ths statements be true, the fact is most disheartening after the efforts, reli- gious and educational, of the last 30 years. Few or no new public-house licences, except, perhaps, to the new railway station, have been granted by our Bench during that period, and, therefore, other causes muet be sought for the alleged ' demoralization of our female population. I wish, if possible, ,land so far as I can gather, there is a general feeling to the same effect, to have the accusation either proved or dis- proved; and as a practical course I venture to sugg,st that the magistrates should hold a meeting, and by examination of their officers, by communications with neighbouring towns, and in other ways, investigate the charge, both for the sake of the present and the coming generation. Hardly any subject can be of greater importance, and if it is found that there is a prima facie case, we must I- aye a public in- quiry, probe the plague spot, and end 'your to find a remedy. It will not be right to fold our arms in apathetic despair, and allow the evil to go on unchecked. If money is required for such an inquiry, I am prepared to contribute, and doubtless many who have the cause of temperance and the welfare of the town at heart will assist, Should the present discussion be the means of enabling someone to suggest how the drunkards, male or female, many or few, cam be gradually reached, and show that the miserable homes which exist amongst us can be made brighter and happier, it will not have taken place in vain.—Yours, ROBERT DAVIES. • September, 1885.

THE ANTIATACCINATORS' FIASCO. Sir,-1 notice in your last issue a letter under the above heading, and purporting to be the effusion of an anti-vacci- nator, and I should feel obliged by the favour of a little space for a reply. In the first place, let me say there is a clear attempt of a wolf to assume the garb of the meek and lowly sheep. The writer of the letter referred to is not what he would have us believe, viz., an anti-vaccinator, and I advise him to make no further attempt to sail under false colours, which can only discredit him. With regard to his covert sneers at the character of the "demonstration " on the day of the sale, and which he styles a failure, miserable, and discouraging, I miy siy— though that is possibly as he would have wished it to turn out—when the attendant circumstances are considered, which in all fairness ought to be done, the demonstration I was fairly successful, and to the anti-vaccinators anything but discouraging. Just consider, sir, that very few perscns indeed knew of the day of sale until announced by the bell- man, just 1 hours previous to its taking place, thus pre- venting any reasonable attempt to publish it. Again, that the sale took place on the Friday afternoon—our local pay and market day—and most inconvenient for either workmen or tradespeople to attend ; for you must be aware, sir, we are not all overseers and clerks who can at any moment rush from our desks for a few hours, and our salaries not be affected thereby. Also, that the goods were conveyed to Newton for sale, over one mile from whence they were taken. Further, the day was remarkable for heavy thunderstorms and showers, when many who migbt otherwise have been able to attend, would not venture so far from home and risk getting a rood soaking ; and also that the friends with the banner started for the salubrious atmosphere of Newton within half an hour after the bellman had announced the sale. It is no wonder, therefore, considering these circuin- stances, that comparatively few followed the banner. How- ever, as it was, a number came later, and at the sale there were over 100 persons present, at least twe-thirds of these being. well-knewn Anti-Vaccinators. Had the services of the Warrington Union Band been se- cured, there is no doubt that things would be more success- ful than they were. Your correspondent says the auctioneer was more than a match for his " persecutors." I cannot see that—be only did just what was expected ; and I may add that in my opinion he seemed well qualified for carrying out such a questionable business; he had quite a number of new, original, and elaborate items in his conditions of sale, showing that someone had been puzzling their brains not a little.

As the Anti-Vaccinators went to Newton fully prepared not only to see the goods sold, but to buy them in again, it Is simply childish to talk of either defeat or discomfiture In this direction. With respect to the projected public meet- ing in the evening, when there were only about 18 persons present, the fact of its being Friday night and the meeting unannounced, except verbally, though not positively, at thl' sale, and, as your report of the meeting states, the weather extremely wet, will fully explain to any reasonible being why the attendance was not larger.. I cannot now deal with the reference to the supposed 400 or 600 Anti-Vaccina- tors ; I think it is fairly understood, and when the time comes they are prepared to exercise their power and in- fluence to the utmost to show the absurdity, and bring about the repeal of (at least) the compulsory clauses of the ob- noxious and tyrannical Vaccination Acts. There will be an opportunity in a week or so of seeing whether there are not a few more Anti-Vaccinators in this neighbourhood than those who were able to make their ap. pearance at the sale.—l am, sir, yours most respectfully. AriTl-VAC.
Earlestown, 16th September, 1885.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 19, 1885. LATEST NEWS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 19, 1885. LATEST NEWS.

TORYISM AND FREEDOM. Sir,—l have been much interested in a correspondence that has been going on in one of your contemporaries. The subject relates to the freedom, or otherwise, of the employes of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and residing at Crewe. It is to me peculiarly significant that the directors of nearly all our railways are chiefly Tones. Why this is so is soon explained, and should, I think, be a strong reason why working-men should refrain from sup- porting anything in the shape of vested interests. Tiae late Government tried hard to carry into law two measures that especially struck at "vested interests," and were calculated to benefit trade, and save human life. I refer to Mr. Chamberlain's efforts to limit the privilege of railway direc- tors, and bring them within the control of the Board of Trade, and to the same gentleman's untiring energy in try- ing to carry a Merchant Shipping Bill. The Government failed to carry these measures, and why ? Simply because the Opposition brought to bear was of such a colossal char- acter that it bad to bend or break.. I need not now go into the merits of the two measures referred to. It is sufficient to know that they aroused a strong feeling of opposition in the minds of railway directors and ship-owners, and a strong determination on the part of these patriotic gentlemen to do all that lay in their power to keep out of office men who be- lieved in "human rights." To accomplish this the screw is pat on, and the workmen at Crewe are given to under- stand that they ," must all pull together "to place the Tory candidate at the head of the poll. One writer says :—"No man occupying any position under the railway company dared openly associate with the Liberal candidates and work on Liberal committees." Sir, I submit that this is not politics, and the working-man who is blinded by it is something of a fool. It is an attempt to make the general interests minister to the selfieh and grasp- ing instincts of railway capitalists. Why should working-men help such unprincipled candi- dates into power? Surely they know that men like Mr. Stephen, the candidate for the Crewe Division of Cheshire, will take no step towards reducing railway freights, or plac- ing the railway system more in harmony with British trade. On the other band, Mr. Latham is, judging by the speech I recently heard him give, brimful of that progressive spirit that would preserve the best interests of the nation, and ' that would make etch part of our commercial system work in harmony with the rest. I read:—"Mr. Latham openly challenged Mr. Stephen, the Tory candidate for the Crewe Division, that if he did not mean to fight unfairly to let it be known from the Board of Directors that the railway em- ployee might vote and work as they liked, and as their con- viction.; dictated." Mr. Stephens has never replied to this challenge, but has purposely avoided it. The more one sees of the ways of Toryism, and the more one gets disgusted at the mean, underhanded shifts to which it will resort. There cannot be a doubt of one thing, that there is not a Tory working-man in this:England of ours, net one, call- ing himself a Tory, dare coma forward and place on record the reasons why he will support a Tory candidate at the next election. When I heard Mr. Chamberlain refer, in his grand speech, to freedom of contract, I was reminded of a speech delivered in Warrington by Sir G. Greenall. Speaking at the open. ing of the Conservative bowling green, Sir Gilbert said : " What he would say to the farmers present was, don't attend to other people. They were quite capable of judging for themselves and going to their landlords for anything they wanted; and he was sure that their landlord and themselves could settle any business they might have with- out the interference of any outside people." This, if true, ' would prove the possibility of freedom of contract, but in the same paper containing this report I read : "A number of Cheshire farmers have sent memorials, through the various farmers' clubs, to the county landlords appealing for reduction of rents, on the ground that the decreased value of agricultural prodncts warrants complete revision of rents. The result of the application has been wholly un- satisfactory, some four landlords only even condescending to reply." Also the following words to which I draw the special attention of Tory Trade Unionists:—" The four replies were to the effect that proper consideration would be given to tiny personal memorials from the tenantry only." Trade Unionists will know the meaning of this Tory squires refuse the right to unite with the tenant farmers. So we see what Freedom of Contract means to the Tories. At the Crewe works the Tory director puts the screw on in such a fashion that the workman is compelled to take one or two courses; either he must submit to stultify all his political aspirations, or he must be prepared to face the streets, break UD his home and see his family reduced to want. The farmer must, single-hauled, be prepared to meet and argue with his landlord questions that in nine cases out of ten he knows before-hand will go against him, might, not right, nearly always ruling the squire's verdict. The Tory has reduced to a science his methods for control- ling the political actions of those who are his servants. September 15, 1885. CLIFFORD DIX.

The doctors last evening consider Mr. Forsteee condi- tion to be on the whole satisfactory. A Royal proclamation directs the militia called eat /est spring to be forthwith disembodied. George .fohnson, a grocer, returning borne from Lyric, jumped from a train as it was passing through East Winch station, on the Great Eastern Railway, and received such terrible injuries that he died sbort.y afterwards. The Central News learns that notification has been given to the respective owners of the vessels fitted as armed cruisers that her Majesty's Government will not require them on the termination of their present charters. WRECK' OP A HARTLEPOOL STEAMER.—A Lloyd's tele- gram from Alexandria on Friday states that the steamer Lady Frances, of Hartlepool, was totally wrecked last Fri- day, 170 miles west of Alexandria. Eight men were saved, but one was drowned in landing. Two boats with the cap- tain and nine men are missing, and the British Consulate is sending a steam tug in search. The Lady Frances was bound from Shields for Alexandria. A BEDRIDDEN WOMAN BPENT TO DEATIL—On Friday, an old woman, named Sarah Cole, was found roasted alive In a house in Workhouse Lane, Tipton. The old woman was dropsical, and, owing to her not being able to get up- stairs, a bed was made for her in the kitchen. On Friday morning she was round dead, her body presenting a shock- ing appearance through being burnt to a cinder. The bed was also destroyed. It is supposed that the bed clothing became ignited by the kitchen are.

div.head: OLDHAM STRIKE.
div.p: THE OLDHAM STRIKE.

The ballot of cotton operatives on the question of pro. posing to the employers an unconditional five per cent. reduction in wages took place on Friday. The result is three to one against *ccepting any reduction.

div.head: RAILWAY ACCIDENT.-THREE MEN KILLED.
div.p: RAILWAY ACCIDENT.-THREE MEN KILLED.

On Friday morning an accident occurred on the loop line of the Eastern and Midland Railway, now in course of construction at Saddlebow, sear Lynn, whereby three men lost their lives. A ballast train was being pushed down an incline when the engine coupling broke and some ten or 12 trucks broke away at a fearful speed. About 40 men were riding in the tracks, but most of them jumped off safely, but several remained urvtil the edge of the bank was reached. Of these, three men, John Long, R. Sparks, and John Laws were thrown off as the waggons overturned, and were buried beneath the ballast and killed. Other two men, Robert Smith and William Chamberlain, were badly injured.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE'S MANIFESTO.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE'S MANIFESTO.

Mr. Gladstone issued on Thursday an address to the eleo tors of Midlothian, in which he 'submits ' himself for- re-election. The right hon. gentleman glances briefly at the labours which his Government was called on to perform at home and abroad. He reiterates his desire to see the British troops withdrawn from Egypt at the earliest moment consistent with honour. He admits that the late Government made errors, and serious errors, too, with cost of blood and treasure, in Egypt, but he lays the responsibility for our intervention at the door of the Beaconsfield Cabinet, which concluded an agreement with France by which we were bound to oppose Arabi. With respect to the Afghan and Russian controversies, Mr. Gladstone commends a policy of prudent preparation. On domestic topics be urges the neces- sity of reform in the methods of local government, co that the balance of taxation may be rectified and the liquor question settled. He advocites such changes in the land laws swill give freedom of bequest and transfer and registration, and ensure the equitable taxation of land during life and at death. He impresses on the Liberal party the vital necessity of unity and comprehensiveness. He presses upon the country the need of reforming procedure in the House of Commons. He reserves his final judgment on the subject of free primary eduCation and the severance of Church and State. The condition of the House of Lords is such as to justify im- portant changes. If the country should demand the sever- ance of the Church from the State, he believes the Church will be found equal to all the needs of the occasion. Refer- ring to Ireland, he says that the claims of that c•untry should be discussed without reference to the prejudices of the last few years. He urges that the first duty of states- men is to maintain the authority of the Crown and the supremacy of the law. He hopes that the political genius of this country will be found equal to the solution of the problem without the heavy drawback of embittered civil strife.
COLLISION IN THE CHANNEL-A STEAMER SUNK WITH LOSS OF MANY LIVES.

The screw steamer Brenda, of VVest Hartlepool, from Bussorah for London, arrived off Dover on Friday morn- ing with bows smashed in, having been in collision with a steamer believed to be the Dolphin, of London, and bound to Havre. Later telegrams from Deal state that the 'steamer sunk by collision in the Downs is the General Steam Navigation Company's boat Dolphin, bound from London to Havre. A portion of the crew and passengers were landed at Kings. down by the lifeboat, and the captain proceeded to London by train:,

The Press Association Ramsgate correspondent tele- graphs :—At about one o'clock on Flidav morning, when between Ramsgate and Deal, the General Steam Naviga- tion Company's paddle steamer Dolphin' 404 registered tonnage, bound from London to Havre with general cargo and passengers, was run into on her starboard side near the stern, her side being stove in. Thinking the damage was above water line, the captain made for Dover, but one of the passengers named John Phillips, commercial traveller, of 11, High-street, Marylebone, who occupied a berth close to where the collision occurred, found that the water was bubbling up through the floor of the saloon. He at once rushed on deck and informed the captain, whereupon an at- tempt was made to get out the boats, but they were fastened rather too securely, and could not be cut away as soon as desired. After a brief delay, however, one boat was launched and was immediately filled with men, altheugh five women were on board. An attempt was made to get out other boats, bat as the vessel was fast settling down, Mr. Phillips secured a life-buoy and on proceeding towards the stern was carried under water. He clang, however, to the buoy, and on coming to the sur- face clutched a raft seat which had floated off the deck. He then drifted towards the South Foreland and, after be- ing in the Bea for three hours and a half, he was picked up by a Hastings smack, the crew of which had hoard his cries for help. When taken on board he expressed his opinion that he conld not have held out another quarter of an hoar. He was very cold about the loins, hut the upper part of his body had not suffered so much. He was very kindly treated on the smack, cud soon recovered. Thirteen of the passen- gers and crew have been landed at Kingsdown. 1 A Lloyd's telegram from Kingsdown says 'the Dolphin was sunk between Weimer' Castle and Kingsdown, in seven fathoms of water. Twenty-eight passengers and crew have been saved and landed at Kingsdows, but there are several missing.

div.head: CHOLERA IN FRANCE.
div.p: THE CHOLERA IN FRANCE.

TODLON, FRIDAY, 10 35 A.m.—Three deaths from cholera in the suburbs have been registered since last night. The general sanitary condition of the tqwn is, however, greatly improving. The suddenly fatal cases occurred yesterday have created a strong impression.

SIR W. HARCOURT AT hormonTß.—Speaking at Ply- mouth, on Thursday night, Sir William Harcourt said he agreed with Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain in opposing the separatist demands of Mr. Parnell. He did not wish to embarass the Government, but he must say that Sir H. D. Wolff's mission to Constantinople up to the pre- sent had failed. Adverting to home affairs, he said the Go. vernment had no home policy, their object simply being to oppose domestic reforms. The new Parliament, however, would have to deal with the land question and provide free education, and Mr. Gladstone was the only possible leader who could give effect to those reforms. WWII ORDEft TIII2OIIMI JELLOUSY.-At the Central Criminal Court, oo Thursday, before Jnatice Hawkins, Henry Norman, 45, painter, was indicted for wife murder. It was alleged that prisoner was jealous of the landlord of the house in which he and the deceased lived, and that he had told his mother the deceased bad been unfaithfu.l, that he had forgiven her two or three times, and that he could not do so again. Next night deceased WAS found dead in bed, stabbed through the heart with a knife. The prisoner, after committing the act, proceeded at once to the police station and gave himself up. The jury, without leaving the box; found him guilty, and he was sentenced to death. . .

Suocirwo Ass,kuvr UPON A Gult.—At the Town Hall, St. Helens. on Monday, before Major R. Pilkington and Aklerman J. Mcgrycle, Joseph Williams' an aged married man, and a greengrocer residing at 77, Raglan-street, Enolee- ton, was charged with attempting to Indecently assault Ann Gdashan, 12 years of age, residing with her parents, at 102, Lyon street.—Mr., ff. L. Riley appeared for the prisoner. —After Superintendent Johnston had stated the case, the prosecntrix wan called. She said that about a quarter to nine o'clock on Saturday night she was talking with another girl near the prisoner's shop. When the other girl left the prisoner opened the door and called to her (prosecutrix). She went into the shop, and he gave her two pennies. He shut the door and took her through the house into the yard, where he behaved indecently towards her. While he was so engaged the shop bell rang, and he left her. As he was go- ing the prisoner said she bad to remain in the yard till he came back. When be returned be again acted improperly, —ln cross-examination by Mr. Riley, prosecutrix said she could give no reason why she did not shout or scream,— 'James Stirrup, a bottle hand, stated that on Saturday night, while be wis standing at his own door, which was opposite Williams's premises, he saw the little girl go into the shop. I lie saw the prisoner give her something out of the window, and then behave improperly to hers—Mrs. Stirrup, the wits of last witness, stated that the girl Galashal told her wbat had happened, and she told the girl's patents.—Prisoner wits committed for trial at the sessions,
