div.head: SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.

About eleven o'clock yesterday morning an accident oc- curred at the Camden Soap Works, Runcorn, by which two men narrowly escaped a violent death. Thomas Booth, of Church-street, John Evans, of New Egerton-street, and Samuel Prince, of Higher Runcorn, were engaged in repair ing a vitriol chamber, and for this purpose had erected a scaffold composed of planks. From 800 unknown cause part of the scaffold gave way. Evana was precipitated to the ground, a distanee of 30 feet, and dislocated his left elbow. He had also contusions on various parts of the body, and sustained a severe shock to the system. Booth was more fortunate He alighted en an intermedi- ate stage, only seven feet below the other,. and beyond a contused wooed on the tread and one or two other bruises, not of a dangerous character, he sustained no injury. Trince was mr the top of the chamber, and he therefore did not fall, but his nerves were so deranged by the sight that he had to be conveyed home in a cab along with the other man. At the works the men were attended to by Mr. Anslow. assistant to Dr. MacDougall. and subsequent/y Dr. Robinson saw Booth and Evans at their homes.

div.head: FOOTBALL MATCH AT WIDNES. BATLEY v. WEST LANCASHIRE.
div.p: FOOTBALL MATCH AT WIDNES. BATLEY v. WEST LANCASHIRE.

Three thousand persons gatheredmpen the ground of the Widnes Football Club last evening, when the West Lanca- shire Union Football Clubs opened their season with a match, against the crack Yorkshire team, Batley. The Union is yet in its infancy, but already it hae achimd mach popularity amongst the football fraternity, and the interest in the game was not by any means represented by the number who paid frr admission to the field_ A wide area is covered by the Union, and no less than eleven clubs were represented in the team that faced the fifteen from the county of big acres, Runcorn contribu'ing one and Wid- nes three. As was to be expected in a team so com- posed, the want of combination was palpable, and from the start at 5-25 to almost the finish at 6.35) Batley displayed a superiority. that the spectators, ripe for adverse criticism, could not help recognising by hearty applaase. In the first half Batley obtained one goal, three tries, and several minor points to nil. In the second half the game was a little more evenly balanced, and when only fifteen minutes remained to be played the Union played up with spirit and dash, and at last their perseverance was re- warded by Farrell (Widnes) obtaining a magnifitent try, which he converted into a goal. The game ended, Batley one goal, four tries, and several minor points to West Lan- cashire one goal. The teams were as follows :. BATLEY.—G.. Wines, back; T. Haslam, A. Ineson, H. Simms three quarters; J. Naylor, A. Hirst, half backs; J. Parker, A. Parker,A, Scholes, J. W. Sykes, H. Hatcl,ffe, W. Wolstenhelme, T. Nicholson, F. Bennett, and E. Jackson, forwards.

Bancks (Wigan); forwards, R. Willcox (Wavertree), F. Turner (Warrington), C. Holt (Wigan, captain), J. U.. Smith (Widnes), F. Tattersall (Wal- ton), E. Brown (Walton), E. Beszant ( vVevertree)) A.Bortb- wick (St. Helens), and S. Rimmer (Newton). The umpires were Messrs. C. A. Cronshavr (Wigan) and P. Fox (Batley). Mr. A. T. Campbell was the referee.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

STACK ON FIRE.—k haystack belonging to MT. Thomas Stelfox, jan., Higher-lane, Lymm, was discovered to be on fire early on Sunday morning. The stack was insured for DIO, but the Lymm Fire Brigade being soon in attend- ance, the damage was fortunately confined to a little over £37. Spontaneous combustion is supposed to have been the cause of the outbreak. • r PROPOSED MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.r—OD Mon- day evening a meeting of the inhabitants of Lymm was held, when the question of the formation of a Mutual im- provement Society was under discussion. A society of an undenominational character, to be called "The Lymm Mutual Improvement Society," was formed, and the officers and committee were appointed. The place of meet- ing is to be the Wesleyan Chapel, and Monday night has been selected for the weekly meeting. The meeting on Monday being only of a preliminary character, another is to be held next week, when the syllabus will be arranged.

DRUNXENNBSS.—WiIIiam 'Lee was charged with being drunk on the licensed premises of C. IL Kane' on the 10th August. The case was dismissed owing to Mr Kane stating that although defendant refused to leave his premises, he did not think he was drunk.—Job Collins Campbell Mars- den was fined 5s and costs for having been drunk at Heat- ley on the 26th July.—John Ryan and Denis Ryan, two young Irishmen, were fined 5s and costs each for having been drunk and disorderly on the 16th inst.. at Lymm.— John Platt, labourer, Lymm. Who was stated to be under the influence of drink whilst in the dock, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on the 14th September, and was fined 10a and costs.—Thomas Devine was ordered to pay costs for having been drunk at Lymm on the 6th Instant.

A CARELESS CARTER —Mired Hewitt, a young man, was fined Is and costs for having driven a horse and cart without reins at Thelwall.—Allan Wright was ordered to pay costs for a similar offence at High,Leigh. SCHOOL ATTENDANCR Casgs,—Elizabeth Philip and Charles Drinkwater were summoned in respect of the ir• regular attendance of their children at school, and in the first case an order to attend was made, and the latter was adjourned. Deareorrao GRAM—Thomas Davies and Thomas Wilson were each ordered to pay ad damage and costs for having damaged grass belonging to John, Winstanley, at Rush (3reen.

A LABOURER'S CLW4.—John Martin, a, teamsman, sued Elizabeth Percival, farmer, High Leig,h, for the suns of £8 18s 64 in respect of 18, weeks' wages at Ss 3d per week. Mr. T. Addenbrooke appeared on behalf of the complainant.—An order was made for the defendant to pay £4 3s 2d and costs.

Tua GROUND Gams Acr.—Thomas Etiastney, a young labmrer, was charged with snaring.garne on land in the oc- cupation of Samuel Wareham, at Warburtoo, on the 13th inst.—Ellis Green, gamekeeper, to Mr. Hargreaves, who has the right of shooting over the land, proseented.—The son of Mr. Wareham, however,, stated that his father had given defendant the right under the Ground. Game Act to catch ground game over his farm,, and the caors was accordingly dismissed.

WASTING WATER.—John Lake,. landlord of the Fleece Inn, Lyeam, was summoned by the Lymm Waterworks Company for having unlawfully suffered his water tap to be out of repair, so that water supplied by the company was wasted.—Mr. Ridgway, who prosecuted on behalf of the Water Company, said that case had been brought by the &molly because they felt it to be their duty to prevent the waste of water.. Another charge might also have been brought against the defendant, but that being the first case of the kind the company had simply charged him with waste of water. On the 27th, 28th. and 29th July the at- tention of Sergeant Harrington was called to the dripping of water on defeadantl premises, and as he still heard it on the 30th he gave Information to an officer of the Water Company, who also heard it on the 31st. Oa the let August the officer called the attention of the defendant to the waste of water, and asked him to stop it. Defendant, however, told the officer that he could not attend to the matter, as be iraa too busy, and that he could not do any- thing to it till the Tueelay. In addition to that he asked Vie officer whattbe was sneaking about his premises for, and that he would not have it. On Monday morning, between nine and ten o'clock, the officer again found that the waste continued, and he then told defendant if it was not stopped by twelve o'clock the water would be cat off. He went again at one o'clock, but they found that tap had been re- p tired.—Henry Diamond, the officer of the company referred to, Sergeant. Harrington, and Samuel Cowsall, another offi- cer of the Wet Company, gave corroborative evidence.— In defence, Mr. Lake said that at the time of the officer's first visit he was just getting ready to catch the express to Manclustes, and consequently had not time to attend to the mater just then, and on the Monday he was again very busy —The Beech stated that as that was the first case of the kind they would dismiss it, but all consumers of water must understand that the rights of the company would be , protected..

A meeting of Cape merchants was held on Wednesday afternoon in London, to protest against the recall of Sir Charles Warren hem South Africa. Ttax RAID, 01.1 BETTING HOUSES —The cases of several of the men who were arrested by the Salford police in the raid upon betting-hanses on the 100 inst. came before the Stipendiary Magistrate at the Borough Police Court on Thursday. In the case of Thomas Lee, the licensee and occupier of a heerhoase called the Horse and Jockey, in Broad-street, Pendleton, a fine of £3O and costs was im- posed. A charge brought against a son of the defendant of using the licensed premises for betting purposes was not sustained. Nicholas Burke, of the Greyhound Inn, Woden- street, and John Fletcher, were charged with using the Bigland-street Club for the purpose of betting. The "club" in question was a small cottage adjoining Burke's liceesed house. Burke was fined £2.5 and costs, and Fletcher £5 and costs. In the cases at one or two other defendants the charges were dismissed. Several were adjnurned. Stu MICHAEL HIC7C73•BEACH AT CIP.ANCESTED, Sir IMichael Hicks-Beach (Chancellor of the Exchequer), speaking at a meeting at Cirencester on Thursday evening, accused the late Government of having, made promises it had never been able to fulfil, and traced its failures and the disgrace which he said it had brought on itself to the want of unity in the Cabinet. He criticised the prorsals of Mr. Chamberlain as to the disestablishment of the Gourd), and contrasted his ontspeken policy with the caution of Mr. Gladstone and Lord Hartington, who were awaiting the development of public opinion ora the subject. In regard to Mr. Parnell's demands he expressed on behalf of the Go, vernment strong disapproval of them, and emphatically 'de- nied that there was any foundation for the charge that the Cabinet favoured any such suggestion. He expressed him- self, however, in favour of an expended system of local government in the three kingdoms, and of a modified pea- sant proprietary of laud. In conclusion, he declared the. determination of tht Qoveraraent to Rick to a trio policy at home and abroad.

I FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT. A SINOtTLAH CASE. Yesterday afternoon Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquiry at the Bowling Green Inn, Bank Qtrny, Warrington, respecting the death of James Knight (44), a hraliesman, in the employ, of the London and North-Western Railway Company, which took place on Saturday lasti.—Mr. Irerrand appeFed on Wulf of the railway company.—The inquiry was one adjourned from Wednesday, when merely preliminary evidence was taken. The Coroner said that the facts were shortly these. On the morning of the third of April last, deceased was on the brake' van of a train of empty waggons. The vantwas at a standstill in a siding near V.Alge Hill station. Whit there a light engine, in charge of an engine driver and fireman, by some means or another, which they' would hear of in evidence, came along the same•line, and dashed into a brake van in wltach deceased was, and' he received injur- ies. Their - duty would be to inquire inta,the cir- cumstances surrounding the smashing of the van by the light engine, and in due course •to say whether or no they thought that any person was to blame for the deathof Knig.htt, Dr. Fox, surgeon, Warrington, said that en April 24th deceased came to tituand said he had been in a railway accident, and that he was suffering from the effects of it. He also said that he had been in the infirmary a fortnight or three weeks. Witness attended him upto the time of his death on Satur- day last. Deceased went to Southport in July, but came back worse. Witness had. made tkplist mortera examination, from .which he was of opinion' that deceased died from, consumption.—By the Coroner: Do you think fife death of , deceased was hastened or accelerated by the injuries be sustained on the 3rd April? ' I should say yes.—ln other words if he had not received 3rd April you do not think he would have in the ordinary course oft events died' on the•l2th inst ? The probability is that he would have lived a littlb

longer. Mrs Knight, wife of the deceased, said'that heri husband was 44 years of age. Several times since he had been at home 'after the accident,„ deceased' had said that it was neglect and drink.that had. caused it. He said that he was .in his brake wait- ing for a signal to go home, when the light engine- went into the brake and he recollected, nothing' more. Thomas Hardy, driverof the goods train of 'which • deceased was brakesman—a • train which• consisted of 40 waggons, an engine, and a brake—described the position of the tram shortly before the accident.. He had seen deceased an hour or two before, when he appeared to be in his usual herali. He assisted to get Knight, who wasconscious,out of thevan. The light engine was against the brake, the draw. bar hoop of the brake van being in the smoke box of the engine. He afterwards saw the driver of the engine—Thomas Hume—who said that the brake van being stood in the • curve he could not just " twig " it, as the night was hazy. Hume was sober, but a little fluttered. James Starkey, assistant superintendent of -the section of the line where the accident occurred; said that, after the accident, from what the engine-man told Iftm, he went to Rob3r signal box, where ,he found the signalman, Peter Pomfret, a distant flitg- man connected with a gang of platelayers, And' another man not in the service of the company.. The. signalman had no right to have anyone else in .his box. There was no light engine booked as having passed the box, and on asking Pomfret where the, entry for the light engine. that followed the goods. train was, he replied that he 'had seen no light en- gine. He appeared to be under the influence of drink, and admitted having had a drop of whiskey, i which he said some one had brought nto the box. Witness put some one else in charge of the box, and Pomfret was suspended. The signalman was sup— posed to book everything that passed, but neither the light engine or the- goods train was booked: Pomfret he knew as a steady.man. John Munday, signalman in the employ of the company, then gave evidence, and the inquiry Was adjourned to enable other • signalmen that the engine would have to pass to be called, and, to. bring forward other evidence bearing OR the subject.

div.head: SUSPICIOUS DEATH AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE SUSPICIOUS DEATH AT WARRINGTON.

The adjourned inquest on the body of Bridget Murphy was held yesterday morning, at the War- rington Workhouse, before Mr. Brighouse, coroner. Deceased died at the Workhouse, on the 31st ult., under circumstances previously reported_ in our columns, and it was alleged that she had been pushed down during ai quarrel. The investigation was therefore adjourned to obtain more evidence.— Patrick Murphy, husband of the deceased, general labourer, Wainwright's-yard,. Buttermarkett-street, said that he remembered the 22nd ult., when it was supposed his wife and her married daughter, Catherine Hankinson, had a quarrel. On. coming home at night witness saw a wound on the- top of deceased's head, .and her handkerchief full of-blood. Deceased was remeNed on the Thursday to. the Workhouse. He did.not sea his wife again dilater her death. Deceased never told him .of ;any. qgarrel between her and her daughter.—ln answer to, Mr. Browne, solicitor, who appeared on behalf of the relatives, witness said deceased had not, been 'well for a short time previous to the quarrel. She, was brought home.oueoniglit with her fate covered with blood, and bruises caused by a fall in Bridge-street about ten weeks ago. He did not notice- whether she was drunk. or sober.—The two women had always been good friends.—Questioned. by In- spector Spinks, witness said when they, lied on Cropper's-brow: the woman did not quarrel every Saturday night.—Mary Belly, wife orThomas Kelly, 6,Wainwright's-yard, said she heard.deceased and her daughter quarrelling, on the 22nd ult,,about the latter's child. A neighbour took a knife. from Hankinson's hand, and subsequently witness saw the deceased in her own house. Deceased, holding up one of her-arms, which was bleeding, said, "See what she has dime." The cut was the ugliest she ever saw. It seemed as if somebody had. put the knife in and "scooped it out." Witness- had not seen or heard of deceased falling, since' the quar- rel, and shawaii not aware that she was. in the habit of fainting.—Josiah Wain.wright,, Buttermar- ket-street,stoposed that Catherine Hankinson had an ordinary dinner knife in her hand:dUriug a quar- rel with,her mother. She was not doing anything with the knife, which he took from ,her. In answer to Mr, Broome.witness paid he • gave. the knife to the deceased, who said itwas hers. Deceased had been in &delicate state of health. Examined by In- spector-Spinks :witness said he • did, net see any blood, about Bridget Murphy when he took the knife from Hankmson. In answer to, Mr. dukland (foreman), witness stated that Hankinsou was like a mad woman at the time.—Honor Fleming said deceased showed her &wound on the- left arm, and said that it had been done by,her daughter. On the Sunday following witness applied some sticking plaster to a wound on her head.. Deceased did not, say how she had sustained that wound.—Ellen Carr. son said that on the 22nd nit she. saw Hankinsoni slightly push her mother; who fell into the yard on: her back. Witness afterwards asked Hankinson I why she did that to her own mother. Hankiusoth did . not reply. Witness saw deceased on tho.fol- . towing Tuesday; and she said she, had fallen out of ' bed on the previous night, and • had hurt her- leg. . —Dr. Spinks, surgeon, said deceased was brought to the workhouse, and he attended her. She was suf- , tering from erysipelas in the face. There was a , wound on the back of the head, and one on the back of each arrao• and- on, the right arm_ a long wound about an inch and a half' tong, which he could not say was incised or not. On the. left"arm. the wound was triangular, appearing to,him to have been done by &puncture, passing through and lifting up the skin; sideways, so as to make a flap. There was a contused wound on the lower. part of the. spine, 'which was very- black and about three inches in diameter. Deceased- was in a low feverish. state from erysipelas, and on the next day it was seen. that she was suffering ! from blood poisbning. She died on the 31st. Wit- ness afterwards maga *post mortent examination. He thought the cause of death was. erripelas ex- cited by the wounds producingblood poisoning anch' exhaustion. The primary cause of the-erysipelas was the wound on the hack of the head. That wound, and the contused wound on the lower part of the I spine, could have been produced by a fall. He had examined the. yard where the deceased lived, and about six feet from the door where deceased was, pushed from witness found a stone seven inches long, coming to a point and slightly raised above the others in the yard.—The jury, after a consulta- tion, returned a verdict to the effect that death re- Suited from erysipelas, but how that was caused the jurors were unable to say. The inquiry lasted about five hours,

Parties tendering for the supply of the above-mentioned goods will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free of cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter to my office, in Frodsham, for a printed Form of Tender (and none other can be entertained), where a schedule of the various articles requtred and further particulars may be obtained. The tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guardians to be held in the Board Room, Dutton, on the 18th September, 1885, at Two p.m. Parties whose tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be prepared to enter into a bond with two sureties, if re- quired by the Guardians.
